title: Djibouti Marks 25 Years of Its National University with Presidential Ceremony
excerpt: Djibouti, March 31, 2026 - The President of the Republic, Ismail Omar Guelleh, presided over a ceremony on Tuesday celebrating the 25th anniversary of the University of Djibouti, highlighting the institution’s role in training skilled professionals and advancing national developm
title_en: Djibouti Marks 25 Years of Its National University with Presidential Ceremony
excerpt_en: Djibouti, March 31, 2026 - The President of the Republic, Ismail Omar Guelleh, presided over a ceremony on Tuesday celebrating the 25th anniversary of the University of Djibouti, highlighting the institution’s role in training skilled professionals and advancing national developm
body_en:
Djibouti, March 31, 2026 - The President of the Republic, Ismail Omar Guelleh, presided over a ceremony on Tuesday celebrating the 25th anniversary of the University of Djibouti, highlighting the institution’s role in training skilled professionals and advancing national development.
Held at the Balbala campus, the event showcased the university’s academic and research programs, reflecting a broad offering that spans undergraduate studies to strategic doctoral research. Presentations emphasized the institution’s contributions to technological innovation, scientific research, and specialized engineering.
During the visit, President Guelleh toured several state-of-the-art facilities, including the Energy and Systems Research Laboratory, focused on renewable energy solutions tailored to local climatic conditions. He also visited the Multidisciplinary Chemistry Laboratory, which studies environmental chemical transformations across land, sea, and air, as well as the Advanced Construction Research Laboratory, dedicated to civil engineering and urban planning expertise. The tour concluded at the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, where research in digital technologies and innovation is underway.
Addressing a packed amphitheater of academics, researchers, and students, President Guelleh praised the university’s achievements, describing it as a cornerstone of the country’s human capital development.
“The university trains essential professionals for the development of our nation-engineers, teachers, healthcare workers, and legal experts,” he said. “It represents a significant human capital built for our country.”
The head of state also reflected on the institution’s origins, noting that its creation marked a decisive shift in national education policy. He described the establishment of the university as a “major political decision” that broke with a system previously reliant on limited scholarships for studies abroad.
Looking ahead, President Guelleh reiterated his ambition to transform the University of Djibouti into a regional center of excellence. He called for strengthened academic programs, expanded research capacity, and closer collaboration with industry, alongside greater support for innovation and student entrepreneurship.
The ceremony was attended by several senior government officials, including Prime Minister Abdoulkader Kamil Mohamed, Minister of Higher Education and Research Nabil Mohamed Ahmed, Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, and political figure Abdallah Abdillahi Miguil.
The President of the university, Djama Mohamed Hassan, was also present, alongside senior university officials.

title: Djibouti Showcases Water Infrastructure and Training Ambitions During French Delegation Visit
excerpt: Djibouti, April 8, 2026 - The National Water and Sanitation Office of Djibouti hosted a French delegation on Tuesday, including the ambassador of France and the Director General of the French Development Agency, for a visit focused on key water infrastructure and capacity-buildin
title_en: Djibouti Showcases Water Infrastructure and Training Ambitions During French Delegation Visit
excerpt_en: Djibouti, April 8, 2026 - The National Water and Sanitation Office of Djibouti hosted a French delegation on Tuesday, including the ambassador of France and the Director General of the French Development Agency, for a visit focused on key water infrastructure and capacity-buildin
body_en:
Djibouti, April 8, 2026 - The National Water and Sanitation Office of Djibouti hosted a French delegation on Tuesday, including the ambassador of France and the Director General of the French Development Agency, for a visit focused on key water infrastructure and capacity-building projects.
The visit highlighted two flagship initiatives: the Douda wastewater treatment plant and ONEAD’s newly established training center, both central to Djibouti’s strategy for sustainable water management.
Commissioned in 2014, the Douda plant has become a cornerstone of the country’s wastewater treatment system. Initially designed to process 2,000 cubic meters per day-serving approximately 40,000 residents-the facility was expanded in 2025 to handle up to 3,300 cubic meters daily, effectively doubling its coverage to around 80,000 inhabitants. The plant integrates flows from eleven pumping stations, reflecting significant investment in network infrastructure.
Officials described the expansion as a tangible demonstration of ONEAD’s long-term planning and operational capacity in addressing growing urban water needs.
Alongside infrastructure development, ONEAD is investing in human capital through its new training center, aimed at strengthening technical expertise in the water sector. The facility is equipped with modern classrooms, digital tools, and collaborative workspaces designed to support both theoretical and practical instruction.
According to the Office, an ambitious training program has been set for the year, with 58 sessions planned and more than 1,000 employees expected to benefit. A certification process will assess both academic knowledge and field competencies.
The presence of the French delegation underscored the importance of bilateral cooperation in advancing these projects. Officials highlighted the role of international partnerships in supporting Djibouti’s efforts to modernize essential public services and build long-term technical autonomy in water management.

title: EU Launches €962,000 Civil Society Grants Programme in Djibouti
excerpt: Djibouti, April 1, 2026 - The European Commission has launched the “Djibouti Civil Society Grants 2026” initiative, aimed at strengthening democratic governance, inclusive development, and the role of civil society organizations (CSOs) in the country. Implemented under the Commis
title_en: EU Launches €962,000 Civil Society Grants Programme in Djibouti
excerpt_en: Djibouti, April 1, 2026 - The European Commission has launched the “Djibouti Civil Society Grants 2026” initiative, aimed at strengthening democratic governance, inclusive development, and the role of civil society organizations (CSOs) in the country. Implemented under the Commis
body_en:
Djibouti, April 1, 2026 - The European Commission has launched the “Djibouti Civil Society Grants 2026” initiative, aimed at strengthening democratic governance, inclusive development, and the role of civil society organizations (CSOs) in the country.
Implemented under the Commission’s thematic programme for civil society, the initiative seeks to empower local and international CSOs as independent actors in governance and public policy processes. The programme emphasizes institutional capacity-building, inclusive participation, and socio-economic resilience.
With a total budget of €962,000, the grants will support projects designed to enhance civil society engagement in decision-making and regional development planning. Priority areas include policy advocacy, institutional strengthening, and economic empowerment, with a particular focus on women, youth, and vulnerable groups.
According to programme guidelines, selected projects must demonstrate sustainability, measurable impact, and strong collaboration with regional councils and local stakeholders. The initiative also aims to foster partnerships that can improve long-term development outcomes.
Eligible applicants include legally registered non-profit organizations, NGOs, and civil society groups operating in Djibouti. Both national and international organizations may apply, provided they are officially registered in the country and can demonstrate solid operational and financial capacity, as well as relevant experience in governance, development, or social inclusion.
Applicants are required to submit detailed project proposals outlining objectives, target beneficiaries, implementation strategies, and expected results. Emphasis is placed on inclusivity, collaboration, and long-term sustainability.
The application deadline for the Djibouti Civil Society Grants 2026 is April 16, 2026. Officials encourage interested organizations to submit proposals ahead of the deadline to avoid potential technical issues during the application process.

body_en:
Ouagadougou, April 3, 2026 - Burkina Faso’s transitional president, Ibrahim Traoré, has said the country will only hold elections once national security is fully restored, stressing that democratic processes cannot succeed amid ongoing armed threats.
Speaking in an interview on April 2, Traoré said that instability caused by terrorist groups remains the main obstacle to organizing elections, and argued that “fake democracy” could have harmful consequences if implemented under current conditions.
He reiterated that governance priorities must focus on restoring peace and stability before a return to electoral politics.
Traoré, who came to power following a coup in September 2022, had previously promised elections for 2024, but they have been postponed as security challenges persist.
His remarks highlight ongoing debate in Burkina Faso over the timing of a return to constitutional rule while the country continues to face militant insurgencies.

body_en:
Yaoundé, April 4, 2026 - Cameroon’s Parliament has approved a constitutional amendment reinstating the position of Vice President, a post that had been abolished in 1972.
The amendment was passed by an overwhelming majority of lawmakers in the National Assembly and Senate, according to official parliamentary figures.
The new provisions establish that the Vice President would assume the presidency in the event of death or incapacitation of the Head of State, while certain constitutional powers would remain reserved exclusively for the President.
The revised framework also allows the President to appoint and dismiss the Vice President, who would serve alongside the Head of State for a defined term.
The move is widely seen as part of efforts to formalize succession arrangements in Cameroon’s political system, amid ongoing discussions about long-term governance stability.
President Paul Biya has remained in office since 1982, making him one of the world’s longest-serving heads of state. The last time Cameroon had a Vice President was in the early 1970s before the position was abolished.

title: Chinese to build three factories including transformer plant in Nyagatare
excerpt: Nyagatare, Rwanda, March 25, 2026 - Chinese investors are set to establish three factories in Nyagatare District, including a transformer manufacturing plant, in a move expected to boost industrial capacity and agricultural production in the region. District authorities said the
title_en: Chinese to build three factories including transformer plant in Nyagatare
excerpt_en: Nyagatare, Rwanda, March 25, 2026 - Chinese investors are set to establish three factories in Nyagatare District, including a transformer manufacturing plant, in a move expected to boost industrial capacity and agricultural production in the region. District authorities said the
body_en:
Nyagatare, Rwanda, March 25, 2026 - Chinese investors are set to establish three factories in Nyagatare District, including a transformer manufacturing plant, in a move expected to boost industrial capacity and agricultural production in the region.
District authorities said the projects will include two factories producing electrical equipment and one facility dedicated to manufacturing fertilizer from cow dung mixed with other substances.
The development follows a March 11 meeting between Eastern Province Governor Pudence Rubingisa and a delegation of Chinese investors who visited the province to assess investment opportunities and explore potential partnerships.
After the meeting, the investors traveled to Nyagatare District, where local officials presented a range of opportunities. Several proposals attracted immediate interest, with investors agreeing to move forward without delay.
Acting Mayor Kakooza Henry said key areas of interest included the construction of electrical equipment factories and a fertilizer plant.
“The first factory will focus on fertilizer production using manure mixed with other substances,” he said. “Another will manufacture electrical equipment, including transformers, while a third will produce wires and related components.”
He added that the investors are also looking to expand into agriculture, with plans to grow crops and supply them to markets.
One investor has already committed to launching the transformer factory project and is expected to begin construction soon after securing one hectare of land in the district’s industrial park. The investor is currently preparing and is expected to return in April, with construction scheduled to begin no later than August.
Other investors have temporarily returned to their home country to finalize internal consultations before proceeding.
Meanwhile, development continues at the Rutaraka industrial park, where additional projects are underway, including a chia seed processing plant, an animal feed factory, and a planned coal processing facility.
District authorities highlighted that the 256-hectare industrial park is equipped with water and electricity infrastructure, with road development planned to improve access and attract further investment.
Chinese investment in Rwanda continues to grow, reaching an estimated $108.6 million in 2024, reflecting strengthening economic ties between the two countries.

title: Digital lending platform Numida launches in Rwanda to expand access to business loans
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, March 25, 2026 - A technology-driven lending company has officially launched operations in Rwanda, offering quick, collateral-free loans to small business owners in a move aimed at improving financial inclusion. The platform, Numida, enables users to apply for bus
title_en: Digital lending platform Numida launches in Rwanda to expand access to business loans
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 25, 2026 - A technology-driven lending company has officially launched operations in Rwanda, offering quick, collateral-free loans to small business owners in a move aimed at improving financial inclusion. The platform, Numida, enables users to apply for bus
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 25, 2026 - A technology-driven lending company has officially launched operations in Rwanda, offering quick, collateral-free loans to small business owners in a move aimed at improving financial inclusion.
The platform, Numida, enables users to apply for business loans via a mobile application, with approvals and disbursements made within 24 hours. Loan amounts range from 800,000 Rwandan francs to 12 million francs, with repayment periods of up to 30 days.
The launch event took place in Kigali on March 24, 2026, and marks the company’s formal entry into the Rwandan financial market.
To access the service, applicants are required to have a smartphone, a national ID, a passport photo, and a legally registered business operating in Rwanda for at least six months, along with documentation from the Rwanda Development Board.
Numida Chief Executive Officer Mina Shahid said the platform is designed to support small businesses and aligns with Rwanda’s long-term development goals under Vision 2050, which aims to broaden access to financial services and drive economic growth.
Officials from the Central Bank of Rwanda (BNR) confirmed that the company has received the necessary authorization to operate as a non-deposit-taking lending institution, emphasizing that it meets regulatory requirements.
A representative from the BNR noted that expanding access to credit is part of the country’s strategy to support entrepreneurship and business development.
Early beneficiaries have already reported positive experiences, with small business owners stating that the platform provides faster and easier access to funding compared to traditional financial institutions.
Since beginning operations in Rwanda, Numida has reportedly disbursed around 120 million Rwandan francs in loans to approximately 150 entrepreneurs.
The company already operates in Uganda and Kenya and has facilitated over 150 million dollars in loans across the region, supporting thousands of small businesses. It aims to expand its reach further in Rwanda throughout 2026.

Early beneficiaries have already reported positive experiences, with small business owners stating that the platform provides faster and easier access to funding compared to traditional financial institutions.

title_en: Rwanda’s tech minister outlines five steps for East Africa to accelerate AI development
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 30, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of ICT and Innovation, Paula Ingabire, has called on member states of the East African Community (EAC) to adopt a coordinated approach to advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) across the region. Speaking at a regional conference
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 30, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of ICT and Innovation, Paula Ingabire, has called on member states of the East African Community (EAC) to adopt a coordinated approach to advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) across the region.
Speaking at a regional conference in Kigali, she outlined five key priorities: establishing AI governance laws, creating a regional research and innovation center, developing shared data infrastructure, harmonizing regulations, and investing in large-scale skills training.
Ingabire emphasized that AI could significantly boost economic growth, citing projections that the technology could contribute up to $1 trillion to Africa’s GDP by 2035.
She also highlighted the need to increase African language content online, noting that less than 3% of global internet content is currently available in African languages.
Officials say the initiative aims to position East Africa as a competitive player in the global digital economy while ensuring inclusive access to emerging technologies.

title: President Ruto Calls for Deep Reform of African Union Governance Structures
excerpt: Kenya April 11, 2026 - Kenyan President William Ruto has called for urgent reforms within the African Union, warning that the institution is currently hampered by weak and dysfunctional governance structures. Speaking at a Security Cooperation Summit on April 10, 2026, President
title_en: President Ruto Calls for Deep Reform of African Union Governance Structures
excerpt_en: Kenya April 11, 2026 - Kenyan President William Ruto has called for urgent reforms within the African Union, warning that the institution is currently hampered by weak and dysfunctional governance structures. Speaking at a Security Cooperation Summit on April 10, 2026, President
body_en:
Kenya April 11, 2026 - Kenyan President William Ruto has called for urgent reforms within the African Union, warning that the institution is currently hampered by weak and dysfunctional governance structures.
Speaking at a Security Cooperation Summit on April 10, 2026, President Ruto, who also chairs the AU Reform Commission, said the continent’s potential remains vast due to its natural resources and demographic strength, but emphasized that effective leadership and institutional restructuring are essential to unlock it.
“We need leaders with good ideas, we need wise leaders who think about how we can improve,” he said, adding that African leaders have entrusted him with advancing reforms to strengthen AU institutions and improve their effectiveness.
Ruto argued that the African Union is not fully delivering on its mandate, stating that its current structure limits its ability to provide governance solutions for the continent’s evolving challenges. He stressed that comprehensive reforms are necessary to make the institution more functional and responsive.
He also highlighted the importance of implementing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as a key pillar of continental integration and economic transformation.
The AU reform process, launched in 2016, was previously led by former Kenyan President Paul Kagame, who oversaw early institutional changes, including efforts to strengthen the African Peace Fund. According to previous AU statements, significant progress was made in increasing financial contributions for peace operations and improving cooperation with the United Nations.
Ruto said his current mandate is to build on those reforms and ensure that AU institutions are better aligned with long-term continental priorities, including governance, security, and economic integration.

title: Senegalese Prime Minister Criticizes Global Military Interventions at Dakar Conference
excerpt: April 12, 2026 - The Senegalese Prime Minister, Ousmane Sonko, has sharply criticized recent Western military interventions, stating that they have contributed to global instability rather than peace. His remarks were delivered during an international conference on state sovereig
title_en: Senegalese Prime Minister Criticizes Global Military Interventions at Dakar Conference
excerpt_en: April 12, 2026 - The Senegalese Prime Minister, Ousmane Sonko, has sharply criticized recent Western military interventions, stating that they have contributed to global instability rather than peace. His remarks were delivered during an international conference on state sovereig
body_en:
April 12, 2026 - The Senegalese Prime Minister, Ousmane Sonko, has sharply criticized recent Western military interventions, stating that they have contributed to global instability rather than peace. His remarks were delivered during an international conference on state sovereignty held in Dakar on April 9, 2026.
Speaking at the forum, Sonko argued that recent and historical military campaigns led by Western powers have failed to achieve their stated objectives and have instead left long-term political and humanitarian consequences in several regions.
He cited conflicts including Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, and Syria as examples of what he described as unsuccessful attempts to reshape political outcomes through military force.
According to the Prime Minister, similar dynamics are now being observed in the ongoing tensions involving Iran, where military pressure has not produced the intended political results. He suggested that despite escalating confrontation, diplomatic engagement is gradually becoming the preferred path for the parties involved.
“The goal of overthrowing the Iranian regime has not been achieved. It still exists and has, in some respects, become stronger than before,” Sonko stated during his address.
The Prime Minister also directly criticized US President Donald Trump, linking him to what he described as destabilizing global policies. He argued that the current trajectory of international relations reflects a pattern in which powerful states impose decisions under the banner of democracy, often without regard for national sovereignty.
“Donald Trump is not a person who wants peace. He is a person who is concerned with disrupting the stability of people,” he said.
Sonko further stated that continued reliance on military solutions should be reconsidered, urging a shift toward dialogue and cooperation in resolving international disputes. He emphasized that unilateral interventions by powerful nations should give way to approaches that respect the sovereignty and independent choices of states.
He concluded that sustainable peace can only be achieved through negotiation rather than military confrontation, given the far-reaching consequences of modern conflicts on global stability.

excerpt_en: Benin April 14, 2026 - Benin’s National Electoral Commission has announced that Romuald Wadagni, the candidate of the ruling party, has won the presidential election with 94% of the vote, according to provisional results released on April 14, 2026. The vote was held on April 12,
body_en:
Benin April 14, 2026 - Benin’s National Electoral Commission has announced that Romuald Wadagni, the candidate of the ruling party, has won the presidential election with 94% of the vote, according to provisional results released on April 14, 2026.
The vote was held on April 12, 2026. According to the Electoral Commission, Wadagni secured a decisive victory over his main challenger, Paul Hounkpè, who obtained 6% of the vote.
Paul Hounkpè reportedly conceded defeat even before the official provisional results were made public.
Romuald Wadagni, an economist and senior political figure, has served in Benin’s Ministry of Finance since 2016, where he has been closely associated with key economic reforms.
He is credited with contributing to improvements in tax revenue collection and public financial management, and has built a profile as one of the country’s leading technocrats in economic policy.
Before entering government, Wadagni worked in the private financial sector, including at Deloitte, where he gained experience in auditing and financial advisory services.
Widely regarded as a close ally of the current administration and a potential successor to President Patrice Talon, Wadagni is expected to serve a seven-year presidential mandate.
The Constitutional Court is expected to deliver the final validation of the results in the coming days.

title: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Peace Talks Open Amid Rising Tensions
excerpt: Switzerland April 14, 2026 - Peace talks between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance opened in Switzerland on April 13, 2026, but began in a tense atmosphere marked by disagreement over delegation composition and allegations of contin
title_en: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Peace Talks Open Amid Rising Tensions
excerpt_en: Switzerland April 14, 2026 - Peace talks between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance opened in Switzerland on April 13, 2026, but began in a tense atmosphere marked by disagreement over delegation composition and allegations of contin
body_en:
Switzerland April 14, 2026 - Peace talks between the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the AFC/M23 alliance opened in Switzerland on April 13, 2026, but began in a tense atmosphere marked by disagreement over delegation composition and allegations of continued violence in eastern Congo.
The discussions, facilitated by international partners including Qatar, the United States, and the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the DRC (MONUSCO), brought together representatives from both sides in an effort to revive stalled peace efforts in the region.
Delegations and early tensions
The AFC/M23 delegation was led by its Permanent Secretary, Benjamin Mbonimpa, and included six representatives accompanied by six additional experts, some of whom previously served in senior government positions under both former President Joseph Kabila and current President Félix Tshisekedi.
Among the experts present were Claude Ibalanky Ekolomba, former ambassador and coordinator of the national monitoring mechanism for the Addis Ababa Peace Agreements, and Franck Mwe di Malila, former minister of tourism and deputy foreign minister.
The inclusion of former senior Congolese officials reportedly surprised members of the government delegation, which had expected a more strictly defined AFC/M23 representation.
Sources familiar with the negotiations indicated that AFC/M23’s participation had initially been contested by the government side, but was ultimately accepted as part of the mediation framework.
Review of prior agreements
Before substantive negotiations began, participants reviewed the implementation of earlier agreements, including commitments on ceasefire arrangements, monitoring mechanisms, and the release of detainees-several of which were reported to have been only partially implemented.
Discussions also focused on humanitarian access in eastern DRC, including proposals to facilitate aid delivery and reopen Goma airport as a key logistical hub.
MONUSCO officials had previously raised the issue during a visit to Goma in February 2026, while international partners, including France, had also supported limited humanitarian flight operations through the airport.
Renewed accusations of violence
While talks were underway in Switzerland, AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka issued statements alleging renewed military activity by government forces in eastern DRC on April 13.
He claimed that clashes and drone strikes targeted several areas in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces, including Kalehe, Masisi, and Minembwe territories.
According to AFC/M23, government forces used drones in multiple locations, resulting in civilian casualties and renewed insecurity in affected communities.
The Congolese government has not independently confirmed these allegations.
Fragile diplomatic context
The talks in Switzerland reflect ongoing international efforts to stabilize eastern DRC, where multiple armed groups continue to operate despite repeated ceasefire agreements.
However, the opening session highlighted persistent mistrust between the parties, with both sides exchanging accusations of violations even as negotiations were being initiated.
Mediators have urged restraint and continued engagement, emphasizing the importance of maintaining dialogue despite ongoing tensions on the ground.

title_en: Belgium Raises Concerns Over Rising Number of Congolese Asylum SeekersApril 14, 2026 Belgium has expressed growing concern over an increase in asylum applications from nationals of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), according to the country’s Minister for Refugees and Migration, Anneleen Van Bossuyt.
excerpt_en: Speaking at the start of an official visit to the DRC on April 13, 2026, the minister indicated that the issue would be a key topic of discussion with Congolese authorities, particularly in light of the rising number of applicants recorded in recent years. According to figures pr
body_en:
Speaking at the start of an official visit to the DRC on April 13, 2026, the minister indicated that the issue would be a key topic of discussion with Congolese authorities, particularly in light of the rising number of applicants recorded in recent years.
According to figures provided by the minister, the number of Congolese asylum seekers in Belgium has doubled over a two-year period, increasing from 1,250 in 2023 to 2,500 in 2025. The upward trend has continued into 2026, with more than 450 additional applications registered in the first three months of the year.
“This is a significant increase that Belgium has been facing for several months,” she said.
Minister Van Bossuyt noted that a large proportion of applicants reportedly originate from Kinshasa, a region not directly affected by the armed conflict in eastern DRC. She suggested that this raises questions regarding the grounds on which some asylum claims are based.
The minister also warned that individuals found to have provided false information during the asylum process could face legal consequences, including rejection of their applications, deportation, or restrictions affecting their ability to live and work in Belgium.
Belgian authorities say they intend to continue discussions with Congolese officials as part of broader cooperation on migration management and asylum procedures.

title: Togo Calls for Revision of World Maps to Reflect Africa’s True Size
excerpt: April 15, 2026; Togo has formally called on the United Nations to promote the use of world maps that more accurately reflect the true size of Africa, challenging the continued dominance of the Mercator projection in global institutions. The country’s Foreign Minister, Robert Duss
title_en: Togo Calls for Revision of World Maps to Reflect Africa’s True Size
excerpt_en: April 15, 2026; Togo has formally called on the United Nations to promote the use of world maps that more accurately reflect the true size of Africa, challenging the continued dominance of the Mercator projection in global institutions. The country’s Foreign Minister, Robert Duss
body_en:
April 15, 2026; Togo has formally called on the United Nations to promote the use of world maps that more accurately reflect the true size of Africa, challenging the continued dominance of the Mercator projection in global institutions.
The country’s Foreign Minister, Robert Dussey, raised the issue on April 13, 2026, arguing that commonly used maps significantly distort the relative size of the African continent.
“The size of Africa shown on many world maps is not accurate. We are asking for representations based on scientific truth,” he said.
The African Union (AU) has backed the initiative, encouraging Togo to spearhead efforts aimed at phasing out the Mercator projection in government and international use.
Originally developed in 1569 by Gerardus Mercator, the projection has long been used for navigation but is widely criticized for distorting the size of landmasses-making regions near the equator, such as Africa, appear smaller than they are relative to areas closer to the poles.
Advocacy groups including Africa No Filter and Speak Up Africa are supporting the initiative, calling for the adoption of maps that more accurately depict the true proportions of countries and continents.
Moky Makura, Executive Director of Africa No Filter, emphasized that the issue goes beyond cartography. “This is not just about maps, but about ensuring that Africa is seen as it truly is,” she said.
According to organizers, a proposal outlining potential revisions to global mapping standards is being prepared for discussion at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, where member states are expected to debate and potentially vote on the initiative.
Earlier this year, the African Union urged its 55 member states to reconsider the use of the Mercator projection and advocate for more accurate geographic representations in official and educational materials.

title: Sudan Suspends Private Broadcaster Sudania 24 Over Alleged Hate Speech
excerpt: Sudan April 8, 2026 ; Sudan’s Ministry of Information has suspended the private television channel Sudania 24 and revoked its operating licenses, accusing it of professional misconduct and incitement of tribal tensions. The broadcaster, owned by businessman Wajdi Mirghani, has be
title_en: Sudan Suspends Private Broadcaster Sudania 24 Over Alleged Hate Speech
excerpt_en: Sudan April 8, 2026 ; Sudan’s Ministry of Information has suspended the private television channel Sudania 24 and revoked its operating licenses, accusing it of professional misconduct and incitement of tribal tensions. The broadcaster, owned by businessman Wajdi Mirghani, has be
body_en:
Sudan April 8, 2026 ; Sudan’s Ministry of Information has suspended the private television channel Sudania 24 and revoked its operating licenses, accusing it of professional misconduct and incitement of tribal tensions.
The broadcaster, owned by businessman Wajdi Mirghani, has been operating from outside Sudan since the outbreak of war in April 2023 forced the closure of its Khartoum headquarters. It has primarily continued its reporting through digital platforms and social media.
According to a ministry statement, the suspension followed recent coverage of a protest in the Dalgo locality of Northern State. The channel had aired footage showing local residents opposing the presence of displaced people from Darfur, which authorities said contributed to the spread of hate speech and regional division.
The ministry further ordered the suspension of work permits for the channel’s correspondents until all licenses are renewed and editorial compliance commitments are made.
Sudania 24 has previously faced government restrictions. In December 2024, it was forced to cancel its “Circle of Events” program after hosting opposition figures accused of insulting the military.
Officials said they are working with the Ministry of Telecommunications to block the specific content cited in the violation. They also emphasized that the government does not hold ownership in the channel and is not responsible for its editorial output.
Authorities justified the decision as necessary to protect national unity and social stability, noting that the broadcaster currently operates without an authorized studio inside the country.

title: Detained Sudanese Students in Egypt Risk Missing National Exams
excerpt: Egypt April 5, 2026 ; Sudanese families in Egypt are voicing growing concern as several secondary school students remain in detention just days before national exams are set to begin on April 13, raising fears they could miss a critical academic milestone. The detentions come ami
title_en: Detained Sudanese Students in Egypt Risk Missing National Exams
excerpt_en: Egypt April 5, 2026 ; Sudanese families in Egypt are voicing growing concern as several secondary school students remain in detention just days before national exams are set to begin on April 13, raising fears they could miss a critical academic milestone. The detentions come ami
body_en:
Egypt April 5, 2026 ; Sudanese families in Egypt are voicing growing concern as several secondary school students remain in detention just days before national exams are set to begin on April 13, raising fears they could miss a critical academic milestone.
The detentions come amid a broader crackdown by Egyptian authorities on foreign nationals, a campaign that has affected thousands of Sudanese residents, including some with valid documentation.
Families say the situation threatens to prevent the students from sitting for the Sudan School Certificate examinations, potentially jeopardizing their academic futures.
One parent said her son has been held for several weeks, prompting the family to consider sending him back to Sudan to ensure he does not lose the school year, despite ongoing insecurity there. Another parent described the prospect of returning as both difficult and psychologically taxing, particularly given the uncertainties surrounding travel and safety.
Officials at the Sudanese Embassy in Cairo said the number of detained students remains limited, adding that efforts are underway to secure their release or facilitate their return to Sudan in time for the exams. Authorities are also exploring alternative arrangements to allow affected students to sit for exams individually or in small groups if necessary.
Coordination between Sudanese and Egyptian officials is ongoing, with a focus on ensuring that students can access examination centers under stable conditions.
In a joint statement, rights organizations called on Egyptian authorities to expedite legal procedures for detained students and consider temporary documentation measures to allow them to move freely during the examination period.
They also urged all parties to safeguard the education sector from the impact of conflict. Since the outbreak of war in April 2023, Sudan’s national examination system has faced significant disruptions, including delays, damage to educational infrastructure, and widespread displacement of students and teachers.

title: RSF Accused of Killing 16 Civilians in Ethnically Motivated Attack in El Fasher
excerpt: Sudan March 25, 2026 ; At least 16 civilians, including three women, were killed in what has been described as an ethnically motivated attack in El Fasher, according to a medical network monitoring the conflict in the region. In a statement released on Wednesday, the Sudan Doctor
title_en: RSF Accused of Killing 16 Civilians in Ethnically Motivated Attack in El Fasher
excerpt_en: Sudan March 25, 2026 ; At least 16 civilians, including three women, were killed in what has been described as an ethnically motivated attack in El Fasher, according to a medical network monitoring the conflict in the region. In a statement released on Wednesday, the Sudan Doctor
body_en:
Sudan March 25, 2026 ; At least 16 civilians, including three women, were killed in what has been described as an ethnically motivated attack in El Fasher, according to a medical network monitoring the conflict in the region.
In a statement released on Wednesday, the Sudan Doctors Network alleged that members of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) carried out summary executions targeting unarmed residents in the city. The victims were reportedly buried in three separate mass graves on the outskirts of El Fasher, in what the group described as a reflection of the scale of the tragedy facing civilians in conflict zones.
The group condemned the killings as a “heinous crime” and a blatant violation of international law and fundamental human values.
The RSF has faced repeated accusations of systematic abuses in El Fasher since launching a major offensive in May 2024. Allegations include the destruction of hospitals and water infrastructure, as well as widespread violence against civilians. Reports of mass killings intensified after the paramilitary group seized full control of the city in October.
On February 19, 2026, a United Nations fact-finding mission concluded that the RSF had committed acts amounting to genocide during its takeover of El Fasher. Earlier findings by the UN Human Rights Office documented more than 6,000 deaths during the first three days of the assault, with thousands more killed during the subsequent occupation or while attempting to flee.
Assessments by the International Criminal Court and the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights indicate that war crimes and crimes against humanity may have been committed in the North Darfur capital.
The Sudan Doctors Network warned that the continued targeting of civilians based on identity reflects an escalating pattern of systematic violence across the Darfur region. It called on the international community and human rights organizations to take urgent action to halt ongoing violations, which have displaced thousands of women and children since October.
The statement also held RSF leadership responsible and urged global powers to take more decisive action to address the humanitarian crisis. Since consolidating control over the city, the RSF has imposed strict restrictions on humanitarian access and banned satellite internet services-moves observers say are intended to limit the flow of information and conceal evidence of atrocities.

title: MSF Reports Over 3,300 Sexual Violence Cases in Darfur
excerpt: Darfur, March 31, 2026 - A new report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has revealed that more than 3,300 survivors of sexual violence were treated in Sudan’s Darfur region over a period of less than two years, underscoring the scale of abuses in the conflict-affected areas. The
title_en: MSF Reports Over 3,300 Sexual Violence Cases in Darfur
excerpt_en: Darfur, March 31, 2026 - A new report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has revealed that more than 3,300 survivors of sexual violence were treated in Sudan’s Darfur region over a period of less than two years, underscoring the scale of abuses in the conflict-affected areas. The
body_en:
Darfur, March 31, 2026 - A new report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has revealed that more than 3,300 survivors of sexual violence were treated in Sudan’s Darfur region over a period of less than two years, underscoring the scale of abuses in the conflict-affected areas.
The findings, released Tuesday, show that 3,396 survivors received care at MSF-supported facilities in North and South Darfur between January 2024 and November 2025. The report draws on medical data, survivor testimonies, and interviews with local actors working closely with affected communities.
Women and girls accounted for 97% of the victims, with MSF warning that the actual number of cases is likely far higher due to limited access to medical services and the risks associated with seeking care.
According to the report, fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias were responsible for widespread and systematic sexual violence. Patterns of abuse indicate that in North Darfur, armed men were involved in more than 95% of reported cases, while in South Darfur, around 60% of assaults involved multiple perpetrators.
The report, titled “I Have Something to Tell You: Surviving the Sexual Violence Crisis in Darfur,” highlights a sharp escalation in violence following the capture of El Fasher in October 2025. In the aftermath, MSF treated more than 140 survivors who had fled to Tawila, with 94% reporting attacks by armed men.
Many survivors said they were assaulted while fleeing violence, often in front of family members and frequently by multiple perpetrators. The report also notes that non-Arab communities were deliberately targeted as part of a broader pattern of humiliation and intimidation.
Between December 2025 and January 2026, MSF recorded 732 additional cases in displacement camps around Tawila. Women reported facing attacks both during their journeys and within the camps themselves.
At the Daba Naira camp in Tawila, at least 206 survivors received consultations specifically related to rape. Most victims were only able to access medical care approximately three months after the assault, reflecting both the dangers of travel and the lack of immediate services.
The report highlights that overcrowding, poor security, and unsafe living conditions-including distant water points and unprotected sanitation facilities-have significantly increased the vulnerability of displaced women.
Tawila, now under the control of the Sudan Liberation Movement led by Abdul Wahid al-Nur, has become a refuge for more than 715,000 displaced people living in dire humanitarian conditions.
MSF also documented testimonies from 150 survivors in the weeks following the RSF takeover of Zamzam camp, located southwest of El Fasher, further illustrating the widespread nature of the abuses.
The organization warned that the continued lack of protection and access to essential services is exacerbating the crisis, calling for urgent international action to safeguard civilians and support survivors.

title: Drone Strike Kills Dozens at Wedding in North Darfur’s Kutum
excerpt: Kutum April 9, 2026 ; More than 40 people were killed and over 100 others injured after a drone strike hit a wedding gathering in Kutum on Wednesday evening, according to local sources. The strike targeted a residential home in the Al-Salam neighborhood, where a wedding ceremony
title_en: Drone Strike Kills Dozens at Wedding in North Darfur’s Kutum
excerpt_en: Kutum April 9, 2026 ; More than 40 people were killed and over 100 others injured after a drone strike hit a wedding gathering in Kutum on Wednesday evening, according to local sources. The strike targeted a residential home in the Al-Salam neighborhood, where a wedding ceremony
body_en:
Kutum April 9, 2026 ; More than 40 people were killed and over 100 others injured after a drone strike hit a wedding gathering in Kutum on Wednesday evening, according to local sources.
The strike targeted a residential home in the Al-Salam neighborhood, where a wedding ceremony was underway. Witnesses said the explosion caused extensive destruction, leveling dozens of houses and displacing multiple families.
Kutum has been under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since the early stages of the conflict that erupted in April 2023. The town has experienced repeated drone strikes in recent months, widely believed to be carried out by the Sudanese army, often targeting RSF positions as well as civilian infrastructure, including a rural hospital and the main market.
A spokesperson for a political coalition aligned with the RSF claimed the death toll had risen to 56, including 17 children, with 107 others wounded. The group attributed the attack to the Sudanese military and condemned it in strong terms.
The incident comes amid rising internal tensions within RSF ranks in North Darfur. Military sources indicate that RSF leadership recently attempted to disarm a prominent field commander in Kutum amid suspicions over his loyalty to tribal leader Musa Hilal.
A force reportedly deployed from El Fasher to enforce the order, but the commander refused to surrender his weapons and instead sought protection from his community, raising concerns of potential internal clashes.
Relations between the RSF and Musa Hilal have deteriorated significantly in recent months. In February, Hilal survived a drone strike targeting his residence in Misteriya. The incident was followed by a ground offensive by RSF forces to seize the Mahameed stronghold.
Hilal later relocated to Al Dabbah in Northern State before traveling to Khartoum.
Since taking control of Misteriya, the RSF has faced accusations of abuses against members of the Mahameed community in North and West Darfur, including killings, arrests, and increased surveillance of individuals linked to the group.
The latest strike underscores the intensifying violence in Darfur, where civilians continue to bear the brunt of ongoing fighting and internal divisions among armed groups.

title: Protests Block Key Highway to Egypt Over Ongoing Power Cuts in Northern Sudan
excerpt: Northern Sudan April 8, 2026 ; Dozens of residents in the town of Abri blocked a major highway linking Sudan and Egypt on Wednesday in protest against prolonged electricity shortages, disrupting a key trade and transport route. Demonstrators set tyres on fire and obstructed the r
title_en: Protests Block Key Highway to Egypt Over Ongoing Power Cuts in Northern Sudan
excerpt_en: Northern Sudan April 8, 2026 ; Dozens of residents in the town of Abri blocked a major highway linking Sudan and Egypt on Wednesday in protest against prolonged electricity shortages, disrupting a key trade and transport route. Demonstrators set tyres on fire and obstructed the r
body_en:
Northern Sudan April 8, 2026 ; Dozens of residents in the town of Abri blocked a major highway linking Sudan and Egypt on Wednesday in protest against prolonged electricity shortages, disrupting a key trade and transport route.
Demonstrators set tyres on fire and obstructed the road connecting Dongola to Wadi Halfa, a strategic corridor for cross-border movement and commerce between the two countries.
A member of a local emergency response group in Wadi Halfa said residents were angered by the inclusion of Abri in a recent electricity rationing schedule, arguing that the area should not be affected due to its supply connection with Egypt.
Protesters claim that electricity transmitted from Egypt is sufficient to meet local demand without the need for scheduled outages. They argue that the rationing decision is unjustified and has severely disrupted daily life.
Egypt supplies electricity to several towns in northern Sudan under a long-standing arrangement, with these areas historically exempt from national grid load-shedding measures implemented to manage fuel shortages and infrastructure constraints.
In a statement issued by demonstrators, local authorities were criticized for attributing the power cuts to external geopolitical tensions, including instability in global energy markets and maritime security concerns in the Strait of Hormuz. Protesters rejected this explanation, calling it disconnected from local realities.
They warned that continued blackouts have paralyzed markets, disrupted public services, and worsened living conditions in the region.
The protesters said they would escalate their demonstrations and maintain the highway blockade until authorities reverse the rationing decision and restore stable electricity supply.

title: Sudan Seeks to Revive World Bank Partnership for Reconstruction and Debt Relief
excerpt: Washington, April 18, 2026 - Sudan has stepped up efforts to restore cooperation with international financial institutions, as officials push to secure funding for reconstruction and accelerate debt relief amid the ongoing crisis. A Sudanese delegation held talks on Saturday with
title_en: Sudan Seeks to Revive World Bank Partnership for Reconstruction and Debt Relief
excerpt_en: Washington, April 18, 2026 - Sudan has stepped up efforts to restore cooperation with international financial institutions, as officials push to secure funding for reconstruction and accelerate debt relief amid the ongoing crisis. A Sudanese delegation held talks on Saturday with
body_en:
Washington, April 18, 2026 - Sudan has stepped up efforts to restore cooperation with international financial institutions, as officials push to secure funding for reconstruction and accelerate debt relief amid the ongoing crisis.
A Sudanese delegation held talks on Saturday with representatives of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on the sidelines of the Spring Meetings, focusing on reactivating partnerships suspended in recent years.
The World Bank froze approximately $1.8 billion in grants to Sudan following the October 2021 political upheaval. Despite this, limited engagement has continued through programs implemented by United Nations agencies in key sectors such as health, education, water, and agriculture.
During the discussions, Sudanese officials emphasized that restoring full cooperation with the World Bank is critical to financing reconstruction and development initiatives. They also called for faster progress on resolving the country’s external debt, seen as a prerequisite for unlocking concessional financing for infrastructure and productive sectors.
Sudan’s external debt reached an estimated $66.8 billion by late 2023, with a significant portion consisting of accumulated interest. Earlier debt relief efforts-amounting to roughly $50 billion-were suspended following the 2021 crisis, despite Sudan having advanced under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative.
Officials highlighted ongoing economic reform efforts, noting progress despite the severe disruptions caused by the war. The government reaffirmed its commitment to meeting the conditions required for debt relief and implementing structural reforms aimed at restoring financial stability and economic growth.
International partners signaled cautious support. Representatives at the meetings expressed willingness to assist Sudan in re-engaging with global financial institutions, including through technical support, while underscoring the importance of transparency and continued data sharing.
The economic toll of the conflict remains severe. The war has significantly reversed development gains, with sharp declines in economic output and a surge in poverty levels, further intensifying the urgency of securing international financial support for recovery and reconstruction.

title: Burhan Receives Defecting RSF Commander in Northern State
excerpt: Dongola, April 19, 2026 - Sudan’s army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has received a senior commander who defected from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in what marks a significant development in the country’s ongoing conflict. Major General Al-
title_en: Burhan Receives Defecting RSF Commander in Northern State
excerpt_en: Dongola, April 19, 2026 - Sudan’s army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has received a senior commander who defected from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in what marks a significant development in the country’s ongoing conflict. Major General Al-
body_en:
Dongola, April 19, 2026 - Sudan’s army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has received a senior commander who defected from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in what marks a significant development in the country’s ongoing conflict.
Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, widely known as “Al-Qubba,” arrived in the northern city of Dongola after leaving RSF-controlled areas in North Darfur. His defection is considered one of the most notable since previous high-profile departures from the paramilitary group.
Al-Burhan, accompanied by senior military officials, formally welcomed the commander and his entourage. The move is seen as a symbolic and strategic gain for the Sudanese Armed Forces amid continued fighting with the RSF.
A founding member of the RSF, Al-Qubba played a key role in major battles, particularly in El Fasher. His departure is reportedly linked to internal disputes within the RSF leadership, including grievances over appointments and alleged marginalization.
According to military sources, the commander’s departure followed a tense standoff, during which he reportedly avoided arrest and led a convoy of fighters and vehicles through desert areas toward northern Sudan.
The operation was supported by Sudanese army units, which provided aerial cover and protection along the route. The convoy eventually reached northern territory under military escort before proceeding to Dongola.
The defection has drawn reactions from tribal and political actors. The Revolutionary Awakening Council, led by Musa Hilal, welcomed the move as a step toward national unity.
However, reports from Darfur suggest that the development has triggered reprisals, with allegations of abuses against communities perceived to have links to the defecting commander. These include raids, arrests, and looting in parts of North Darfur.
The episode underscores growing internal fractures within the RSF, even as the broader conflict continues to reshape alliances and dynamics on the ground.

title: Sudan and Saudi Arabia to Hold Investment Forum in Riyadh
excerpt: Khartoum, April 19, 2026 - Sudanese and Saudi stakeholders are preparing to convene a major investment forum in Riyadh this June, in a bid to revive economic cooperation and address key financial and investment challenges between the two countries. The initiative, announced by th
title_en: Sudan and Saudi Arabia to Hold Investment Forum in Riyadh
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 19, 2026 - Sudanese and Saudi stakeholders are preparing to convene a major investment forum in Riyadh this June, in a bid to revive economic cooperation and address key financial and investment challenges between the two countries. The initiative, announced by th
body_en:
Khartoum, April 19, 2026 - Sudanese and Saudi stakeholders are preparing to convene a major investment forum in Riyadh this June, in a bid to revive economic cooperation and address key financial and investment challenges between the two countries.
The initiative, announced by the Sudanese Employers Federation, will focus in particular on resolving constraints related to banking transfers and facilitating business operations. It marks the first large-scale economic gathering of its kind since the outbreak of conflict in Sudan in April 2023.
The forum follows recent diplomatic steps to strengthen bilateral ties, including plans to establish a joint coordination council aimed at enhancing economic and strategic cooperation.
Sudanese authorities have identified around 100 priority projects for potential partnerships with Saudi investors, with a combined estimated value exceeding $50 billion. These projects span several key sectors, including agriculture, energy, mining, infrastructure, and technology.
Organizers indicate that the event will bring together senior political and economic leaders from both countries, alongside private sector representatives. An exhibition showcasing Sudanese and Saudi products is also planned, with discussions expected to highlight reforms to Sudan’s investment framework and opportunities for public-private partnerships in reconstruction efforts.
Saudi Arabia remains Sudan’s leading Arab investment partner, with significant capital concentrated in agricultural ventures. Trade between the two countries is substantial, driven largely by exports of livestock and agricultural goods from Sudan.
The upcoming forum is seen as a step toward reactivating economic engagement and attracting foreign investment at a time when Sudan faces mounting reconstruction needs following prolonged conflict.

title: Sudan Industrial Body Calls for Austerity and Reallocation of Seized Assets
excerpt: Khartoum, April 20, 2026 - The Secretary-General of the Federation of Sudanese Industries, Abbas Ali al-Sayyid, has called for the implementation of a strict national austerity programme and the reallocation of assets seized from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to support the reco
title_en: Sudan Industrial Body Calls for Austerity and Reallocation of Seized Assets
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 20, 2026 - The Secretary-General of the Federation of Sudanese Industries, Abbas Ali al-Sayyid, has called for the implementation of a strict national austerity programme and the reallocation of assets seized from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to support the reco
body_en:
Khartoum, April 20, 2026 - The Secretary-General of the Federation of Sudanese Industries, Abbas Ali al-Sayyid, has called for the implementation of a strict national austerity programme and the reallocation of assets seized from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to support the recovery of Sudan’s struggling industrial sector.
He said the country requires a two- to three-year austerity plan focused on reducing public spending and eliminating what he described as non-essential expenditures, including luxury government vehicles and costly foreign missions maintained on high-value foreign currency leases despite limited activity.
Al-Sayyid urged authorities to confiscate RSF-linked assets within Sudan and pursue funds allegedly transferred abroad, arguing that such resources should be redirected toward industrial rehabilitation and national reconstruction. He noted that before the conflict, the RSF controlled significant real estate holdings and financial institutions.
He warned that Sudan’s industrial base has been severely damaged by the ongoing war, with an estimated 70% of industrial activity currently halted. According to his assessment, around 3,493 industrial facilities have been affected, including more than 1,800 that sustained major damage and several dozen that were completely destroyed.
To support recovery, he proposed long-term tax exemptions, concessional financing for factories, and the establishment of a national reconstruction fund financed through confiscated assets and revenues from anti-smuggling operations.
Al-Sayyid also highlighted Sudan’s widening trade imbalance, citing central bank data showing a $3.86 billion deficit in 2025, with exports at $2.64 billion compared to imports totaling $6.49 billion. He stressed the need to reduce dependence on raw material exports and shift toward value-added manufacturing in sectors such as food processing, edible oils, and meat production.
In addition, he called for the creation of an independent anti-corruption authority, reforms to integrate the informal economy into the tax system, and improved energy allocation policies, including prioritizing electricity for industrial use during daytime hours while expanding solar power for households to ease pressure on the national grid.

title: Sudan Finance Minister Orders Urgent Measures to Address Trade Crisis
excerpt: Khartoum, April 22, 2026 - Sudan’s Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim has directed immediate measures to address severe bottlenecks affecting exports and imports, as the country’s economy continues to struggle under the weight of a prolonged conflict. The Ministry of Finance said th
title_en: Sudan Finance Minister Orders Urgent Measures to Address Trade Crisis
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 22, 2026 - Sudan’s Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim has directed immediate measures to address severe bottlenecks affecting exports and imports, as the country’s economy continues to struggle under the weight of a prolonged conflict. The Ministry of Finance said th
body_en:
Khartoum, April 22, 2026 - Sudan’s Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim has directed immediate measures to address severe bottlenecks affecting exports and imports, as the country’s economy continues to struggle under the weight of a prolonged conflict.
The Ministry of Finance said the minister, who is heading a special economic task force, has ordered “instant solutions” to ongoing trade disruptions while preparing broader structural reforms aimed at stabilizing the national economy.
Since the outbreak of war in April 2023, Sudan’s economy has contracted by more than 42% compared to pre-conflict levels. Officials estimate that around 60% of the population has lost reliable sources of income, while the national currency has sharply depreciated, now trading at over 4,000 Sudanese pounds per U.S. dollar.
During a high-level meeting at the central bank in Khartoum, the finance minister emphasized the need for coordinated policies to secure agricultural inputs and revive industrial production. He called in particular for upgrading livestock processing and slaughterhouse systems to increase value-added exports and expand access to international markets.
The task force also agreed on stronger anti-smuggling enforcement measures and greater support for the private sector through structured partnerships aimed at import substitution. Authorities say these steps are intended to protect domestic industries and ensure a steady supply of essential goods through formal financial channels.
Business representatives have expressed support for the reforms, stating that the private sector is prepared to play a central role in reconstruction efforts, particularly in food processing and textile industries.
However, the broader economic outlook remains highly challenging. Recent assessments indicate that Sudan’s GDP fell by 29.4% in 2023 and a further 13.5% in 2024, with projections suggesting a return to pre-war economic levels may take several years.
Government revenues have also declined sharply, dropping from around 10% of GDP in 2022 to less than 5% in 2024. Trade data for 2025 show a deficit of approximately $3.86 billion, with exports totaling $2.64 billion against imports of $6.49 billion.

title: Sudan Union Warns of Sugar Sector Collapse Amid War and Funding Shortages
excerpt: Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - Sudan’s General Union of Industrial Workers has warned that the country’s sugar industry is at risk of total collapse due to persistent funding shortages, lack of production inputs, and the escalating impact of the ongoing conflict. In a statement issue
title_en: Sudan Union Warns of Sugar Sector Collapse Amid War and Funding Shortages
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - Sudan’s General Union of Industrial Workers has warned that the country’s sugar industry is at risk of total collapse due to persistent funding shortages, lack of production inputs, and the escalating impact of the ongoing conflict. In a statement issue
body_en:
Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - Sudan’s General Union of Industrial Workers has warned that the country’s sugar industry is at risk of total collapse due to persistent funding shortages, lack of production inputs, and the escalating impact of the ongoing conflict.
In a statement issued Thursday, the union’s sugar sector committee urged the Sovereign Council and relevant government institutions to take urgent action to rescue the industry and secure the upcoming agricultural season, which is expected to begin within weeks.
The committee said major sugar factories, particularly those in Sennar and El Guneid in central Sudan, have suffered extensive looting and vandalism following the entry of Rapid Support Forces into key production areas. The destruction of infrastructure, equipment, and raw materials has forced several facilities to shut down completely.
According to the union, the sector is now facing “serious risks,” with officials calling for emergency financing to restart production and protect the planting season. Delays in cultivation have already placed the current cycle in jeopardy, with around 4,000 acres of seed cane still unplanted, including 2,500 acres at New Halfa and 1,500 acres at Assalaya. Authorities warned that failure to complete planting before mid-May could trigger a significant drop in output.
The union also highlighted worsening humanitarian conditions among workers, many of whom are surviving on severely reduced wages that have been eroded further by inflation and currency depreciation. It warned that continued financial strain is pushing employees deeper into hardship.
The memorandum called for the urgent provision of essential agricultural inputs, including fuel, fertilizers, and pesticides, cautioning that further delays could lead to the near collapse of a sector considered strategically important to the national economy.
The warning comes as authorities attempt to address broader trade and supply chain disruptions affecting Sudan’s economy. Recent government directives have emphasized securing agricultural inputs and stabilizing industrial production as part of wider recovery efforts.
At the same time, Sudan has become increasingly reliant on sugar imports. Official trade data for 2025 indicate that the country imported about $1.8 billion worth of food products, with sugar accounting for approximately $552 million of that total.
Before the outbreak of war in April 2023, domestic production was estimated to meet roughly 65% of national sugar consumption, a share that has since sharply declined due to widespread damage to the sector.

title: Bank of Uganda Signs Shs592 Billion Gold Supply Deal Under Domestic Purchase Programme
excerpt: Kampala April 9, 2026 - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has signed a contract worth $160 million (approximately Shs592 billion) with two local companies, including Euro Gold Refinery, to begin supplying gold under its Domestic Gold Purchase Programme. The agreement marks a key step in U
title_en: Bank of Uganda Signs Shs592 Billion Gold Supply Deal Under Domestic Purchase Programme
excerpt_en: Kampala April 9, 2026 - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has signed a contract worth $160 million (approximately Shs592 billion) with two local companies, including Euro Gold Refinery, to begin supplying gold under its Domestic Gold Purchase Programme. The agreement marks a key step in U
body_en:
Kampala April 9, 2026 - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) has signed a contract worth $160 million (approximately Shs592 billion) with two local companies, including Euro Gold Refinery, to begin supplying gold under its Domestic Gold Purchase Programme.
The agreement marks a key step in Uganda’s strategy to strengthen national reserves, curb gold smuggling, and promote value addition in the mineral sector through direct central bank purchases.
The contract follows BoU’s decision to procure gold for treasury purposes as part of efforts to diversify reserve assets and reduce dependence on foreign currencies.
According to Benard Feni, the contract was awarded after a competitive bidding process involving multiple local and international bidders.
“The central bank made an open call for bids, and Euro Gold emerged the best bidder among several international companies. We have signed the contract and received confirmation,” Feni said.
The Bank of Uganda’s Domestic Gold Purchase Programme targets the acquisition of between seven and ten tonnes of locally mined gold annually. The initiative is designed to strengthen foreign exchange reserves and support artisanal and small-scale miners.
BoU Executive Director for Research and Economic Analysis Adam Mugume confirmed that the institution plans to purchase at least 100 kilogrammes of gold between March and June 2026.
“If all goes as planned, we should be able to purchase at least 100 kilogrammes of gold between March and June 2026,” Mugume said.
Uganda exported gold worth $5.8 billion in 2025, though much of the production remains driven by artisanal and small-scale mining operations.
Euro Gold Refinery, Uganda’s first fully locally owned refinery, has positioned itself as a key player in formalizing the sector. Launched in July 2025 by Energy and Mineral Development Minister Ruth Nankabirwa, the refinery processes gold to 99.9% purity and aims to align Uganda’s output with international standards.
Feni said the refinery is working with mining communities in Mubende, Abim, and Yumbe to improve production standards and expand access to formal markets. These partnerships reportedly benefit thousands of artisanal miners and aim to strengthen traceability in the gold value chain.
“We are helping miners move from raw gold to refined products so they can fetch better prices on the international market,” he said.
The refinery has also expanded its workforce, with more than 70% of employees being Ugandan nationals trained in modern refining standards.
Feni added that the company’s long-term ambition is to position Uganda as a continental gold hub.
“By 2030, we want Uganda to be recognised as a gold hub-not just exporting raw materials, but producing high-quality, 24-karat bullion for the global market,” he said.
The Bank of Uganda said gold purchased under the programme will be sourced from artisanal miners, licensed dealers, and small-scale operators across the country, before being refined and certified for reserve use.
Officials say the initiative is expected to enhance transparency in the gold sector, reduce illicit trade, and increase domestic value addition in Uganda’s mining industry.

title: Danish Companies Target Uganda’s Agriculture and Manufacturing Sectors as Investment Ties Deepen
excerpt: Kampala April 9, 2026 - Denmark is stepping up efforts to expand its commercial footprint in Uganda, with a renewed focus on attracting investment and supporting Danish firms already operating in the country, according to Ambassador Signe Winding Alberg. She made the remarks duri
title_en: Danish Companies Target Uganda’s Agriculture and Manufacturing Sectors as Investment Ties Deepen
excerpt_en: Kampala April 9, 2026 - Denmark is stepping up efforts to expand its commercial footprint in Uganda, with a renewed focus on attracting investment and supporting Danish firms already operating in the country, according to Ambassador Signe Winding Alberg. She made the remarks duri
body_en:
Kampala April 9, 2026 - Denmark is stepping up efforts to expand its commercial footprint in Uganda, with a renewed focus on attracting investment and supporting Danish firms already operating in the country, according to Ambassador Signe Winding Alberg.
She made the remarks during a visit to Uganda’s State House Investors Protection Unit, underscoring strengthening bilateral economic relations anchored in trade, investment, and sustainable development.
Alberg highlighted growing Danish interest in sectors such as agriculture, food processing, and safety technologies. She cited examples including a Danish-linked pineapple processing facility that adds value to Ugandan agricultural produce, as well as Fire Express, which is introducing modern fire safety solutions in the country.
“We remain very committed to strengthening the Danish business community here in Uganda to deepen our commercial engagement,” Alberg said. “We have a very active business community that is growing here, and we value Uganda as an investment destination for foreign investors.”
She also announced that the Danish Agriculture and Food Council is expected to visit Uganda on April 22, 2026, accompanied by ten companies in the agri-food sector. The delegation will explore partnerships and investment opportunities, while engaging government institutions on market entry strategies.
Alberg emphasized that supporting existing investors remains central to Denmark’s approach, noting that successful established companies encourage further investment. She pointed to Motorcare, a Danish-affiliated company operating in Uganda for over 30 years, which is seeking improved clarity on public procurement processes in the automotive sector.
“We are very focused on attracting new Danish investment while supporting our existing investors,” she said.
Ugandan officials welcomed the engagement, reaffirming commitment to improving the investment climate. The meeting was hosted by Col. Edith Nakalema, who said Uganda values partnerships that support industrialization and value addition.
“We remain fully committed to creating an investor-friendly climate for Danish investors in Uganda,” Nakalema said, noting that the State House unit works closely with government agencies to fast-track investor concerns.
She highlighted the electronic Investors Protection Portal, which allows investors to coordinate with multiple government departments through a single platform aimed at reducing bureaucratic delays.
Officials said the discussions also focused on strengthening procurement transparency and improving coordination for foreign companies operating in Uganda.
The engagement reflects Uganda’s broader strategy to attract foreign direct investment, expand industrial capacity, and deepen partnerships in key sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, and infrastructure as part of its long-term economic transformation agenda.

title: Deepen Investment Ties as Chinese Delegation Explores Coffee, Industry and Tourism Opportunities
