body_en:
Ihula, April 17, 2026 - A tense calm has settled in Ihula, in Walikale territory, a day after heavy fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters forced residents to flee.
Clashes erupted on April 16 in the locality, located in the Balindu area of the Kisimba group, when Wazalendo elements launched an offensive on positions held by AFC/M23. The fighting triggered widespread panic, with civilians fleeing toward nearby Kalembe or seeking refuge in surrounding bush areas.
The human toll remains unclear, though local sources report that a rebel position was set on fire during the brief incursion by Wazalendo fighters.
Following the clashes, Wazalendo forces withdrew from the area, allowing AFC/M23 elements to reassert control over the locality.
Despite the lull in fighting, the situation remains volatile. Many residents have yet to return to their homes, opting to remain in safer areas amid fears of renewed violence.

title: DRC-AFC/M23 Talks: Parties Agree on Urgent Humanitarian Measures
excerpt: Montreux, April 17, 2026 - Delegates from the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion have agreed on the urgent need to facilitate humanitarian aid and protect essential civilian infrastructure, following a new round of talks held in Switzerland. The negotiations,
title_en: DRC-AFC/M23 Talks: Parties Agree on Urgent Humanitarian Measures
excerpt_en: Montreux, April 17, 2026 - Delegates from the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion have agreed on the urgent need to facilitate humanitarian aid and protect essential civilian infrastructure, following a new round of talks held in Switzerland. The negotiations,
body_en:
Montreux, April 17, 2026 - Delegates from the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebellion have agreed on the urgent need to facilitate humanitarian aid and protect essential civilian infrastructure, following a new round of talks held in Switzerland.
The negotiations, mediated by Qatar and conducted from April 13 to 17 in Montreux, resulted in what both sides described as “substantial progress” toward a protocol on humanitarian access and legal protection, according to a joint communiqué issued at the close of the discussions.
Both parties reaffirmed their commitment to respecting international humanitarian law, human rights law, and refugee law, while also adhering to the constitutional principles of the DRC.
The communiqué further highlights a pledge to refrain from targeting or damaging infrastructure critical to civilian survival. This includes food supplies, agricultural land, livestock, water installations, irrigation systems, as well as telecommunications, energy services, hospitals, and schools.
The renewed engagement marks a shift after months of stalled negotiations and comes against the backdrop of a deteriorating security situation in eastern DRC, where ongoing clashes have continued to impact civilian populations.
Observers say the outcome could represent a step toward easing humanitarian conditions, though its implementation will depend on sustained commitment from both sides on the ground.

title: Armed Attack on National Route 4 Leaves Seven Injured
excerpt: Kisangani, April 18, 2026 - Seven people were injured in an armed attack on a passenger bus along National Route 4, about 54 kilometers from Kisangani, in the Bakumu-Mandombe sector. The incident occurred on Friday afternoon when a vehicle belonging to a transport agency en route
title_en: Armed Attack on National Route 4 Leaves Seven Injured
excerpt_en: Kisangani, April 18, 2026 - Seven people were injured in an armed attack on a passenger bus along National Route 4, about 54 kilometers from Kisangani, in the Bakumu-Mandombe sector. The incident occurred on Friday afternoon when a vehicle belonging to a transport agency en route
body_en:
Kisangani, April 18, 2026 - Seven people were injured in an armed attack on a passenger bus along National Route 4, about 54 kilometers from Kisangani, in the Bakumu-Mandombe sector.
The incident occurred on Friday afternoon when a vehicle belonging to a transport agency en route to Butembo was ambushed by armed men reportedly wearing military uniforms. According to eyewitnesses, the assailants opened fire, wounding several passengers.
Five of the injured were transported back to Kisangani for medical treatment due to the severity of their condition, while two others continued their journey toward Bafwasende.
Passengers reported that a soldier aboard the bus responded to the attack, leading to an exchange of gunfire that lasted several minutes. During the incident, the driver was forced off the road and taken toward a nearby forest before later managing to return, reportedly after the attackers withdrew.
Despite the violence, no property was reported stolen. Witnesses also noted that military reinforcements arrived at the scene after the attack had ended.
In a separate development, three young men were arrested at a checkpoint on the Ituri road several hours after the incident. Authorities said the suspects raised suspicion due to their appearance and were found in possession of a mobile phone they were unable to unlock. They were taken into custody in Kisangani as investigations continue.

title: Authorities Warn of Alleged Rwandan Military Camp in Kabare
excerpt: Kabare, April 20, 2026 - The provincial government of South Kivu has raised concerns over reports of a Rwandan military presence in Kabare territory, warning of what it describes as a serious violation of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s sovereignty. In a statement, provincial
title_en: Authorities Warn of Alleged Rwandan Military Camp in Kabare
excerpt_en: Kabare, April 20, 2026 - The provincial government of South Kivu has raised concerns over reports of a Rwandan military presence in Kabare territory, warning of what it describes as a serious violation of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s sovereignty. In a statement, provincial
body_en:
Kabare, April 20, 2026 - The provincial government of South Kivu has raised concerns over reports of a Rwandan military presence in Kabare territory, warning of what it describes as a serious violation of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s sovereignty.
In a statement, provincial authorities said local residents had reported the establishment of a military camp in the village of Mumosho, an area currently under the control of AFC/M23 rebels. Officials allege that Rwandan soldiers recently entered the area and began setting up a base.
The provincial government described the development as a “grave attack” on the country’s territorial integrity and a violation of ongoing peace efforts aimed at stabilizing eastern DRC.
Authorities also warned of the risks posed to civilian populations, citing concerns over the militarization of inhabited areas and the potential consolidation of a foreign presence on Congolese soil.
The South Kivu administration called for the immediate halt to any construction linked to the reported camp and demanded the withdrawal of all foreign forces from the territory. It also urged the central government to take urgent measures to restore state authority in the affected areas.
Officials said they would continue to document alleged violations while working with national institutions to support efforts aimed at protecting civilians and preserving territorial integrity.
The province remains one of the main theaters of conflict in eastern DRC, where AFC/M23 rebels continue to operate across several territories despite previous withdrawals from key urban centers.

title: MONUSCO Urges End to Drone Use and GPS Disruptions
excerpt: Kinshasa, April 20, 2026 - The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo has called for the suspension of offensive drone operations and an end to GPS signal interference to ensure effective monitoring of the ceasefire between Kinshasa and the AFC/M2
title_en: MONUSCO Urges End to Drone Use and GPS Disruptions
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, April 20, 2026 - The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo has called for the suspension of offensive drone operations and an end to GPS signal interference to ensure effective monitoring of the ceasefire between Kinshasa and the AFC/M2
body_en:
Kinshasa, April 20, 2026 - The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo has called for the suspension of offensive drone operations and an end to GPS signal interference to ensure effective monitoring of the ceasefire between Kinshasa and the AFC/M23 rebellion.
In a statement issued on April 19, the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) welcomed recent progress made during talks in Montreux, Switzerland, where both parties agreed on measures related to humanitarian access, detainee exchanges, and the protection of civilian infrastructure.
However, the UN mission stressed that several key conditions must be met to allow the ceasefire monitoring mechanism to function “credibly, securely, and effectively.” These include halting the use of offensive drones, ending the jamming and spoofing of GPS signals, ensuring full freedom of movement for MONUSCO personnel, and guaranteeing safe access to airspace and airport facilities.
MONUSCO emphasized the importance of establishing a transparent and operational monitoring system capable of verifying compliance with the ceasefire and helping to reduce violence on the ground. The mission also highlighted the role of such mechanisms in strengthening civilian protection and supporting the gradual restoration of state authority in conflict-affected areas.
The UN mission reaffirmed its readiness to support the deployment of initial verification missions through logistical and technical assistance, in line with its stabilization mandate and relevant UN Security Council resolutions.
MONUSCO further encouraged both parties to maintain the current diplomatic momentum and translate commitments into concrete improvements on the ground, while continuing negotiations on outstanding issues.
The appeal comes as ongoing mediation efforts, supported by international partners including Qatar, the United States, and the African Union, seek to consolidate fragile progress toward a broader peace agreement in eastern DRC.

title: New Drone Strike Allegations Undermine Montreux Commitments
excerpt: Kinshasa, April 20, 2026 - Just days after the conclusion of the latest round of peace talks in Montreux, Switzerland, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the AFC/M23 rebellion have exchanged fresh accusations over alleged drone strikes in eastern DRC
title_en: New Drone Strike Allegations Undermine Montreux Commitments
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, April 20, 2026 - Just days after the conclusion of the latest round of peace talks in Montreux, Switzerland, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the AFC/M23 rebellion have exchanged fresh accusations over alleged drone strikes in eastern DRC
body_en:
Kinshasa, April 20, 2026 - Just days after the conclusion of the latest round of peace talks in Montreux, Switzerland, the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the AFC/M23 rebellion have exchanged fresh accusations over alleged drone strikes in eastern DRC, casting renewed doubt on the fragile implementation of recent agreements.
The talks, held under Qatari mediation and involving observers from the United States, Switzerland, and the African Union, had ended with commitments to strengthen humanitarian access, release detainees, and operationalize a joint ceasefire verification mechanism.
However, tensions quickly resurfaced over the weekend. The Congolese army accused AFC/M23, allegedly supported by the Rwandan military, of carrying out drone strikes on April 18 targeting FARDC positions in Mikenge and Kakenge, as well as civilian areas in the Mwenga and Fizi highlands of South Kivu.
According to the military spokesperson, the attacks caused civilian casualties, including four deaths and eight injuries, among them women and children.
The AFC/M23, for its part, rejected the accusations and instead alleged that government forces and their allies conducted drone and artillery strikes on populated areas in South Kivu and North Kivu, including Minembwe and Masisi territories.
The mutual accusations of aerial attacks highlight the continuing fragility of the ceasefire process, despite recent diplomatic advances. Observers note that the use of drones and long-range strikes has become a central point of contention between the two sides.
In response to rising tensions, the United Nations peacekeeping mission (MONUSCO) reiterated its call for an end to the use of offensive drones and electronic interference with navigation systems, stressing that such practices undermine efforts to monitor the ceasefire effectively.
Meanwhile, the Montreux negotiations produced additional commitments, including an agreement to proceed with the release of detainees within ten days, as part of a broader prisoner exchange mechanism previously agreed in September 2025. Although the exact figures were not formally published in the final communiqué, AFC/M23 representatives indicated that over 300 detainees linked to the movement and more than 160 government-held prisoners could be affected.
The parties also signed a memorandum of understanding to operationalize an expanded joint verification mechanism aimed at monitoring compliance with the ceasefire and investigating violations on the ground.
Despite these diplomatic steps, the rapid exchange of accusations underscores the continued volatility of the conflict and the challenges facing efforts to translate agreements into lasting stability in eastern DRC.

title: MONUSCO Chief Begins Field Visit to Assess Security and Civilian Protection
excerpt: Beni, April 20, 2026 - The head of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO), James Swan, has begun a field visit to eastern DRC aimed at assessing the worsening security situation and reinforcing civilian protection effor
title_en: MONUSCO Chief Begins Field Visit to Assess Security and Civilian Protection
excerpt_en: Beni, April 20, 2026 - The head of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO), James Swan, has begun a field visit to eastern DRC aimed at assessing the worsening security situation and reinforcing civilian protection effor
body_en:
Beni, April 20, 2026 - The head of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (MONUSCO), James Swan, has begun a field visit to eastern DRC aimed at assessing the worsening security situation and reinforcing civilian protection efforts.
Arriving in Beni on Monday, Mr. Swan launched his first on-the-ground mission since taking office, with planned engagements involving provincial authorities, political representatives, and civil society actors.
MONUSCO officials said the visit is intended to gather direct assessments of local security conditions and identify ways to improve the mission’s operational response, particularly in areas affected by recurring violence.
The mission’s communications office noted that the itinerary also includes a visit to Beni territory, a region frequently targeted by armed groups, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), where attacks on civilians have persisted.
Upon arrival, Mr. Swan held discussions with North Kivu Governor General Evariste Somo, focusing on the evolving security challenges in the province and coordination between MONUSCO and local authorities.

title: Fragile Calm Returns After Heavy Clashes in Mitimingi
excerpt: Masisi, April 21, 2026 - A precarious calm was observed on Monday evening in the Ufamandu 2 area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, following several days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters allied with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Co
title_en: Fragile Calm Returns After Heavy Clashes in Mitimingi
excerpt_en: Masisi, April 21, 2026 - A precarious calm was observed on Monday evening in the Ufamandu 2 area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, following several days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters allied with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Co
body_en:
Masisi, April 21, 2026 - A precarious calm was observed on Monday evening in the Ufamandu 2 area of Masisi territory, North Kivu, following several days of intense fighting between AFC/M23 rebels and Wazalendo fighters allied with the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC).
According to local sources, hostilities began on Sunday, April 19, and escalated sharply on Monday, April 20, particularly in the village of Mitimingi. Residents reported hours of sustained gunfire involving both heavy and light weapons, forcing civilians to remain confined to their homes or flee into surrounding areas.
Civil society representatives said the Wazalendo launched a counter-offensive early Monday morning, targeting rebel positions as AFC/M23 elements advanced toward Mitimingi. The operation followed an earlier assault attributed to the rebels on a Wazalendo position in the nearby village of Kashuka.
After a full day of fighting, the guns fell silent on Monday evening, but the security situation remains highly unstable. Residents continue to fear renewed clashes, as armed movements persist in the area.
Local organizations have warned of a deepening humanitarian crisis in Ufamandu 2, where repeated violence has triggered large-scale displacement and left communities in increasingly precarious living conditions.
Conclusion
The period from April 6 to April 20, 2026, reflected a Democratic Republic of Congo navigating a delicate balance between diplomatic advancement, economic repositioning, and persistent security and governance challenges.
On the diplomatic front, the implementation of the Washington Peace Agreement showed limited but notable progress, with execution indicators rising to 27.5%. However, tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali persisted, with mutual distrust continuing to slow the translation of formal commitments into concrete security improvements on the ground. This external diplomatic fragility was mirrored internally by heightened political contestation, particularly through the “Save the DRC” opposition movement, which intensified its criticism of the government’s handling of governance, rights, and security issues.
At the same time, the country recorded a significant shift in its international economic posture. The successful issuance of a $1.25 billion Eurobond-branded “Mbote”-marked a milestone in the DRC’s integration into global capital markets and signaled growing investor confidence in its macroeconomic trajectory. This momentum was reinforced by the expansion of strategic partnerships, notably with the United States, alongside intensified defense and security cooperation initiatives with partners such as Turkey and France, reflecting a broader effort to modernize state capacity and diversify international alliances.
Yet, these developments unfolded against a backdrop of continued instability in the eastern provinces. Ongoing violence involving armed groups such as the AFC/M23, the ADF, and various local militias continued to drive displacement, insecurity, and humanitarian pressure. These conditions underscore a widening gap between diplomatic and economic achievements on one hand, and the lived realities of populations affected by conflict on the other.
Overall, the trajectory of this period suggests a country in transition: increasingly active on international financial and strategic fronts, but still constrained by unresolved internal security challenges. The coming months will largely depend on the government’s ability to convert diplomatic agreements and external partnerships into tangible improvements in security, governance, and public trust.
By Glad Musema
Jeff Buleli

title_en: DRC government plans Kakobola 2 hydropower project to expand electricity supply in Kwilu province
excerpt_en: Kikwit March 28, 2026 - The Congolese government is considering the construction of a second hydroelectric facility, Kakobola 2, following the commissioning of the Kakobola Dam in Kikwit. The proposed project, announced on March 26 in Bandundu by Water Resources Minister Aimé Mol
body_en:
Kikwit March 28, 2026 - The Congolese government is considering the construction of a second hydroelectric facility, Kakobola 2, following the commissioning of the Kakobola Dam in Kikwit.
The proposed project, announced on March 26 in Bandundu by Water Resources Minister Aimé Molendo Sakombi, would be located about two kilometers from the existing site in Gungu territory. It is expected to generate 15 megawatts of electricity, increasing the overall production capacity of the Kakobola complex to approximately 25 megawatts.

title_en: Rubaya landslide kills at least 9 miners in Masisi territory amid renewed safety concerns
excerpt_en: Rubaya March 28, 2026 - At least nine artisanal miners have been killed and 12 others injured following a landslide at the Gasasa mining site in Rubaya, located in Masisi territory in North Kivu province. The accident occurred on Friday when two mining shafts collapsed as workers
body_en:
Rubaya March 28, 2026 - At least nine artisanal miners have been killed and 12 others injured following a landslide at the Gasasa mining site in Rubaya, located in Masisi territory in North Kivu province.
The accident occurred on Friday when two mining shafts collapsed as workers descended underground to extract coltan. Several of the injured are reported to be in critical condition, according to local sources.
Rescue efforts were severely hindered by unstable ground conditions and a lack of adequate equipment, highlighting persistent safety challenges in the region’s artisanal mining sector.
The Rubaya mining area, one of the most significant coltan-producing zones in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, is currently under the control of the AFC/M23 armed group. In this context, mining activities continue largely without formal regulation, increasing risks for workers operating in informal and hazardous conditions.
Authorities and local actors say such incidents have become increasingly frequent in recent weeks, with multiple collapses reported across mining sites in Rubaya and surrounding areas of Masisi and Walikale territories.
Civil society organizations have renewed calls for stronger oversight of artisanal mining operations and improved safety standards, particularly in zones affected by armed conflict and limited state presence.
Families of victims continue to mourn in a region where the economic importance of mineral resources contrasts sharply with the dangerous working conditions faced by miners.

title: Community radio director arrested by AFC/M23 in Minova amid tensions in South Kivu
excerpt: Minova March 29, 2026 - The director of community radio station Top Buzi FM, Espoir Mbata, was arrested on Sunday in Minova, located in Kalehe territory in South Kivu province, according to local sources and station staff. He was reportedly apprehended by members of the AFC/M23 m
title_en: Community radio director arrested by AFC/M23 in Minova amid tensions in South Kivu
excerpt_en: Minova March 29, 2026 - The director of community radio station Top Buzi FM, Espoir Mbata, was arrested on Sunday in Minova, located in Kalehe territory in South Kivu province, according to local sources and station staff. He was reportedly apprehended by members of the AFC/M23 m
body_en:
Minova March 29, 2026 - The director of community radio station Top Buzi FM, Espoir Mbata, was arrested on Sunday in Minova, located in Kalehe territory in South Kivu province, according to local sources and station staff.
He was reportedly apprehended by members of the AFC/M23 movement. The arrest is believed to be linked to an on-air comment concerning a possible withdrawal of AFC/M23 forces from Minova, a subject considered sensitive in the current security context.
In eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, areas under the control of the AFC/M23 continue to experience growing pressure on media professionals, with journalists reporting increased restrictions, intimidation, and security risks.
The incident has heightened concern among local journalists, several of whom reportedly left Minova shortly after the arrest, fearing further detentions.
Top Buzi FM, a community broadcaster operating in the region, has not yet issued an official statement on the arrest. The station’s staff describe an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty following the incident.
The arrest comes amid ongoing uncertainty over reported internal movements and possible redeployments within AFC/M23-held areas, which have fueled tension and speculation among local populations.
Press freedom organizations and local media workers warn that journalists in conflict-affected zones are increasingly exposed to reprisals, particularly when reporting on armed group activity.
The case of Espoir Mbata underscores the fragile conditions under which media operate in parts of eastern Congo, where security dynamics continue to shift and access to reliable information remains highly constrained.

title: Over 200 suspects arrested in large security sweep at Lubumbashi military camp in Haut-Katanga
excerpt: Lubumbashi March 30, 2026 - Security forces in southeastern Democratic Republic of Congo arrested more than 200 suspected criminals during a large-scale cordon-and-search operation at Major Vangu Camp in Lubumbashi, Haut-Katanga province. The joint operation was conducted under t
title_en: Over 200 suspects arrested in large security sweep at Lubumbashi military camp in Haut-Katanga
excerpt_en: Lubumbashi March 30, 2026 - Security forces in southeastern Democratic Republic of Congo arrested more than 200 suspected criminals during a large-scale cordon-and-search operation at Major Vangu Camp in Lubumbashi, Haut-Katanga province. The joint operation was conducted under t
body_en:
Lubumbashi March 30, 2026 - Security forces in southeastern Democratic Republic of Congo arrested more than 200 suspected criminals during a large-scale cordon-and-search operation at Major Vangu Camp in Lubumbashi, Haut-Katanga province.
The joint operation was conducted under the supervision of provincial Interior Minister Jean-Jacques Kashiba and the provincial police commissioner, Blaise Kilimbalimba. It involved units of the National Police, supported by elements of the 22nd Military Region and other security services.
Authorities reported the seizure of 19 AK-47 rifles, along with ammunition, military uniforms, and various bladed weapons including machetes, crowbars, hammers, and shears. Security forces also recovered items such as alcoholic beverages and narcotics during the searches.
Police spokesperson Major Charles Bin Lwamba stated that those arrested included civilians, soldiers, and women, describing the group as suspected of involvement in criminal activity within and around the camp area.
The operation involved systematic searches of residential homes, shops, informal markets, and other structures inside and outside the camp perimeter, according to security officials.
The sweep followed a recent military gathering at Major Vangu Camp where the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Lt. Gen. Jules Banza Mwilambwe, called for stronger unity and discipline within the ranks to reinforce national security and territorial integrity.

title: DRC NGO highlights rural women’s role in forest conservation during closing of Women’s Month
excerpt: Kinshasa March 31, 2026 - The NGO National Alliance for Support and Promotion of Indigenous and Community Heritage Areas and Territories in the Democratic Republic of Congo (ANAPAC DRC) has emphasized the central role of rural women in forest conservation and local development as
title_en: DRC NGO highlights rural women’s role in forest conservation during closing of Women’s Month
excerpt_en: Kinshasa March 31, 2026 - The NGO National Alliance for Support and Promotion of Indigenous and Community Heritage Areas and Territories in the Democratic Republic of Congo (ANAPAC DRC) has emphasized the central role of rural women in forest conservation and local development as
body_en:
Kinshasa March 31, 2026 - The NGO National Alliance for Support and Promotion of Indigenous and Community Heritage Areas and Territories in the Democratic Republic of Congo (ANAPAC DRC) has emphasized the central role of rural women in forest conservation and local development as part of activities marking the closing of Women’s Month.
The event, held in Kinshasa alongside celebrations linked to the International Day of Forests, highlighted women’s contribution to agriculture, forest product processing, and the supply of urban markets in a country where forests remain a key pillar of economic and social life.
According to ANAPAC DRC, its Inclusive Conservation Initiative (ICI) project has supported Indigenous and local women across several provinces through income-generating activities and financial assistance aimed at strengthening both livelihoods and environmental stewardship.
Project representatives reported that women’s committees established under the initiative have received grants ranging between 5,000 and 10,000 US dollars, alongside agricultural tools and processing equipment designed to reduce workload and improve productivity in rural communities.
Officials involved in the program said the initiative has contributed not only to income growth but also to social empowerment, citing increased participation of women in public meetings and community decision-making processes. Participation levels were reported to have risen significantly, with women now taking a more active role in local development discussions.
The project, implemented across multiple biocultural landscapes, supports activities such as cassava, maize, rice, peanut, bean cultivation, livestock farming, and fish farming, with the goal of strengthening economic autonomy while promoting sustainable resource management.
Speaking during the event, representatives of ANAPAC DRC stressed that conservation efforts cannot succeed without integrating local communities, particularly women, who play a major role in managing forest-based livelihoods.
They also called on public authorities to take greater ownership of such initiatives to ensure long-term sustainability beyond external funding cycles, especially in areas where rural women face limited access to processing infrastructure and markets.
The organization further underscored the importance of continued support for Indigenous and local women, noting that strengthening their economic resilience is closely linked to environmental protection and biodiversity conservation in the country.

title: DR Congo declares national holiday after historic World Cup qualification
excerpt: Guadalajara April 1, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has qualified for the 2026 FIFA World Cup for the first time in 52 years, prompting the government to declare Wednesday, April 1, a paid public holiday nationwide. The decision, announced by the Ministry of Employment a
title_en: DR Congo declares national holiday after historic World Cup qualification
excerpt_en: Guadalajara April 1, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has qualified for the 2026 FIFA World Cup for the first time in 52 years, prompting the government to declare Wednesday, April 1, a paid public holiday nationwide. The decision, announced by the Ministry of Employment a
body_en:
Guadalajara April 1, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo has qualified for the 2026 FIFA World Cup for the first time in 52 years, prompting the government to declare Wednesday, April 1, a paid public holiday nationwide.
The decision, announced by the Ministry of Employment and Labour, aims to allow citizens to celebrate what officials described as a moment of national unity and pride following a landmark sporting achievement.
According to the ministry, the measure applies across the entire national territory and gives workers a paid day off in recognition of the national team’s success.
The qualification was secured after the national team, known as the Leopards, defeated Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz 1-0 after extra time in the final of the intercontinental playoffs held in Guadalajara, Mexico.
The victory marks a return to football’s biggest stage for the DRC after more than five decades of absence, with the team becoming one of the African representatives at the 2026 World Cup.
Under coach Sébastien Desabre, the Leopards delivered a tightly contested performance, managing to break through in extra time after a disciplined defensive display and sustained pressure from their opponents.
The result has sparked nationwide celebrations, with authorities and supporters hailing the achievement as a historic milestone for Congolese football and a moment of collective national pride.

title: Gims placed in police custody in money laundering investigation in France
excerpt: Paris March 25, 2026 - Congolese-French singer and rapper Gims has been taken into police custody for questioning in connection with an investigation into alleged organized money laundering activities. According to judicial sources, the 39-year-old artist is being questioned unde
title_en: Gims placed in police custody in money laundering investigation in France
excerpt_en: Paris March 25, 2026 - Congolese-French singer and rapper Gims has been taken into police custody for questioning in connection with an investigation into alleged organized money laundering activities. According to judicial sources, the 39-year-old artist is being questioned unde
body_en:
Paris March 25, 2026 - Congolese-French singer and rapper Gims has been taken into police custody for questioning in connection with an investigation into alleged organized money laundering activities.
According to judicial sources, the 39-year-old artist is being questioned under a rogatory commission issued by investigating magistrates and overseen by France’s National Anti-Organized Crime Prosecutor’s Office. He is reportedly being examined as part of inquiries into suspected complex financial operations involving significant monetary flows.
Gims, whose birth name is Gandhi Djuna, was apprehended on Wednesday upon his arrival at Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport from Dubai. Investigators are seeking to clarify his possible role in financial transactions described as suspicious, although no formal charges have been publicly announced at this stage.
A prominent figure in Francophone music and a self-described ambassador of Congolese culture, Gims was appointed cultural ambassador for the Democratic Republic of Congo in January 2022 by President Félix Tshisekedi. He was also granted a diplomatic passport in recognition of his role in promoting Congolese culture abroad.
Alongside his international career, he has frequently highlighted Congolese musical heritage, collaborating with and drawing inspiration from major figures such as Koffi Olomide. His work often incorporates Congolese rhythms, helping broaden their reach across global Francophone audiences.
Beyond music, Gims has been involved in cultural and humanitarian initiatives linked to the Democratic Republic of Congo, including proposals for modern recording studios in Kinshasa and Lubumbashi and support for cultural events aimed at promoting Congolese music internationally. He has also used his platform to speak out on humanitarian crises in eastern Congo and to call for international attention to ongoing violence in the region.

body_en:
Walikale, March 22, 2026 - Heavy fighting broke out early Sunday in the village of Kanune, located in the Ikobo grouping of Walikale territory, North Kivu, as clashes opposed fighters of the AFC/M23 coalition to Wazalendo militias.
According to local sources, the confrontation began around 5:00 a.m. when Wazalendo elements launched an offensive on positions held by AFC/M23 forces. Residents reported sustained gunfire involving both heavy and light weapons, forcing civilians to remain confined to their homes amid growing panic.
The area of Ikobo has been under AFC/M23 control for nearly a year, following earlier confrontations that saw Wazalendo fighters pushed out of the zone. Since then, the security situation has remained fragile, with recurring tensions and sporadic violence.
Recent movements of rebel reinforcements toward nearby areas, particularly Kisimba, are believed to have altered the balance on the ground. Observers suggest that this redeployment may have weakened certain AFC/M23 positions, especially in the western parts of Buleusa, prompting the latest attempt by Wazalendo forces to regain lost territory.
As fighting continues, the humanitarian situation remains a major concern. Civilians, already affected by prolonged instability, face increasing risks as clashes intensify in and around populated areas. Local authorities have yet to provide an official update on casualties or displacement, while the situation on the ground remains highly fluid.

title: Fighting for Bule intensifies amid suspicions of external support to armed groups
excerpt: Djugu, March 23, 2026 - Clashes continue in the locality of Bule, in Djugu territory of Ituri province, as fighting persists between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Convention for the People’s Revolution (CRP), an armed group linked to Thomas
title_en: Fighting for Bule intensifies amid suspicions of external support to armed groups
excerpt_en: Djugu, March 23, 2026 - Clashes continue in the locality of Bule, in Djugu territory of Ituri province, as fighting persists between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Convention for the People’s Revolution (CRP), an armed group linked to Thomas
body_en:
Djugu, March 23, 2026 - Clashes continue in the locality of Bule, in Djugu territory of Ituri province, as fighting persists between the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Convention for the People’s Revolution (CRP), an armed group linked to Thomas Lubanga.
Since January, Bule has remained a strategic flashpoint, with control of the area shifting between the two sides. In early February, heavy fighting led to the CRP pushing FARDC forces to the outskirts of the town, despite a counter-offensive launched the same day by government troops. The situation has since remained contested, with both sides maintaining positions in and around the area.
The conflict has also taken a toll on civilians. Reports indicate that several non-combatants have been killed in the violence, including individuals accused of collaborating with opposing forces. In nearby localities, additional clashes have resulted in civilian casualties caused by stray bullets, further heightening fear among residents.
Tensions have been exacerbated by targeted violence against specific communities. In some cases, civilians have reportedly been killed or threatened for refusing to support armed groups, contributing to an atmosphere of intimidation and deepening ethnic divisions in the region.
The situation is further complicated by suspicions within the FARDC regarding possible external support to the CRP. Congolese military sources have expressed concern over alleged links between the armed group and elements of the Ugandan army, citing observed interactions and a perceived lack of intervention during certain attacks. These allegations have not been officially confirmed.
The broader security context in Djugu remains fragile, with ongoing clashes between armed groups and government forces continuing to drive displacement and humanitarian needs. The province of Ituri has been under a state of siege since 2021, with military authorities overseeing security operations. While officials argue that some progress has been made, the persistence of violence highlights the challenges facing efforts to restore lasting stability.
As fighting continues around Bule and surrounding areas, civilians remain the most vulnerable, caught between competing forces in a conflict that shows little sign of immediate resolution.

body_en:
Masisi, March 23, 2026 - Intense clashes broke out early Monday in Kazinga, a locality in the Osso Banyungu sector of Masisi territory, North Kivu, as AFC/M23 fighters launched a new offensive against Wazalendo positions.
According to local security and community sources, the fighting began around 5:00 a.m., with heavy and light weapons used on both sides. Loud explosions were reported across nearby villages, triggering panic among residents, many of whom sought shelter as violence escalated.
Kazinga, considered a strategic area, has in recent weeks been under the control of Wazalendo groups. The latest offensive is widely seen as an attempt by AFC/M23 to regain control of the locality amid shifting frontlines in the region.
The renewed fighting highlights the ongoing volatility in Masisi territory, where clashes between AFC/M23 and pro-government forces, often backed by Wazalendo militias, continue to intensify. Civilians remain at high risk, with repeated cycles of displacement and insecurity affecting already vulnerable communities.

title: Report alleges journalists detained in inhumane conditions by M23 in Goma
excerpt: Goma, March 24, 2026 - Armed group M23 has been accused of detaining civilians, including at least two journalists, in shipping containers under harsh and inhumane conditions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to a new investigation by the Reporters Without Border
title_en: Report alleges journalists detained in inhumane conditions by M23 in Goma
excerpt_en: Goma, March 24, 2026 - Armed group M23 has been accused of detaining civilians, including at least two journalists, in shipping containers under harsh and inhumane conditions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to a new investigation by the Reporters Without Border
body_en:
Goma, March 24, 2026 - Armed group M23 has been accused of detaining civilians, including at least two journalists, in shipping containers under harsh and inhumane conditions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to a new investigation by the Reporters Without Borders.
The report, based on testimonies and visual evidence, indicates that several of these containers are located within the compound of the Goma Provincial Assembly in the Himbi neighborhood, as well as near the premises of the national broadcaster in the city. These sites have reportedly been used as informal detention centers since M23 took control of Goma in early 2025.
Former detainees describe extremely harsh conditions, with dozens of people confined in metal containers lacking light and ventilation. According to testimonies, detainees were allowed outside only once per day and received minimal food. Some survivors also reported acts of violence, including beatings, and deaths occurring inside the containers.
Visual material analyzed as part of the investigation reportedly shows individuals held under armed supervision near the containers. Satellite imagery comparisons suggest that the structures appeared after M23 established control over the city.
The findings align with previous concerns raised by human rights groups over the use of unofficial detention sites in conflict zones, where abuses such as torture and summary executions are alleged to occur.
The AFC/M23 leadership has strongly denied the accusations. Spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka dismissed the report as unfounded, claiming it is part of a campaign aimed at discrediting the movement, and insisting that journalists are free to operate in areas under their control.
Meanwhile, the broader media environment in eastern DRC continues to deteriorate. Dozens of journalists have reportedly fled the region over the past year due to threats and insecurity, while others have faced violence, intimidation, or restrictions on their work.
The situation underscores growing concerns over press freedom and civilian protection in conflict-affected areas of the Great Lakes region, as insecurity and competing narratives continue to shape the information landscape.

excerpt_en: Walikale, March 24, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), backed by Wazalendo fighters, repelled an attempted incursion by AFC/M23 rebels near Mungazi in Walikale territory, North Kivu. According to local security and administrative sources, the reb
body_en:
Walikale, March 24, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC), backed by Wazalendo fighters, repelled an attempted incursion by AFC/M23 rebels near Mungazi in Walikale territory, North Kivu.
According to local security and administrative sources, the rebels attempted to advance through the Usuka River corridor, using forest routes to bypass army positions and carry out a surprise attack on the town of Mungazi, located in the Luberike grouping and currently under government control.
The operation was intercepted by a joint FARDC-Wazalendo patrol in the surrounding forest, triggering intense exchanges of gunfire that caused panic among residents. Following a counteroffensive, government forces managed to push the attackers back toward their initial positions near Kibati.
By Tuesday, calm had largely returned to Mungazi and nearby areas, with daily activities gradually resuming. FARDC and allied fighters remain deployed in the area, maintaining a heightened state of alert as the broader security situation in Walikale continues to be volatile.

title: ADF commander Difenda Kasibandi killed in joint FARDC-UPDF operation
excerpt: Mambasa, March 24, 2026 - A senior leader of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), Difenda Kasibandi, has been killed during a joint military operation conducted by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Ugandan army (UPDF) in the Asangwa area, near th
title_en: ADF commander Difenda Kasibandi killed in joint FARDC-UPDF operation
excerpt_en: Mambasa, March 24, 2026 - A senior leader of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), Difenda Kasibandi, has been killed during a joint military operation conducted by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Ugandan army (UPDF) in the Asangwa area, near th
body_en:
Mambasa, March 24, 2026 - A senior leader of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), Difenda Kasibandi, has been killed during a joint military operation conducted by the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and the Ugandan army (UPDF) in the Asangwa area, near the Lindi River.
According to the Congolese army, Kasibandi was killed alongside four other fighters in an operation targeting a key ADF stronghold located along the border between Lubero and Mambasa territories. The offensive also led to the rescue of three civilians who had been held hostage by the armed group.
Military sources indicate that the operation was part of broader efforts to dismantle ADF networks operating between North Kivu and Ituri provinces. The targeted group was reportedly linked to a faction led by a senior ADF figure known for directing attacks against civilians in the Bapere region.
Recent movements of ADF fighters between Lubero and Mambasa have reinforced concerns about the group’s mobility and its ability to regroup across territories despite ongoing military pressure.
Following the operation, army officials reiterated their warning to individuals suspected of collaborating with the ADF, stating that all those involved with the group would be tracked down and held accountable.

excerpt_en: Rutshuru, March 25, 2026 - A new armed attack targeting civilians was reported on the Kiwanja-Goma road, a key route crossing Virunga National Park, highlighting persistent insecurity in the area. According to local sources, a public transport vehicle was ambushed by armed men be
body_en:
Rutshuru, March 25, 2026 - A new armed attack targeting civilians was reported on the Kiwanja-Goma road, a key route crossing Virunga National Park, highlighting persistent insecurity in the area.
According to local sources, a public transport vehicle was ambushed by armed men between Buvunga and Bugomba. The attackers opened fire to force the vehicle to stop before robbing passengers of their belongings.
The driver was seriously wounded after being shot in the jaw and was rushed to a nearby hospital in Rutshuru for treatment. Another passenger was briefly abducted during the incident but later released.
The attack is part of a growing pattern of insecurity along this strategic road. Just a day earlier, two separate robberies were reported in the same corridor, including one targeting funds intended for teachers and another involving motorcycle taxi drivers and their passengers.
This road, essential for trade and civilian movement in North Kivu, has remained highly vulnerable due to the presence and influence of armed groups, including areas under AFC/M23 control. The situation continues to expose travelers to significant risks despite its economic importance.
Local authorities and community leaders are calling for increased vigilance among road users, while residents stress the urgent need for stronger security measures to ensure safe movement and protect civilians in the region.

title: Army reinforces Okapi Wildlife Reserve after ADF drone activity
excerpt: Mambasa, March 25, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have deployed reinforcements to the Okapi Wildlife Reserve following reported drone activity attributed to the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) over key positions in the area. According to source
title_en: Army reinforces Okapi Wildlife Reserve after ADF drone activity
excerpt_en: Mambasa, March 25, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have deployed reinforcements to the Okapi Wildlife Reserve following reported drone activity attributed to the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) over key positions in the area. According to source
body_en:
Mambasa, March 25, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have deployed reinforcements to the Okapi Wildlife Reserve following reported drone activity attributed to the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) over key positions in the area.
According to sources within the reserve, drones flew over the headquarters and several patrol posts on March 18 and 19, raising alarm among rangers. The overflights come amid growing concerns about the presence of ADF fighters, who are believed to have infiltrated parts of the reserve.
The situation escalated in recent weeks after earlier incidents in nearby villages, including Babesua, where armed elements reportedly forced rangers to abandon their positions before setting fire to parts of the locality. No casualties were reported in that incident, but it highlighted the increasing reach of the group.
In response, FARDC units were deployed from Bunia to reinforce ranger positions and secure the reserve. While the arrival of troops has been welcomed, local sources indicate that the current deployment may not be sufficient given the scale of the threat.
Several surrounding villages, including Muchacha and Babesua, remain deserted as residents continue to flee insecurity. Some patrol activities within the reserve have also been suspended due to safety concerns.
The renewed threat recalls past attacks in the reserve, notably the 2011 incident in which armed elements killed several okapis, an endangered species unique to the region. Conservation efforts have since been ongoing, but continued insecurity poses a serious risk to both wildlife protection and civilian safety in the area.

title: Kinshasa Accuses Kabila After ‘Sudanization’ Remarks Amid Rising Political Tensions
excerpt: KINSHASA, March 26, 2026 - Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have strongly reacted to recent statements by former president Joseph Kabila, interpreting them as an implicit assumption of responsibility for the activities of armed groups operating in the country’s eas
title_en: Kinshasa Accuses Kabila After ‘Sudanization’ Remarks Amid Rising Political Tensions
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, March 26, 2026 - Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have strongly reacted to recent statements by former president Joseph Kabila, interpreting them as an implicit assumption of responsibility for the activities of armed groups operating in the country’s eas
body_en:
KINSHASA, March 26, 2026 - Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo have strongly reacted to recent statements by former president Joseph Kabila, interpreting them as an implicit assumption of responsibility for the activities of armed groups operating in the country’s east.
The controversy follows a renewed public intervention by Kabila after consultations with socio-political actors in North and South Kivu and a Nairobi-based declaration by the “Save the Democratic Republic of Congo” political initiative. The former head of state used the opportunity to criticize the governance of President Félix Tshisekedi, marking one of his most direct political interventions in recent months.
In a recent interview with a Belgian media outlet, Kabila rejected the commonly used term “balkanization” to describe the security crisis in eastern Congo, instead referring to a process of “Sudanization.” He drew parallels with the historical fragmentation of Sudan, which led to the independence of South Sudan in 2011 after years of civil conflict.
Government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya condemned the remarks during a briefing in Kinshasa, describing them as a “form of claim of responsibility” linked to the actions of the AFC/M23 rebellion active in eastern DRC, an armed group Kinshasa alleges is supported by Rwanda.
Muyaya further argued that the timing and framing of Kabila’s statement were politically significant, suggesting they reflected an underlying agenda. He also dismissed the former president’s criticism of current governance, insisting that the present administration has prioritized infrastructure development and institutional reform, while accusing previous leadership of failing to address long-standing national challenges.
The remarks come in the context of continued political mobilization linked to a conclave held in Nairobi in October 2025, where allies and political figures close to Kabila announced the formation of the “Save the DRC Movement.” The platform describes its mission as restoring democratic governance, addressing systemic crisis, and promoting national reconciliation.
The initiative has accused the current government of democratic backsliding and institutional abuse, and has called for an inclusive national dialogue facilitated by religious institutions. It also rejects unilateral political processes led by the presidency.
The movement, also referred to in several local languages as Tobikisa Ekolo, Tuokowe Taifa, and Tupandishayi Ditunga, has indicated plans to coordinate opposition forces and engage regional and international stakeholders regarding the situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

title: Washington Calls for Immediate Withdrawal of Rwandan Forces From Eastern DRC, Imposes Sanctions
excerpt: NEW YORK / WASHINGTON, March 26, 2026 - The United States has called for the immediate withdrawal of Rwandan troops from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, while announcing targeted sanctions against senior Rwandan military officials, during a briefing to the United Nations Se
title_en: Washington Calls for Immediate Withdrawal of Rwandan Forces From Eastern DRC, Imposes Sanctions
excerpt_en: NEW YORK / WASHINGTON, March 26, 2026 - The United States has called for the immediate withdrawal of Rwandan troops from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, while announcing targeted sanctions against senior Rwandan military officials, during a briefing to the United Nations Se
body_en:
NEW YORK / WASHINGTON, March 26, 2026 - The United States has called for the immediate withdrawal of Rwandan troops from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, while announcing targeted sanctions against senior Rwandan military officials, during a briefing to the United Nations Security Council on March 26.
Speaking on behalf of the U.S. administration, Senior Advisor for African Affairs Massad Boulos expressed “deep disappointment” over what Washington described as a recent escalation by Rwanda in eastern DRC, calling it a “direct violation” of commitments made under the Washington peace framework.
The U.S. referred to the implementation of the Washington agreements (December 4, 2025), noting that while some progress had been achieved, recent developments threatened to undermine the fragile process.
According to the U.S. statement, sanctions have been imposed on members of the Rwandan Defence Forces (RDF), including four senior generals, in response to their alleged role in destabilizing activities in eastern Congo.
Washington reiterated its demand for the “immediate withdrawal of Rwandan forces from Congolese territory,” alongside renewed calls for respect of DRC sovereignty and intensified efforts by Kinshasa to neutralize the FDLR armed group.
The U.S. envoy also stressed the importance of restoring state authority in the Kivu provinces and addressing the ongoing illegal exploitation of natural resources, which he said continues to fuel the conflict.
While acknowledging the roles of regional and international mediation efforts - including MONUSCO and Qatari and African-led initiatives - Washington emphasized that lasting peace would require strict adherence to ceasefire commitments and genuine political will from all parties.
The statement also referenced the killing of a French humanitarian worker during a March 11 attack in Goma, extending condolences and underscoring concerns over civilian safety in the conflict zone.

title: AFC/M23 Withdrawal Reported From Several Localities in North Kivu’s Walikale Territory
excerpt: WALIKALE, North Kivu March 27, 2026 - Movements attributed to AFC/M23 elements were observed on March 26 in several localities of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including Minjenje and Mpety in the Kisimba group, as well as Kanune in the Ikobo group, according to local admi
title_en: AFC/M23 Withdrawal Reported From Several Localities in North Kivu’s Walikale Territory
excerpt_en: WALIKALE, North Kivu March 27, 2026 - Movements attributed to AFC/M23 elements were observed on March 26 in several localities of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including Minjenje and Mpety in the Kisimba group, as well as Kanune in the Ikobo group, according to local admi
body_en:
WALIKALE, North Kivu March 27, 2026 - Movements attributed to AFC/M23 elements were observed on March 26 in several localities of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including Minjenje and Mpety in the Kisimba group, as well as Kanune in the Ikobo group, according to local administrative and security sources.
Witnesses reported the departure of armed fighters from Minjenje and Mpety, with personnel and equipment seen moving through the Banakindi area. In Kalembe, a key transit point, residents observed convoys of fighters traveling both by vehicle and on foot, raising further confirmation of a coordinated pullback.
Security sources also indicated that similar movements took place in Kanune, where armed elements reportedly left the area in the early afternoon, heading toward Miriki in neighboring Lubero territory. Residual presence, however, was still reported in parts of the affected zones.
No official communication has been issued by AFC/M23 leadership regarding the reported withdrawals. The movements come days after a meeting of the group’s officers in Minjenje along the Kalembe-Mpety axis, according to local accounts.
On the ground, interpretations remain divided. Some observers describe the movements as a tactical repositioning, while others among the civilian population suspect a maneuver aimed at avoiding security pressure or reshaping frontlines.
The developments occur against a fragile security backdrop in Walikale, where recent clashes between AFC/M23 elements and Wazalendo fighters have triggered population displacement toward safer areas, including Miriki. Many residents remain cautious, awaiting clearer signs of stability and the possibility of safe returns for displaced communities.

title: RSF Report Warns of Mass Exodus of Journalists From Eastern DRC Amid Rising Insecurity
excerpt: KINSHASA / EASTERN DRC March 27, 2026 - A growing number of journalists are fleeing the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo due to escalating threats, violence, and deteriorating working conditions linked to ongoing armed conflict, according to a Reporters Without Borders (RSF)
title_en: RSF Report Warns of Mass Exodus of Journalists From Eastern DRC Amid Rising Insecurity
excerpt_en: KINSHASA / EASTERN DRC March 27, 2026 - A growing number of journalists are fleeing the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo due to escalating threats, violence, and deteriorating working conditions linked to ongoing armed conflict, according to a Reporters Without Borders (RSF)
body_en:
KINSHASA / EASTERN DRC March 27, 2026 - A growing number of journalists are fleeing the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo due to escalating threats, violence, and deteriorating working conditions linked to ongoing armed conflict, according to a Reporters Without Borders (RSF) report reviewed under embargo.
The report, drawing on testimony from the National Union of the Congolese Press (UNPC), indicates that dozens of media professionals have been displaced from conflict-affected provinces, particularly North Kivu and South Kivu. While some have relocated within the country, others have sought refuge in neighboring states including Burundi, Uganda, and Rwanda.
RSF describes a pattern of dangerous displacement journeys, with journalists crossing areas controlled by armed groups or security forces. Several report having faced threats, arrests, interrogations, or temporary detention linked to their professional activities.
Conditions in host countries remain precarious. Some Congolese journalists in exile reportedly face detention in transit centers or administrative uncertainty before release, while others struggle with limited resources and lack of legal status.
The report notes that relocation to Kinshasa is not always a viable alternative, citing high living costs, limited professional opportunities, and unstable income conditions that make continued journalism difficult for displaced reporters.
Multiple testimonies also highlight sustained pressure on media workers, including accusations of collaboration with armed groups and threats following the publication or broadcast of sensitive reporting. In some cases, journalists say they were compelled to relay information dictated by actors in the conflict.
Several journalists interviewed in the report say they have been forced to abandon the profession entirely due to insecurity. One testimony cited by RSF describes a journalist leaving Rutshuru after repeated threats and eventually giving up reporting work.
The report also raises concerns about cross-border risks, noting that exiled journalists may continue to face surveillance, detention, or legal harassment in host countries. It references cases in the region as examples of broader patterns affecting press freedom in conflict contexts.
RSF concludes that the ongoing displacement of journalists is severely undermining access to independent reporting from eastern Congo and calls for stronger protections for media workers both within the country and across borders.

While some have relocated within the country, others have sought refuge in neighboring states including Burundi, Uganda, and Rwanda.
RSF describes a pattern of dangerous displacement journeys, with journalists crossing areas controlled by armed groups or security forces. Several report having faced threats, arrests, interrogations, or temporary detention linked to their professional activities.
Conditions in host countries remain precarious. Some Congolese journalists in exile reportedly face detention in transit centers or administrative uncertainty before release, while others struggle with limited resources and lack of legal status.
The report notes that relocation to Kinshasa is not always a viable alternative, citing high living costs, limited professional opportunities, and unstable income conditions that make continued journalism difficult for displaced reporters.
Multiple testimonies also highlight sustained pressure on media workers, including accusations of collaboration with armed groups and threats following the publication or broadcast of sensitive reporting. In some cases, journalists say they were compelled to relay information dictated by actors in the conflict.
Several journalists interviewed in the report say they have been forced to abandon the profession entirely due to insecurity. One testimony cited by RSF describes a journalist leaving Rutshuru after repeated threats and eventually giving up reporting work.
The report also raises concerns about cross-border risks, noting that exiled journalists may continue to face surveillance, detention, or legal harassment in host countries. It references cases in the region as examples of broader patterns affecting press freedom in conflict contexts.
RSF concludes that the ongoing displacement of journalists is severely undermining access to independent reporting from eastern Congo and calls for stronger protections for media workers both within the country and across borders.

body_en:
WALIKALE, North Kivu March 27, 2026 - The village of Kateku, in the Iremya area of the Ikobo group, was recaptured on March 26 by Wazalendo fighters following clashes with AFC/M23 elements, according to local administrative and community sources.
The fighting reportedly broke out after AFC/M23 fighters had occupied the area. The confrontation lasted around two hours before the armed group withdrew, allowing Wazalendo forces to regain control of the village.
Local sources indicate that at least one combatant from AFC/M23 was killed during the clashes. Following the setback, the group reportedly retreated toward Buleusa, a major locality in the Ikobo area.
The renewed fighting triggered fresh civilian displacement, with residents fleeing toward Buleusa and others moving further into neighboring Lubero territory in search of safety.
Traditional leaders in the area have confirmed the change of control, while warning that the security situation in this part of Walikale remains highly unstable, marked by recurring clashes and shifting control between armed groups.

excerpt_en: WALIKALE, North Kivu March 29, 2026 - Wazalendo self-defense fighters have re-entered and reoccupied the town of Mpety in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, two days after the withdrawal of AFC/M23 elements from the area, according to local sources. Mpety, located in the Banak
body_en:
WALIKALE, North Kivu March 29, 2026 - Wazalendo self-defense fighters have re-entered and reoccupied the town of Mpety in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, two days after the withdrawal of AFC/M23 elements from the area, according to local sources.
Mpety, located in the Banakindi area of the Kisimba group in Walikale territory, had been under the presence of AFC/M23 fighters before their reported pullout earlier in the week. Following their departure, Wazalendo units that had been positioned several kilometers away advanced rapidly to secure the locality.
Local accounts indicate that the groups moved in to establish control and prevent any potential return of AFC/M23 forces. Since March 27, Wazalendo fighters and local commanders have been visibly present in the town, marking a new phase in the shifting control of the area.
The reoccupation reflects a broader pattern of fluid frontlines in North Kivu, where armed groups frequently reposition in response to clashes, withdrawals, or tactical redeployments.
While some residents have welcomed the Wazalendo presence as a relative improvement in security conditions, others remain concerned that the situation could escalate again if AFC/M23 elements attempt to re-enter the area, potentially triggering renewed fighting.
The development comes amid continued instability across Walikale territory and wider parts of North Kivu, where civilian populations remain exposed to recurring insecurity, displacement risks, and unpredictable changes in territorial control.

body_en:
RUTSHURU, North Kivu March 29, 2026 - At least two people were killed and several others injured during an armed incursion in Kanyangohe/Masha, Bwito chiefdom, in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, according to local sources.
The attack occurred during the night of March 27-28, when unidentified armed men stormed the village located near Mwesso in neighboring Masisi territory.
Preliminary reports indicate that among the dead are a commander of a local self-defense group linked to AFC/M23 influence in the area and a civilian. Several wounded victims were treated at a nearby health facility, though the exact number of injured remains unclear.
The assault triggered panic in the area, forcing residents to flee toward Mwesso and surrounding localities in search of safety.
The incident comes amid heightened insecurity in Rutshuru territory, where armed violence continues to affect civilian populations. It also occurs against the backdrop of reported withdrawals by AFC/M23 elements from several localities in North Kivu, a development that appears to be accompanied by renewed instability and sporadic attacks in some areas.

body_en:
MASISI, North Kivu March 29, 2026 - Intense fighting broke out on Sunday in the Osso Banyungu sector of Masisi territory, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, pitting AFC/M23 fighters against Wazalendo self-defense groups, according to local sources.
The clashes reportedly began around 7:00 a.m., when AFC/M23 elements launched coordinated assaults targeting Wazalendo positions near Kazinga and Ngululu. Both localities had been under Wazalendo control in recent weeks and are now at the center of renewed fighting as each side attempts to consolidate or reclaim territory.
Residents reported sustained exchanges of heavy and light weapons fire throughout the day, with gunfire audible across multiple surrounding villages. The violence also affected areas bordering Walikale territory, deepening panic among civilian populations.
The renewed hostilities come amid a volatile security landscape in North Kivu, where reported AFC/M23 withdrawals from parts of Walikale, Lubero, and Rutshuru contrast with continued fighting in Masisi, where no signs of de-escalation have been observed.
Civilians remain exposed to the violence, with many expressing fear of further escalation as armed groups continue to contest control of strategic rural areas in the province.

title: AFC/M23 Describes Troop Movements as “Strategic Rotation,” Kinshasa Questions Intentions
excerpt: Goma, DRC, March 29, 2026 - The AFC/M23 movement says recent withdrawals observed from several front-line positions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo are part of what it describes as a “normal strategic rotation,” amid ongoing uncertainty over the security situation in Nort
title_en: AFC/M23 Describes Troop Movements as “Strategic Rotation,” Kinshasa Questions Intentions
excerpt_en: Goma, DRC, March 29, 2026 - The AFC/M23 movement says recent withdrawals observed from several front-line positions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo are part of what it describes as a “normal strategic rotation,” amid ongoing uncertainty over the security situation in Nort
body_en:
Goma, DRC, March 29, 2026 - The AFC/M23 movement says recent withdrawals observed from several front-line positions in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo are part of what it describes as a “normal strategic rotation,” amid ongoing uncertainty over the security situation in North and South Kivu.
In a statement issued Saturday, March 28, spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka said the troop movements recorded in multiple areas are routine redeployments within the group’s structure.
He described the activity as part of a “normal and strategic rotation of units of the Congolese Revolutionary Army (ARC),” adding that the movement remains committed to what it calls confidence-building measures under the ongoing peace framework.
The AFC/M23 also reaffirmed its stated commitment to civilian protection and said it remains prepared to respond to threats on the ground.
The explanation comes amid heightened attention to recent shifts in territorial presence reported in parts of Walikale, Rutshuru, and Lubero, where local sources have noted withdrawals or repositioning of armed elements in recent days.
However, the government of the Democratic Republic of Congo has expressed skepticism about the group’s claims.
Government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya said Kinshasa is closely monitoring the situation but remains focused on what it considers the core issue: the presence of foreign-linked armed forces on Congolese territory.
He said the government expects a “definitive withdrawal” rather than what it views as tactical or temporary movements, adding that similar redeployments have been observed in the past without leading to lasting de-escalation.
The exchanges take place against the backdrop of the stalled Doha peace process, which was intended to advance implementation of a broader framework agreement signed in late 2025.
Although initial progress had been recorded under the agreement, including early protocol signings, negotiations have since slowed, with no substantive new rounds reported in recent weeks.
Diplomatic sources have cited both regional tensions and logistical constraints affecting mediation efforts, while officials in Kinshasa maintain that they remain committed to the process but want clearer guarantees on implementation.
Despite the diplomatic track, fighting and local insecurity continue in several areas of eastern DRC, with residents frequently reporting shifting frontlines, temporary withdrawals, and renewed clashes between AFC/M23 elements, Wazalendo fighters, and other armed groups.

title: FARDC Launches Operation Against FDLR, Calls for Surrender and Repatriation to Rwanda
excerpt: KISANGANI, Tshopo March 29, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have officially launched a new operation targeting elements of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a Rwandan armed group operating in eastern Congo. The announce
title_en: FARDC Launches Operation Against FDLR, Calls for Surrender and Repatriation to Rwanda
excerpt_en: KISANGANI, Tshopo March 29, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have officially launched a new operation targeting elements of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a Rwandan armed group operating in eastern Congo. The announce
body_en:
KISANGANI, Tshopo March 29, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have officially launched a new operation targeting elements of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), a Rwandan armed group operating in eastern Congo.
The announcement was made on Sunday, March 29, at Camp General Bauma in Kisangani by General Jacques Ychaligonza, who oversaw a military parade marking the start of the campaign.
The operation aims to identify, disarm, and repatriate FDLR fighters still present on Congolese territory. Addressing troops, General Ychaligonza urged members of the group to surrender, stating that they should lay down their weapons “whether willingly or by force” and return to their country of origin, Rwanda.
He emphasized that the operation prioritizes avoiding bloodshed, calling for voluntary surrender and describing Kisangani as a designated reception point for those who give up arms. According to military authorities, a prepared site in the city will host surrendered fighters before their repatriation.
The launch follows what the army described as a completed awareness phase aimed at encouraging defections from the FDLR ranks. Military officials said three battalions have already been assigned to the operation and are expected to be deployed in the coming days.
General Ychaligonza said the campaign is being conducted within the framework of the Washington Agreement (DRC-Rwanda peace framework), and stressed that international actors are expected to monitor its implementation.
He also reassured that surrendered fighters would be treated under supervised conditions before eventual repatriation.
Beyond the launch of the operation, the senior FARDC commander held a series of meetings with military leadership in the 3rd Defense Zone and Kisangani garrison officers, focusing on broader security coordination and stabilization efforts in the region.
The announcement comes amid ongoing security challenges across eastern DRC, where multiple armed groups remain active despite parallel military and diplomatic initiatives aimed at restoring stability.

The launch follows what the army described as a completed awareness phase aimed at encouraging defections from the FDLR ranks. Military officials said three battalions have already been assigned to the operation and are expected to be deployed in the coming days.
General Ychaligonza said the campaign is being conducted within the framework of the Washington Agreement (DRC-Rwanda peace framework), and stressed that international actors are expected to monitor its implementation.
He also reassured that surrendered fighters would be treated under supervised conditions before eventual repatriation.
Beyond the launch of the operation, the senior FARDC commander held a series of meetings with military leadership in the 3rd Defense Zone and Kisangani garrison officers, focusing on broader security coordination and stabilization efforts in the region.
The announcement comes amid ongoing security challenges across eastern DRC, where multiple armed groups remain active despite parallel military and diplomatic initiatives aimed at restoring stability.
