title: Victory Group Secures $15 Million to Expand Fish Farming Operations in Rwanda and Kenya
excerpt: April 14, 2026 - Fish farming company Victory Group, which operates in Rwanda and Kenya, has secured $15 million in new funding from AgDevCo to support the expansion of its aquaculture activities across both countries. The company, which owns Kivu Choice in Rwanda and Victory Far
title_en: Victory Group Secures $15 Million to Expand Fish Farming Operations in Rwanda and Kenya
excerpt_en: April 14, 2026 - Fish farming company Victory Group, which operates in Rwanda and Kenya, has secured $15 million in new funding from AgDevCo to support the expansion of its aquaculture activities across both countries. The company, which owns Kivu Choice in Rwanda and Victory Far
body_en:
April 14, 2026 - Fish farming company Victory Group, which operates in Rwanda and Kenya, has secured $15 million in new funding from AgDevCo to support the expansion of its aquaculture activities across both countries.
The company, which owns Kivu Choice in Rwanda and Victory Farms in Kenya, said the financing will be used to scale up production capacity and strengthen its distribution network, with the aim of improving consistent access to fish in regional markets.
The funding is structured as a loan with the option for conversion into equity, according to the company.
Victory Group operates major fish farming sites on Lake Victoria in Kenya and Lake Kivu in Rwanda, where it produces and supplies tilapia to a growing network of traders and distributors.
In Rwanda, Kivu Choice Chief Executive Officer Emmanuel Bahizi said the company aims to significantly expand production capacity, targeting an increase from 9,000 tonnes to 30,000 tonnes annually by 2029. The expansion is also expected to raise employment from 700 to 1,200 workers.
Founded in 2015 by Joseph Rehmann and Steve Moran, Victory Group has positioned its long-term strategy around expanding access to affordable protein across Africa, with ambitions to reach up to 2 billion consumers over the next two decades.
The company integrates production, processing, distribution, and retail operations within a vertically structured business model.
AgDevCo Chief Investment Officer John Jakobsson said the additional financing reflects continued investor confidence in the company’s performance and growth trajectory.
“This continued funding demonstrates our confidence in Victory Group’s leadership and its ability to scale,” he said.
The latest investment follows previous funding rounds, including $4 million in 2021 from AgDevCo and an additional $35 million in 2023 from Creadev, underscoring sustained investor interest in the company’s expansion strategy.

Rwanda April 15, 2026 - Rwanda’s Chamber of Deputies has called on the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MINICOM) to urgently address persistent challenges affecting cooperatives, particularly delays in inspections that lawmakers say are undermining their performance and sustainability.
The recommendation was adopted on April 14, 2026, following the presentation of a report by the parliamentary Committee on Governance, Gender Equality and related matters during a plenary session.
Presenting the findings, Committee Chairperson Deputy Nabahire Anastase acknowledged that Rwanda has established a comprehensive framework for cooperative management, including a national policy, relevant legislation, and supervisory institutions. However, he noted that significant gaps remain in implementation.
“These shortcomings have led to serious consequences, including poor management, weak performance, and financial losses affecting cooperative members, as highlighted in the 2024/2025 report of the Office of the Ombudsman,” he said.
Data from the Rwanda Cooperatives Regulatory Authority (RCA) indicates that out of approximately 11,000 registered cooperatives, more than 4,200 are currently inactive.
According to the committee, one of the primary causes of these challenges is the prolonged absence of regular inspections and advisory support. Lawmakers noted that some cooperatives have gone more than 17 years without any formal inspection.
In response, the Chamber of Deputies has instructed MINICOM to develop and implement measures to address these delays, improve oversight mechanisms, and strengthen the functioning of cooperatives.
The ministry has been given a deadline of three months to report back on the steps taken to resolve the issue, with the aim of restoring efficiency, accountability, and public confidence in the cooperative sector.

title_en: Cholera Outbreak Worsens in Burundi as Authorities Enforce Sanctions
excerpt_en: Bujumbura, 6 April 2026 - Burundi is grappling with a worsening outbreak of cholera, with cases continuing to rise amid limited access to clean water and environmental contamination following recent floods. Since the beginning of 2026, health authorities have recorded at least 3,
body_en:
Bujumbura, 6 April 2026 - Burundi is grappling with a worsening outbreak of cholera, with cases continuing to rise amid limited access to clean water and environmental contamination following recent floods.
Since the beginning of 2026, health authorities have recorded at least 3,500 cases nationwide, with a sharp increase observed in recent weeks. In just three days, 38 new infections were reported, with patients receiving treatment at the Prince Régent Charles Hospital. Among them, 18 cases originated from heavily affected areas including Bubanza and Bukirasazi.
In response, the government has introduced stricter measures to curb the spread of the disease. The ministries of health, security, and economy have announced sanctions against individuals failing to comply with hygiene regulations, with the measures taking effect on 6 April.
Health Minister Lydwine Baradahana stated that the sanctions are intended to enforce existing public health laws and strengthen efforts to contain the outbreak, which has already mobilized significant government resources.
Authorities attribute the rapid spread of the disease to several factors, including the consumption of contaminated water, unsafe handling of septic systems, and illegal water connections to main supply lines.
Over the past three months, the Burundian government, alongside its partners, has allocated approximately 3 billion Burundian francs to combat the outbreak, funding patient care as well as public awareness and emergency response initiatives.

title: Rising Mental Health Concerns Among Rwandan University Students Amid Financial Strain
excerpt: Kigali April 12, 2026 - Mental health challenges are increasingly emerging as a major public concern in Rwanda, with growing reports indicating that a significant portion of the population has experienced psychological distress linked to depression, anxiety, stress, and substance
title_en: Rising Mental Health Concerns Among Rwandan University Students Amid Financial Strain
excerpt_en: Kigali April 12, 2026 - Mental health challenges are increasingly emerging as a major public concern in Rwanda, with growing reports indicating that a significant portion of the population has experienced psychological distress linked to depression, anxiety, stress, and substance
body_en:
Kigali April 12, 2026 - Mental health challenges are increasingly emerging as a major public concern in Rwanda, with growing reports indicating that a significant portion of the population has experienced psychological distress linked to depression, anxiety, stress, and substance abuse.
Health professionals note that approximately one in five people in Rwanda has been affected by some form of mental health condition. The country’s primary psychiatric treatment facility, Ndera Neuropsychiatric Teaching Hospital, has reported sustained pressure on its services. Operating for nearly 57 years, the hospital has seen patient numbers exceed capacity, reaching about 116% occupancy. In the 2024/2025 period alone, it received 119,859 patients, representing a 17.7% increase compared to the previous year.
University students highlight growing pressures
University students, particularly at the University of Rwanda, report that academic and financial difficulties are contributing to worsening mental health conditions. Students from the Faculty of Medicine in Remera cite limited resources and financial strain as key stress factors that, in some cases, lead to severe depression and dropout risks.
These concerns were raised during discussions held on April 1, 2026, during activities marking Public Health Week. Students described a combination of academic pressure, financial hardship, and challenging living conditions as major contributors to psychological distress.
One student, Amani Joyeuse, explained that the financial support provided to students is often insufficient to meet basic living costs.
“If we are given a scholarship of 40,000 Frw, the cost of food at nearby restaurants is higher than what the government provides. How can we avoid mental problems?” the student said.
Other students reported additional challenges, including compulsory internships or field placements in distant locations, which further strain limited financial resources. Some described difficulties in adapting to new living environments and the psychological impact of poverty and instability.
Another student, Amina, noted that many students are forced to seek additional income sources alongside their studies to supplement their stipends. Similarly, Pontient Ukwivikasa highlighted the high cost of living in Kigali, particularly housing, where rent for a small room can reach around 50,000 Rwandan francs per month, exceeding the monthly student allowance.
Institutional response and government concern
In response to these challenges, a lecturer at the University of Rwanda’s Faculty of Medicine, Prof. Erigene Rutayisire, stated that the institution has established a dedicated unit to study student mental health and develop preventive measures.
“We have a department responsible for conducting research on the mental health of students to monitor these issues and find solutions for both students and the general public,” he said.
The Ministry of Education has also acknowledged the growing concern. Minister Joseph Nsengimana indicated that plans are underway to introduce expanded counseling services in educational institutions to better support students experiencing psychological distress.
His remarks followed recent incidents involving student deaths, including a case reported on March 24, 2026, at Tumba College of Vocational and Technical Education in Rulindo, where a 20-year-old student was found dead in a dormitory. Authorities have indicated that investigations are ongoing, while emphasizing that mental health issues may be a contributing factor in some cases.
The minister added that the government is reviewing additional support measures for students, including strengthened psychosocial services, to complement existing financial assistance programs.
“We must ensure that students in higher education are not only financially supported but also psychologically supported through counseling and related services,” he said.
Authorities say the issue of student mental health remains under review as part of broader efforts to improve well-being in Rwanda’s education system.

title: Rwanda Among Countries Set to Receive Long-Acting HIV Prevention Drug
excerpt: April 15, 2026 - Rwanda is among a group of countries expected to benefit from the expanded rollout of a long-acting HIV prevention drug as part of a global initiative led by the United States and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. The program aims to make t
title_en: Rwanda Among Countries Set to Receive Long-Acting HIV Prevention Drug
excerpt_en: April 15, 2026 - Rwanda is among a group of countries expected to benefit from the expanded rollout of a long-acting HIV prevention drug as part of a global initiative led by the United States and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. The program aims to make t
body_en:
April 15, 2026 - Rwanda is among a group of countries expected to benefit from the expanded rollout of a long-acting HIV prevention drug as part of a global initiative led by the United States and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
The program aims to make the drug, Lenacapavir, accessible to at least three million people by 2028. Developed by Gilead Sciences, the treatment has already been introduced in nine African countries, with plans underway to extend distribution to an additional 12 nations.
Alongside Rwanda, the next phase of the rollout is expected to include countries such as Dominican Republic, Fiji, Indonesia, Morocco, and Thailand.
The Global Fund signed an agreement with Gilead in July 2025 to supply at least two million doses of the drug over a five-year period to low- and middle-income countries.
Humanitarian organization Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) welcomed the initiative but cautioned that current distribution levels remain insufficient compared to global demand.
Lenacapavir is administered via injection twice a year and is designed to prevent HIV infection by inhibiting the virus’s ability to replicate in the body. Health experts highlight its potential advantage over daily oral preventive treatments, as its long-acting formulation may improve adherence among patients.
Global health stakeholders say the expansion of access to such treatments could play a significant role in reducing new HIV infections, particularly in regions with high prevalence rates.

title: Rubavu Mayor Says FDLR Deceived Residents Into Selling Land, as Hundreds Return from Eastern DRC
excerpt: April 17, 2026 - Authorities in Rubavu District say some residents were misled into selling their property by members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), who allegedly convinced them that they would soon take control of Rwanda. The remarks were made by R
title_en: Rubavu Mayor Says FDLR Deceived Residents Into Selling Land, as Hundreds Return from Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: April 17, 2026 - Authorities in Rubavu District say some residents were misled into selling their property by members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), who allegedly convinced them that they would soon take control of Rwanda. The remarks were made by R
body_en:
April 17, 2026 - Authorities in Rubavu District say some residents were misled into selling their property by members of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), who allegedly convinced them that they would soon take control of Rwanda.
The remarks were made by Rubavu Mayor Mulindwa Prosper on April 16, 2026, during the reception of Rwandan nationals who had returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo after being held in areas controlled by the armed group.
Return of civilians from eastern DRC
A total of 403 returnees-including 280 children, 105 women, and 18 men-entered Rwanda through the La Corniche border crossing between Rubavu and Goma. They were subsequently transferred to a temporary reception facility in Nyarushishi, Rusizi District, where they are receiving initial assistance.
The group is part of civilians who had been living in eastern DRC and were recently assisted in returning through coordination involving humanitarian actors.
Allegations of exploitation and misinformation
Mayor Mulindwa warned returnees to remain cautious of misinformation and what he described as manipulation by armed groups operating in eastern Congo.
He stated that some individuals had been persuaded to sell land and assets under the belief that armed groups would soon take control of Rwanda, leaving them impoverished as a result.
“The people you have been with were deceiving some Rwandans into believing they would attack and take over the country, encouraging them to sell their land and fall into poverty through false promises and harmful narratives,” he said.
He urged returnees to rely on official institutions and to share accurate information with relatives who remain outside the country, encouraging voluntary return.
Testimonies from returnees
Some returnees described difficult living conditions in eastern DRC, citing insecurity and lack of access to basic livelihoods.
One returnee, 25-year-old Niyonsenga Segasore, said life in the DRC was marked by fear and instability, making daily survival difficult.
Another returnee, 18-year-old Uwase Jeannette, said insecurity had severely affected agricultural activities, making it impossible to sustain livelihoods.
Reintegration support
Authorities confirmed that returnees are receiving reintegration assistance upon arrival, including financial support and basic supplies to help them restart their lives.
Officials say the program is part of ongoing efforts to facilitate the voluntary return and reintegration of Rwandans from conflict-affected areas in eastern DRC.

excerpt: Kigali April 17, 2026 - Streaming platform Netflix has released a new documentary focusing on the mountain gorillas of Rwanda’s Volcanoes National Park, in a production that highlights both wildlife conservation and community-based environmental efforts. Titled “Rwanda’s Mountain
title_en: Netflix Releases Documentary Spotlighting Rwanda’s Mountain Gorillas
excerpt_en: Kigali April 17, 2026 - Streaming platform Netflix has released a new documentary focusing on the mountain gorillas of Rwanda’s Volcanoes National Park, in a production that highlights both wildlife conservation and community-based environmental efforts. Titled “Rwanda’s Mountain
body_en:
Kigali April 17, 2026 - Streaming platform Netflix has released a new documentary focusing on the mountain gorillas of Rwanda’s Volcanoes National Park, in a production that highlights both wildlife conservation and community-based environmental efforts.
Titled “Rwanda’s Mountain Gorillas,” the film premiered on Netflix on Friday, April 17, 2026. It explores the behavior, social structure, and lineage of one of the world’s most endangered primate populations, with a particular focus on the Pablo gorilla family.
The documentary was produced by Silverback Films in collaboration with Appian Way Productions, an environmental-focused studio founded by actor Leonardo DiCaprio. The Rwanda Development Board (RDB) and the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund also contributed to the project.
The narration is provided by renowned British broadcaster David Attenborough, whose decades-long work on natural history includes early coverage of Rwanda’s gorillas in the 1979 BBC series Life on Earth.
Filmed across different seasons in Volcanoes National Park, the production captures the daily lives and natural behavior of the gorillas in their habitat.
According to the Rwanda Development Board, the release comes at a time when the country continues to record progress in gorilla conservation. Speaking on the film, RDB’s Director of Tourism, Irène Murerwa, said Rwanda’s conservation model has been built over more than two decades.
“For over 20 years, Rwanda has demonstrated a commitment to protecting its remaining gorilla population through a community-based approach and sustainable investment. This film provides an opportunity to share this story with the world in a way that emphasizes the science and human contribution behind it,” she said.
She also welcomed the collaboration with international production partners, noting its contribution to both conservation awareness and tourism promotion.
Beyond its global streaming release, the documentary is scheduled for theatrical screening in London on April 21, 2026. Authorities say the project has also generated economic benefits for local communities involved in its production through employment and field support activities.

title: Kenya Rejects UN Allegations of Abuse by Police Deployed in Haiti

title_en: Kenya Rejects UN Allegations of Abuse by Police Deployed in Haiti
excerpt_en: Nairobi, April 9, 2026 - The Kenyan government has formally rejected allegations by the United Nations that its police officers committed sexual abuse while deployed in Haiti, according to official correspondence sent this week. In a letter addressed to UN Secretary-General Antón
body_en:
Nairobi, April 9, 2026 - The Kenyan government has formally rejected allegations by the United Nations that its police officers committed sexual abuse while deployed in Haiti, according to official correspondence sent this week.
In a letter addressed to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Kenya’s Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi stated that national investigations had found the accusations to be unfounded.
“The allegations have been found to be baseless. We have conducted an impartial investigation and shared the findings with all stakeholders, including the UN Human Rights Office,” the letter said, according to reports.
Mudavadi indicated that the inquiry was carried out by competent Kenyan authorities and that its conclusions had been communicated to relevant international bodies.
The response follows a report by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, which alleged that Kenyan police officers participating in a multinational security mission in Haiti were involved in the sexual abuse of four girls, including minors aged 12 and 16.
Kenyan forces have been deployed to Haiti since 2024 as part of an international effort to support local authorities in addressing armed violence and restoring security. Kenya has taken a leading role in coordinating the multinational mission, which includes contributions from several other countries.
The case highlights ongoing concerns surrounding accountability and conduct in international peace support operations, particularly in contexts involving vulnerable civilian populations.

title: AFC/M23 Sends Delegation to Peace Talks, Accuses DRC of Ongoing Attacks
excerpt: Goma, April 9, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has announced the dispatch of an envoy to upcoming peace talks in Switzerland, while accusing the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of continuing military operations in areas under its control. In a statement released o
title_en: AFC/M23 Sends Delegation to Peace Talks, Accuses DRC of Ongoing Attacks
excerpt_en: Goma, April 9, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has announced the dispatch of an envoy to upcoming peace talks in Switzerland, while accusing the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of continuing military operations in areas under its control. In a statement released o
body_en:
Goma, April 9, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has announced the dispatch of an envoy to upcoming peace talks in Switzerland, while accusing the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of continuing military operations in areas under its control.
In a statement released on April 9, AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka alleged that Congolese armed forces had intensified attacks since April 8 in the Masisi territory, particularly in the localities of Nyabyondo and Gahira. He claimed that the operations involved the use of aircraft and heavy weaponry in densely populated areas.
“The attacks continue with alarming intensity, causing the population to live in constant fear and insecurity,” Kanyuka said.
The coalition said it had communicated its concerns to mediators, including the government of Qatar, which is facilitating dialogue between the parties, as well as to international stakeholders such as the African Union and the United States.
AFC/M23 accused Kinshasa of pursuing a dual approach-publicly supporting negotiations while continuing military operations on the ground. The group reiterated its stated preference for a political resolution to the conflict but said it would continue to defend territories and civilian populations under its control.
Peace talks are scheduled to take place in Switzerland from April 13 to 17, amid broader regional and international pressures. Organizers have indicated that logistical adjustments to the talks were made in part due to ongoing instability in the Middle East, which has affected mediation efforts previously hosted in Qatar.

title: UNECA Chief Warns of Economic Impact of Middle East Crisis, Urges Strategic Shift for Africa
excerpt: April 9, 2026 - The Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, Claver Gatete, has warned that ongoing tensions in the Middle East are exerting significant pressure on African economies, particularly through rising energy costs and disruptions to glo
title_en: UNECA Chief Warns of Economic Impact of Middle East Crisis, Urges Strategic Shift for Africa
excerpt_en: April 9, 2026 - The Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, Claver Gatete, has warned that ongoing tensions in the Middle East are exerting significant pressure on African economies, particularly through rising energy costs and disruptions to glo
body_en:
April 9, 2026 - The Executive Secretary of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, Claver Gatete, has warned that ongoing tensions in the Middle East are exerting significant pressure on African economies, particularly through rising energy costs and disruptions to global trade routes.
Speaking at the 58th session of African ministers of finance, planning, and economic development, Gatete emphasized that instability in the region is already affecting oil prices and trade flows, with broader implications for economic stability across the continent.
“The ongoing conflict in the Middle East is having a negative impact on the energy market and trade in general, and has serious implications,” he said.
Gatete highlighted the vulnerability of many African economies, noting that a large share of petroleum imports-particularly in eastern and southern Africa-originates from the Middle East. Prolonged disruptions, he warned, could force countries to seek alternative supply routes and markets.
He pointed to the strategic importance of global maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, suggesting that any sustained blockage could reshape international trade patterns. In such a scenario, he argued, Africa could position itself as an alternative corridor for global trade.
Despite the challenges, Gatete also underlined emerging opportunities for the continent. He called on African governments to accelerate structural transformation by prioritizing sustainable development, improving the quality of public investment, and strengthening economic resilience.
He stressed the importance of aligning fiscal policies, debt management, and investment strategies with long-term development goals, while also promoting innovation, technology adoption, and more efficient use of financial resources.
The UNECA chief concluded by urging African countries to turn current global disruptions into opportunities for reform and growth, positioning the continent as a more integrated and competitive player in the global economy.

title: RIB Arrests 63-Year-Old Genocide Convict in Karongi District
excerpt: Rwanda April 14, 2026 -The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has announced the arrest of Murakaza Valens, 63, from Karongi District, who is accused of participating in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and had previously been sentenced by a Gacaca court. According to authoritie
title_en: RIB Arrests 63-Year-Old Genocide Convict in Karongi District
excerpt_en: Rwanda April 14, 2026 -The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has announced the arrest of Murakaza Valens, 63, from Karongi District, who is accused of participating in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and had previously been sentenced by a Gacaca court. According to authoritie
body_en:
Rwanda April 14, 2026 -The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has announced the arrest of Murakaza Valens, 63, from Karongi District, who is accused of participating in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and had previously been sentenced by a Gacaca court.
According to authorities, Murakaza was convicted by the Gacaca Court of Kavumu Sector on August 24, 2011, and sentenced to 15 years in prison. He is alleged to have evaded enforcement of the sentence for several years before his arrest.
Officials said he was located in Rutabi Village, Rutabi Cell, Twumba Sector, where he was apprehended following information that led investigators to his whereabouts. He is currently being held at the Twumba RIB station as his case file is prepared for submission to the prosecution service, which is expected to bring the matter before court for enforcement of the sentence.
The case is linked to crimes committed during the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi. Under Rwandan law, genocide is classified as an imprescriptible crime, meaning it does not expire over time.
Authorities noted that genocide includes acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. These acts may include killing members of the group, causing serious physical or psychological harm, deliberately inflicting conditions of life intended to bring about destruction, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children.
RIB spokesperson Dr. Murangira B. Thierry reiterated the institution’s commitment to bringing perpetrators of serious crimes to justice, stressing that genocide-related offences remain prosecutable regardless of how much time has passed.
He urged the public to reject violence and emphasized that individuals implicated in such crimes will continue to be pursued and held accountable under the law.

title: Questions Mount Over Death of Former Communications Minister
excerpt: Burundi, Bujumbura April 18, 2026 - Uncertainty is growing in Burundi following the death of Gabby Bugaga, the former Minister of Communications and Information, as conflicting accounts emerge over the circumstances surrounding his passing on April 16, 2026. The Burundian governm
title_en: Questions Mount Over Death of Former Communications Minister
excerpt_en: Burundi, Bujumbura April 18, 2026 - Uncertainty is growing in Burundi following the death of Gabby Bugaga, the former Minister of Communications and Information, as conflicting accounts emerge over the circumstances surrounding his passing on April 16, 2026. The Burundian governm
body_en:
Burundi, Bujumbura April 18, 2026 - Uncertainty is growing in Burundi following the death of Gabby Bugaga, the former Minister of Communications and Information, as conflicting accounts emerge over the circumstances surrounding his passing on April 16, 2026.
The Burundian government has maintained that Bugaga, who served in office from August 2025 until the day of his death, was killed in a road traffic accident. However, alternative accounts circulating within political and human rights circles have raised suspicions that he may have been assassinated.
According to initial reports, Bugaga’s vehicle was discovered parked in a palm grove in the Kivoga area along the Bujumbura-Bubanza road. His body was found inside the front seat, with one leg reportedly hanging out of the vehicle’s left window. Witnesses who arrived at the scene are said to have repositioned the body, placing it upright inside the car.
Questions have also been raised over the absence of security personnel at the scene, despite claims that senior government officials in Burundi are typically accompanied by bodyguards at all times.
A close associate of the late minister told reporters that Bugaga had expressed fear for his safety prior to his death. The source, based in Europe, said the minister had been making arrangements to leave Burundi for Canada, but later abandoned the plan. He also claimed Bugaga had recently sought urgent assistance to relocate abroad.
Additional accounts suggest the minister had privately considered resigning, but was reportedly discouraged by acquaintances who feared political repercussions with the administration of President Évariste Ndayishimiye.
Human rights activist Pacifique Nininahazwe also raised concerns about inconsistencies in the official version of events. He pointed to irregularities involving the vehicle, including the absence of a license plate and the unusual positioning of the body. He further questioned reports that the car keys were found in Bugaga’s bag rather than in the ignition.
In a statement, government spokesperson Jérôme Niyonzima reiterated that Bugaga’s death was the result of a road accident, adding that no further investigation was necessary.
However, human rights organizations have pushed back against that position. Anschaire Nikoyagize, president of Ligue Iteka, said it would be premature to dismiss other possibilities and called for an independent investigation.
He noted that since President Ndayishimiye came to power in June 2020, thousands of deaths under unclear circumstances have been recorded in Burundi, arguing that this context warrants a thorough inquiry into Bugaga’s death.
As debate continues, the case has intensified scrutiny over political violence and accountability in Burundi’s public life.

The Burundian government has maintained that Bugaga, who served in office from August 2025 until the day of his death, was killed in a road traffic accident. However, alternative accounts circulating within political and human rights circles have raised suspicions that he may have been assassinated.
According to initial reports, Bugaga’s vehicle was discovered parked in a palm grove in the Kivoga area along the Bujumbura-Bubanza road. His body was found inside the front seat, with one leg reportedly hanging out of the vehicle’s left window. Witnesses who arrived at the scene are said to have repositioned the body, placing it upright inside the car.
Questions have also been raised over the absence of security personnel at the scene, despite claims that senior government officials in Burundi are typically accompanied by bodyguards at all times.
A close associate of the late minister told reporters that Bugaga had expressed fear for his safety prior to his death. The source, based in Europe, said the minister had been making arrangements to leave Burundi for Canada, but later abandoned the plan. He also claimed Bugaga had recently sought urgent assistance to relocate abroad.
Additional accounts suggest the minister had privately considered resigning, but was reportedly discouraged by acquaintances who feared political repercussions with the administration of President Évariste Ndayishimiye.
Human rights activist Pacifique Nininahazwe also raised concerns about inconsistencies in the official version of events. He pointed to irregularities involving the vehicle, including the absence of a license plate and the unusual positioning of the body. He further questioned reports that the car keys were found in Bugaga’s bag rather than in the ignition.
In a statement, government spokesperson Jérôme Niyonzima reiterated that Bugaga’s death was the result of a road accident, adding that no further investigation was necessary.
However, human rights organizations have pushed back against that position. Anschaire Nikoyagize, president of Ligue Iteka, said it would be premature to dismiss other possibilities and called for an independent investigation.
He noted that since President Ndayishimiye came to power in June 2020, thousands of deaths under unclear circumstances have been recorded in Burundi, arguing that this context warrants a thorough inquiry into Bugaga’s death.

title: Former Burundian Vice President Questions Presence of Rwandan Troops in Eastern DRC

excerpt_en: Bujumbura, 6 April 2026 - Former Burundian Vice President Gaston Sindimwo has stated that, based on his own assessment, there is no clear evidence of the presence of Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) troops in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Speaking during an interview broadc
body_en:
Bujumbura, 6 April 2026 - Former Burundian Vice President Gaston Sindimwo has stated that, based on his own assessment, there is no clear evidence of the presence of Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) troops in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Speaking during an interview broadcast on the African TV YouTube channel, Sindimwo said he had not personally seen proof supporting claims that Rwandan forces are operating inside Congolese territory. “To this day, I have not seen that the RDF is in Congo,” he said when asked whether such forces could withdraw from the region.
He emphasized that his position was based on personal observation and analysis rather than formal investigation. “I am not a judge, I have not conducted any investigations; I am only stating what I have analyzed, what I have seen,” he added.
Sindimwo also cast doubt on reports alleging the presence of Rwandan troops, arguing that publication by bodies affiliated with the United Nations does not automatically guarantee accuracy. He suggested that such reports can sometimes generate unnecessary alarm.
The government of Rwanda has consistently denied deploying troops to the DRC, maintaining that its actions have been limited to reinforcing border security to prevent attacks by armed groups threatening its territory.
According to Sindimwo, these measures are more likely defensive in nature, aimed at neutralizing potential threats along the border rather than indicating a military presence in the DRC.
He added, however, that if Rwandan troops were indeed operating in Congolese territory, evidence such as captured soldiers would be expected to substantiate such claims.

title: Rwandan Officials Denounce Youth Recruitment into Armed Groups Along DRC Border
excerpt: Rubavu, 7 April 2026 - Local authorities in western Rwanda have raised concerns over past cases of youth being misled into joining armed groups operating across the border in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while reporting a recent decline in such incidents. Nzayisenga Jean
title_en: Rwandan Officials Denounce Youth Recruitment into Armed Groups Along DRC Border
excerpt_en: Rubavu, 7 April 2026 - Local authorities in western Rwanda have raised concerns over past cases of youth being misled into joining armed groups operating across the border in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while reporting a recent decline in such incidents. Nzayisenga Jean
body_en:
Rubavu, 7 April 2026 - Local authorities in western Rwanda have raised concerns over past cases of youth being misled into joining armed groups operating across the border in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while reporting a recent decline in such incidents.
Nzayisenga Jean Pierre, head of Muti Village in Cyanzarwe Sector, Rubavu District, said some young people had previously left under false pretenses. “They told us they were going to farm or herd in Congo, but we later discovered they had joined armed groups,” he said, referring to militias such as the Wazalendo and the FDLR.
Speaking after a field visit by members of the RPF Inkotanyi, Nzayisenga noted that for over a year, no new cases of youth from his area joining such groups had been recorded. He attributed this change to improved border control and shifting dynamics in eastern DRC, particularly following the advance of the M23, which now controls key areas including the city of Goma.
According to Nzayisenga, authorities and residents have become more vigilant. In the past, some individuals attempting to return secretly were apprehended and handed over to security services. He added that several former recruits had since undergone rehabilitation and reintegrated into civilian life.
Local leaders emphasized the importance of civic education and national unity in preventing recruitment into armed groups. Me Niyonkuru Jean Aimé, president of the Cyanzarwe Sector Council, said awareness campaigns aim to discourage divisive ideologies and promote social cohesion.
Rubavu District Mayor Mulindwa Prosper echoed these concerns, linking past recruitment to lingering extremist ideologies tied to groups that fled Rwanda after the 1994 genocide. He stressed the need for continued vigilance along the border and education on national values to counter such influences.
As Rwanda marks the 31st anniversary of the genocide against the Tutsi, authorities in border sectors such as Bugeshi reported that dozens of residents previously recruited by armed groups had recently returned. Local officials said 60 individuals had been repatriated, including 44 who had joined Wazalendo and 14 associated with the FDLR.
Officials maintain that strengthened security measures and community engagement are key to preventing further recruitment and ensuring stability in border regions.

title: CNLG Highlights Key Pre-Genocide Events from 1991 to 1994
excerpt: Kigali, 7 April 2026 - Rwanda’s National Commission for the Fight against Genocide has outlined a series of key events between 1991 and 1994 that it says demonstrate the long-term planning and execution of the Genocide against the Tutsi. As part of ongoing commemoration efforts,
title_en: CNLG Highlights Key Pre-Genocide Events from 1991 to 1994
excerpt_en: Kigali, 7 April 2026 - Rwanda’s National Commission for the Fight against Genocide has outlined a series of key events between 1991 and 1994 that it says demonstrate the long-term planning and execution of the Genocide against the Tutsi. As part of ongoing commemoration efforts,
body_en:
Kigali, 7 April 2026 - Rwanda’s National Commission for the Fight against Genocide has outlined a series of key events between 1991 and 1994 that it says demonstrate the long-term planning and execution of the Genocide against the Tutsi.
As part of ongoing commemoration efforts, the commission is releasing historical records each month to shed light on the preparation, attempted implementation, and eventual execution of the genocide. The initiative aims to document evidence, clarify historical narratives, and identify those responsible.
According to the commission, events dating back to January 1991 marked an escalation in violence and anti-Tutsi persecution. Following an attack by the RPF Inkotanyi in Ruhengeri, authorities allegedly used the incident as justification for retaliatory killings targeting Tutsi civilians in the region.
The report also points to the role of foreign involvement during this period, particularly military support provided to the government of former President Juvénal Habyarimana. French troops deployed under Operation Noroît were said to have assisted government forces, reinforcing confidence within the regime at the time.
Throughout 1992, the commission highlights the arming of militia groups such as the Interahamwe, alongside the emergence of media outlets accused of spreading hate propaganda. These developments coincided with growing political tensions and resistance to power-sharing arrangements.
In January 1993, extremist figures within the government and military openly rejected the Arusha Accords, which aimed to end the conflict through a transitional government. Statements attributed to senior officials indicated an intention to prepare for mass violence, while organized killings of Tutsi civilians were reported in several regions.
The commission further notes that networks of military officers and political actors coordinated efforts to oppose the peace process and promote extremist ideology. Investigations conducted at the time by international experts concluded that senior authorities were implicated in orchestrating violence against Tutsi and political opponents.
By early 1994, preparations had intensified, with increased distribution of weapons, expansion of militia training, and widespread mobilization under the guise of civil defense. Demonstrations and propaganda campaigns were also used to inflame tensions, particularly in Kigali.
The CNLG maintains that these events form part of a broader pattern illustrating that the genocide was not spontaneous, but rather the result of sustained planning and coordination by elements within the former government and its allies.
The publication of these records comes as Rwanda and the international community continue activities marking the annual remembrance period, aimed at honoring victims and reinforcing commitments to prevent future atrocities.

title: Fighting Intensifies in South Kivu as AFC/M23 Reports Government Offensive
excerpt: South Kivu, 7 April 2026 - The AFC/M23 has accused forces aligned with the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of launching a series of major attacks across South Kivu province, escalating tensions in the conflict-hit eastern region. According to AFC/M23 spokespers
title_en: Fighting Intensifies in South Kivu as AFC/M23 Reports Government Offensive
excerpt_en: South Kivu, 7 April 2026 - The AFC/M23 has accused forces aligned with the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of launching a series of major attacks across South Kivu province, escalating tensions in the conflict-hit eastern region. According to AFC/M23 spokespers
body_en:
South Kivu, 7 April 2026 - The AFC/M23 has accused forces aligned with the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of launching a series of major attacks across South Kivu province, escalating tensions in the conflict-hit eastern region.
According to AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, the offensive began early on 7 April, with drone strikes reported in Mikenke and other densely populated areas of Minembwe commune. He alleged that the attacks resulted in civilian casualties, destruction of homes, and loss of livestock.
Further clashes were reported in areas including Lumbishi, Katale, and Tushunguti in Kalehe territory. The group claims that these operations targeted civilian-populated zones, describing them as violations of international humanitarian law.
The reported escalation follows recent remarks by President Félix Tshisekedi, who stated during a public event on 5 April that government forces would move to retake territories held by the AFC/M23.
In response, the rebel coalition has called on both the Congolese population and the international community to take note of what it describes as ongoing abuses against civilians in the region.
The AFC/M23, which controls significant areas in North and South Kivu, reiterated its position that it is prepared to continue its operations, stating that it would use all available means to pursue its objectives as fighting persists.

title: President Kagame Promotes Over 5,700 Police Officers
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda April 9, 2026 - Rwandan President Paul Kagame has approved the promotion of 5,741 officers within the Rwanda National Police, in a sweeping move affecting multiple ranks across the institution. According to an official announcement released on Thursday, five senior
title_en: President Kagame Promotes Over 5,700 Police Officers
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda April 9, 2026 - Rwandan President Paul Kagame has approved the promotion of 5,741 officers within the Rwanda National Police, in a sweeping move affecting multiple ranks across the institution. According to an official announcement released on Thursday, five senior
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda April 9, 2026 - Rwandan President Paul Kagame has approved the promotion of 5,741 officers within the Rwanda National Police, in a sweeping move affecting multiple ranks across the institution.
According to an official announcement released on Thursday, five senior officers were elevated to the rank of Commissioner of Police (CP): Emmanuel Karasi, Bertin Mutezintare, Jean Népomucène Mbonyumuvunyi, Barthélemy Rugwizangoga, and Fidèle Mugengana.
Ten officers were promoted to the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP), including Claude Bizimana, Adolphe Nyagatare, Rango Ndoli, Callixte Kalisa, Vincent Habintwali Bihigi, Antoine Munyampundu, Faustin Kalimba, Hodali Rwanyindo, Christian Safari, and Alexis Nyamwasa.
The promotions span both senior and junior ranks. Among senior officers, five were elevated from Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) to Commissioner of Police (CSP), 94 from Superintendent of Police (SP) retained or advanced within their rank, and 161 officers moved from Chief Inspector of Police (CIP) to SP. Additionally, 574 officers were promoted from Inspector of Police (IP) to CIP, while 17 advanced from Assistant Inspector of Police (AIP) to IP.
At the junior level, 282 officers were promoted from Staff Sergeant (S/SGT) to Chief Sergeant (C/SGT), while 763 advanced from Sergeant (SGT) to Staff Sergeant. A total of 1,886 corporals (CPL) were promoted to sergeant, and 1,949 police constables (PC) advanced to corporal.
The Rwanda National Police stated that the promotions are part of ongoing efforts to strengthen institutional capacity and recognize merit within the force.

title: Rwanda-DRC Tensions Rise After Minister Accuses Congolese Spokesperson of Hate Speech
excerpt: Kigali, April 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, Jean-Damascène Bizimana, has accused the Congolese government spokesperson, Patrick Muyaya, of promoting hate speech targeting Tutsi communities, escalating already strained relations between Rwanda
title_en: Rwanda-DRC Tensions Rise After Minister Accuses Congolese Spokesperson of Hate Speech
excerpt_en: Kigali, April 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, Jean-Damascène Bizimana, has accused the Congolese government spokesperson, Patrick Muyaya, of promoting hate speech targeting Tutsi communities, escalating already strained relations between Rwanda
body_en:
Kigali, April 9, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of National Unity and Civic Engagement, Jean-Damascène Bizimana, has accused the Congolese government spokesperson, Patrick Muyaya, of promoting hate speech targeting Tutsi communities, escalating already strained relations between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The remarks were made during commemorations marking the 32nd anniversary of the Genocide against the Tutsi, where Bizimana alleged that Muyaya had previously described Tutsis as “murderers” during a televised appearance on Télé 50.
Muyaya swiftly rejected the accusation, stating on the social media platform X that the claims were “a lie told on the day of remembrance.”
In response, Bizimana reiterated his position, referencing a July 2024 interview in which Muyaya discussed the long-running conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. The Rwandan minister argued that such statements contribute to dangerous narratives, warning that “genocide is always preceded by hate speech.”
He also criticized what he described as broader rhetoric from certain Congolese officials, drawing parallels with past figures accused of incitement. Bizimana cited historical examples to underline the potential consequences of inflammatory discourse, particularly in a region marked by recurring tensions and armed conflict.
The dispute comes amid ongoing instability in eastern DRC, where fighting involving armed groups, including the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda and the AFC/M23 coalition, continues to fuel diplomatic friction between Kinshasa and Kigali.
Muyaya has also recently commented on the presence and role of armed groups in the region, reportedly questioning the effectiveness of military approaches to addressing the FDLR, a group historically linked to individuals involved in the 1994 genocide.
The exchange highlights the sensitivity of public discourse around ethnicity and conflict in the Great Lakes region, where accusations of hate speech and genocide denial carry significant political and historical weight.

title: U.S. Issues Travel Warning for Nigeria Over Security Concerns
excerpt: Washington/Abuja, April 9, 2026 - The United States has urged its citizens to exercise heightened caution when traveling to Nigeria, citing persistent security threats including terrorism, kidnappings, and armed violence. In a statement released on April 8, the United States Emba
title_en: U.S. Issues Travel Warning for Nigeria Over Security Concerns
excerpt_en: Washington/Abuja, April 9, 2026 - The United States has urged its citizens to exercise heightened caution when traveling to Nigeria, citing persistent security threats including terrorism, kidnappings, and armed violence. In a statement released on April 8, the United States Emba
body_en:
Washington/Abuja, April 9, 2026 - The United States has urged its citizens to exercise heightened caution when traveling to Nigeria, citing persistent security threats including terrorism, kidnappings, and armed violence.
In a statement released on April 8, the United States Embassy in Nigeria warned that several regions of the country remain unstable and advised Americans to avoid travel to high-risk areas.
The advisory highlighted the possibility of attacks in public spaces such as markets, hotels, places of worship, schools, and other crowded locations. U.S. authorities also indicated that some areas have been classified under the highest risk level, with strong recommendations against all travel.
As part of precautionary measures, the embassy announced the suspension of certain visa processing services, urging applicants to monitor their communications for updates on delays or changes.
In addition, the U.S. government has begun reducing its diplomatic presence, with instructions for some personnel stationed in Abuja to depart the country amid the evolving security situation.
According to the advisory, multiple Nigerian states have been designated as particularly dangerous, including Plateau, Jigawa, Kwara, Niger, Taraba, as well as Borno and Yobe in the northeast-regions affected by insurgent activity and communal violence.
The United States maintains Nigeria at an elevated travel advisory level overall, warning that deteriorating security conditions could have broader implications, including potential impacts on economic activity and foreign investment.

title: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Prepare for Switzerland Peace Talks Amid Mutual Accusations
excerpt: April 10, 2026 - Delegations from the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the AFC/M23 coalition are expected to meet in Switzerland from April 13 to 17, 2026, for renewed peace talks aimed at addressing the conflict in eastern Congo. The discussions are being f
title_en: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Prepare for Switzerland Peace Talks Amid Mutual Accusations
excerpt_en: April 10, 2026 - Delegations from the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the AFC/M23 coalition are expected to meet in Switzerland from April 13 to 17, 2026, for renewed peace talks aimed at addressing the conflict in eastern Congo. The discussions are being f
body_en:
April 10, 2026 - Delegations from the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the AFC/M23 coalition are expected to meet in Switzerland from April 13 to 17, 2026, for renewed peace talks aimed at addressing the conflict in eastern Congo.
The discussions are being facilitated by Qatar, with logistical support from Swiss authorities. According to reports, Qatari representatives may participate remotely due to ongoing geopolitical constraints affecting earlier mediation arrangements in the region.
International actors are also expected to take part in the negotiations, including U.S. Special Advisor for African Affairs Massad Boulos, Deputy Head of MONUSCO operations Vivian van de Perre, and Executive Secretary of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region International Conference on the Great Lakes Region representative Mubita Luwabelwa.
The AFC/M23 delegation will be led by its permanent secretary Benjamin Mbonimpa, while the composition of the government delegation has not yet been disclosed.
A key focus of the talks is expected to be humanitarian access in conflict-affected areas, including the possible reopening of Goma International Airport, which has been under AFC/M23 control since January 2025. International partners have repeatedly called for improved access to facilitate relief operations for civilians.
The talks come amid continued mutual accusations between the two sides. AFC/M23 has accused government forces of ongoing attacks involving drones and heavy weapons in areas under its control, while the government maintains its position on restoring territorial authority and national sovereignty.
Previous agreements between the parties, including ceasefire monitoring mechanisms involving MONUSCO and regional forces, have yet to be fully implemented. Similarly, arrangements involving the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) for prisoner transfers and humanitarian coordination have seen limited progress.
Despite these challenges, mediators and international stakeholders continue to push for confidence-building measures, including prisoner exchanges and the operationalization of monitoring frameworks agreed in earlier rounds of negotiations.

title: AFC/M23 Accuses Kinshasa of Attacks Ahead of Switzerland Peace Talks
excerpt: Goma April 12, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of carrying out attacks against civilians in the Minembwe area, alleging that the operations are intended to undermine upcoming peace negotiations scheduled in Switzerla
title_en: AFC/M23 Accuses Kinshasa of Attacks Ahead of Switzerland Peace Talks
excerpt_en: Goma April 12, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of carrying out attacks against civilians in the Minembwe area, alleging that the operations are intended to undermine upcoming peace negotiations scheduled in Switzerla
body_en:
Goma April 12, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo of carrying out attacks against civilians in the Minembwe area, alleging that the operations are intended to undermine upcoming peace negotiations scheduled in Switzerland.
In a statement released by spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, the group claimed that Congolese forces conducted drone and artillery strikes between the night of April 11 and early April 12 in densely populated areas of Minembwe and surrounding localities.
Kanyuka described the operations as a “deliberate attempt to undermine the talks taking place in Switzerland,” adding that continued military activity ahead of negotiations reflects what the group sees as non-compliance with agreed ceasefire commitments.
The peace talks between the two parties are scheduled to take place from April 13 to 17, 2026, with mediation led by Qatar and logistical arrangements involving Swiss hosts, following earlier rounds of discussions held in Doha. Some reports indicate that parts of the dialogue may be conducted remotely, depending on security and logistical constraints.
The upcoming negotiations are expected to focus on humanitarian access, ceasefire implementation, and mechanisms to monitor compliance on the ground in eastern Congo, where fighting between government forces and the AFC/M23 coalition has continued.
The coalition maintains that continued military operations ahead of the talks risk derailing diplomatic efforts, while regional and international actors continue to press both sides to maintain conditions conducive to dialogue.

title: Commemorations Recall Massacres of Tutsi Civilians Across Rwanda (April 13, 1994 Events Highlighted)
excerpt: Rwanda April 13, 2026 - Commemorative accounts marking the events of April 13, 1994, recall a series of mass killings of Tutsi civilians across multiple locations in Rwanda during the genocide period. Testimonies and historical documentation describe coordinated attacks on civili
title_en: Commemorations Recall Massacres of Tutsi Civilians Across Rwanda (April 13, 1994 Events Highlighted)
excerpt_en: Rwanda April 13, 2026 - Commemorative accounts marking the events of April 13, 1994, recall a series of mass killings of Tutsi civilians across multiple locations in Rwanda during the genocide period. Testimonies and historical documentation describe coordinated attacks on civili
body_en:
Rwanda April 13, 2026 - Commemorative accounts marking the events of April 13, 1994, recall a series of mass killings of Tutsi civilians across multiple locations in Rwanda during the genocide period. Testimonies and historical documentation describe coordinated attacks on civilians who had sought refuge in churches, schools, hospitals, and public institutions.
Massacre at Saint André and surrounding religious sites, Nyamirambo (Kigali)
In Nyamirambo, thousands of Tutsi civilians who had taken refuge at Saint André College and nearby religious institutions, including Saint Charles Lwanga Church and Saint Joseph facilities, were killed.
Survivors’ accounts indicate that more than 2,000 people had gathered in these sites seeking protection after fleeing surrounding neighborhoods such as Butamwa, Nyakabanda, Rwezamenyo, and Biryogo. Many were later attacked despite having sought refuge in religious institutions.
Testimonies further indicate that after initial killings at Saint André and Saint Charles Lwanga, attackers moved to other nearby sites where additional civilians had gathered.
Kanyinya killings (Nyarugenge area)
In Kanyinya Sector, Tutsi civilians from surrounding areas reportedly sought refuge after being told they would be protected. However, accounts describe how they were later taken to isolated locations and killed in large numbers.
Only a small number of survivors, including children, are reported to have escaped.
Muhororo and Kibilira (Ngororero region)
In Muhororo and surrounding areas, killings occurred both before and during April 1994. Reports describe civilians being gathered on hillsides and attacked using various weapons.
Survivors recount that some civilians later sought refuge in churches and mission centers, where they were again targeted in subsequent attacks. Local authorities and armed groups are reported in testimonies to have coordinated operations in several locations.
Musha Catholic Parish (Kigali region)
Between April 12-13, 1994, Musha Catholic Parish became a site of mass killings. Survivors and historical records estimate that thousands of Tutsi civilians were killed after seeking refuge there.
Local administrative officials and militia groups are cited in testimonies as having played roles in organizing and executing the attacks, including violence against women and children prior to killings.
Rukara Catholic Parish (Kayonza)
At Rukara Parish, civilians who had taken refuge were also attacked in mid-April 1994. Initial killings were followed by further assaults on those remaining in the area.
Survivors report that local administrative and militia structures were involved in coordinating the attacks.
Ruharambuga (Nyamasheke)
In Ruharambuga, civilians were gathered in several locations before being killed. Some accounts describe mass killings in private homes and other sites, as well as the forced displacement and killing of children.
Testimonies also describe extreme brutality during and after the killings, including violence against women.
Nyakanyinya (Rusizi)
In Mururu Sector, Nyakanyinya became a site where large groups of displaced civilians were killed following coordinated attacks involving militia groups and local security forces.
Survivors recount that shelters such as schools and churches were also attacked, with civilians being forced out or killed inside.
Kirinda (Karongi)
Kirinda is described in accounts as a major site of killings where civilians who had taken refuge in hospitals and schools were later targeted.
Bodies were reportedly disposed of in nearby rivers and other locations. Survivors also describe roadblocks used to identify and kill civilians attempting to flee.
Gitwa Chapel (Rutsiro)
Gitwa Chapel served as a refuge for displaced civilians before becoming a site of mass killings between April 11-13, 1994.
Testimonies estimate that thousands of people were killed after attacks on the chapel and surrounding hills. Local administrative officials and armed groups are cited in accounts as having coordinated the operations.
Mbogo schools (Gikongoro region)
At Mbogo and surrounding schools, thousands of civilians were reportedly gathered and killed on April 13, 1994, in coordinated attacks involving militia groups and security forces.
Muhima “Esikariye” site (Kigali)
In Muhima, civilians were reportedly rounded up and killed between April 13-14, 1994. Accounts describe mass killings at roadblocks and disposal of bodies in unknown locations.
Broader pattern of violence
Across multiple regions, testimonies consistently describe coordinated attacks beginning in early April 1994, targeting Tutsi civilians in homes, public institutions, churches, schools, and hospitals.
These accounts are widely cited in historical documentation of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, which remains one of the most extensively documented mass atrocities of the 20th century.

Survivors recount that some civilians later sought refuge in churches and mission centers, where they were again targeted in subsequent attacks. Local authorities and armed groups are reported in testimonies to have coordinated operations in several locations.
Musha Catholic Parish (Kigali region)
Between April 12-13, 1994, Musha Catholic Parish became a site of mass killings. Survivors and historical records estimate that thousands of Tutsi civilians were killed after seeking refuge there.
Local administrative officials and militia groups are cited in testimonies as having played roles in organizing and executing the attacks, including violence against women and children prior to killings.
Rukara Catholic Parish (Kayonza)
At Rukara Parish, civilians who had taken refuge were also attacked in mid-April 1994. Initial killings were followed by further assaults on those remaining in the area.
Survivors report that local administrative and militia structures were involved in coordinating the attacks.
Ruharambuga (Nyamasheke)
In Ruharambuga, civilians were gathered in several locations before being killed. Some accounts describe mass killings in private homes and other sites, as well as the forced displacement and killing of children.
Testimonies also describe extreme brutality during and after the killings, including violence against women.
Nyakanyinya (Rusizi)
In Mururu Sector, Nyakanyinya became a site where large groups of displaced civilians were killed following coordinated attacks involving militia groups and local security forces.
Survivors recount that shelters such as schools and churches were also attacked, with civilians being forced out or killed inside.
Kirinda (Karongi)
Kirinda is described in accounts as a major site of killings where civilians who had taken refuge in hospitals and schools were later targeted.
Bodies were reportedly disposed of in nearby rivers and other locations. Survivors also describe roadblocks used to identify and kill civilians attempting to flee.
Gitwa Chapel (Rutsiro)
Gitwa Chapel served as a refuge for displaced civilians before becoming a site of mass killings between April 11-13, 1994.
Testimonies estimate that thousands of people were killed after attacks on the chapel and surrounding hills. Local administrative officials and armed groups are cited in accounts as having coordinated the operations.
Mbogo schools (Gikongoro region)
At Mbogo and surrounding schools, thousands of civilians were reportedly gathered and killed on April 13, 1994, in coordinated attacks involving militia groups and security forces.
Muhima “Esikariye” site (Kigali)
In Muhima, civilians were reportedly rounded up and killed between April 13-14, 1994. Accounts describe mass killings at roadblocks and disposal of bodies in unknown locations.
Broader pattern of violence
Across multiple regions, testimonies consistently describe coordinated attacks beginning in early April 1994, targeting Tutsi civilians in homes, public institutions, churches, schools, and hospitals.
These accounts are widely cited in historical documentation of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, which remains one of the most extensively documented mass atrocities of the 20th century.

title_en: Burundi Reinforces Military Presence in Eastern DRC Amid Ongoing FightingApril 15, 2026 - Burundi has deployed additional troops to South Kivu province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in a move aimed at reinforcing ongoing military operations against armed groups active in the region.
excerpt_en: According to local reports, a military vessel carrying Burundian soldiers and equipment was observed departing from the port of Rumonge on Lake Tanganyika on the evening of April 14, 2026. The deployment is believed to be heading toward Baraka in Fizi territory, a key operational
body_en:
According to local reports, a military vessel carrying Burundian soldiers and equipment was observed departing from the port of Rumonge on Lake Tanganyika on the evening of April 14, 2026. The deployment is believed to be heading toward Baraka in Fizi territory, a key operational area in South Kivu.
Sources indicate that the newly deployed troops are expected to be sent to frontline areas including Gakenke, Mikenke, Kalingi, and Mulima, where fighting has intensified in recent months.
Burundian forces are operating alongside Congolese troops and local militias, commonly referred to as Wazalendo, in efforts to regain control of strategic areas such as Minembwe. The area is considered a stronghold of the Twirwaneho group, which emerged claiming to defend the Banyamulenge community.
By December 2025, Burundi was reported to have deployed more than 20,000 troops in South Kivu, although some units were later withdrawn following territorial advances by the AFC/M23 coalition in parts of Uvira territory, including the city of Uvira.
Recent developments suggest a renewed military push by Burundian forces, with reports indicating a return to active operations aimed at recapturing lost positions and stabilizing contested areas.
Meanwhile, the AFC/M23 alliance has continued to accuse Congolese government forces and their allies-including Burundian troops, Wazalendo militias, and other armed groups-of carrying out attacks in several areas across South Kivu, including Gakenke, Kalingi, and Bidegu. These claims have not been independently verified.
The escalation comes as diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict continue, including ongoing talks in Switzerland launched on April 13, 2026. However, persistent fighting on the ground underscores the fragile nature of the peace process and the deep mistrust between the parties involved.
AFC/M23 representatives have reiterated their stated preference for a political resolution to the conflict, while maintaining that they will continue to defend areas under their control amid ongoing hostilities.

title_en: Kenyan Truck Driver Killed After Hijacking in Bunia
excerpt_en: Ituri April 15, 2026 - A Kenyan truck driver, Edwin Njuguna Ngugi, was killed in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), following a hijacking incident that has raised concerns about security conditions along key transport routes. Njuguna,
body_en:
Ituri April 15, 2026 - A Kenyan truck driver, Edwin Njuguna Ngugi, was killed in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), following a hijacking incident that has raised concerns about security conditions along key transport routes.
Njuguna, who originated from the Busia region of Kenya, had reportedly warned his family about deteriorating security conditions shortly before his death. In a conversation on April 2, 2026, he indicated that he had entered a high-risk area and feared for his safety after encountering armed individuals attempting to rob him.
According to accounts from relatives, the driver initially avoided an attack after the arrival of Congolese soldiers. However, in a subsequent development, he reportedly sought protection from the same soldiers when he feared further threats.
Family members allege that instead of providing protection, the soldiers took his money and left the scene, abandoning him in a vulnerable situation. These claims have not been independently verified.
Communication with Njuguna was lost on April 3, when his phone became unreachable. Several days later, fellow Kenyan drivers traveling through Bunia discovered his body along a roadside. They documented the scene and circulated the information through transport networks in an effort to identify him and locate his family.
Preliminary reports suggest that the driver may have been killed by armed assailants who also looted the cargo he was transporting. His body was later transferred to a local hospital in Bunia, while the truck was found abandoned and damaged.
Njuguna’s family was informed of his death approximately 10 days later. They have since appealed to the Kenyan authorities for assistance in repatriating his body, citing financial and logistical challenges in traveling to the DRC.
The incident underscores ongoing security challenges faced by transport operators in eastern DRC, where armed groups and criminal activity continue to pose risks along major trade corridors.

title_en: Rwanda Tells UN Security Council Peace in Great Lakes Depends on Dismantling FDLRApril 16, 2026 ; Rwanda has told the United Nations Security Council that lasting peace in the Great Lakes region will not be achieved unless the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) is fully dismantled in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
excerpt_en: The message was delivered on April 15, 2026, by Rwanda’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Robert Kayinamura, during a Security Council session focused on regional peace and cooperation initiatives. Kayinamura said persistent insecurity in the region must be addressed at
body_en:
The message was delivered on April 15, 2026, by Rwanda’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Robert Kayinamura, during a Security Council session focused on regional peace and cooperation initiatives.
Kayinamura said persistent insecurity in the region must be addressed at its root causes, including the continued presence of armed groups and ongoing violence affecting civilian populations.
He cited hate speech, targeted attacks, and violence against Kinyarwanda-speaking communities in the DRC, including the Banyamulenge, as key concerns contributing to instability.
According to the Rwandan envoy, the continued existence of the FDLR in eastern DRC remains a major obstacle to peace and regional security.
“This group is a problem for Rwanda and for the security of the region. Its continued existence is contrary to the decisions taken under the framework we are discussing. There is no credible path to peace unless it is effectively and irreversibly dismantled,” he said.
Rwanda also argued that the DRC must apply security measures consistently across all armed groups, without selective enforcement or exclusion of certain actors.
Kayinamura added that the issue of the FDLR has been repeatedly raised in regional and international peace processes, including commitments made under earlier agreements.
He referenced the 2013 regional framework on peace and cooperation and a subsequent agreement signed in Washington in June 2025, under which the DRC government reportedly committed to dismantling the group.
Rwanda further stated that despite these commitments, the FDLR remains active in eastern DRC and continues to pose a threat to regional stability.
The remarks come amid ongoing tensions in eastern Congo, where multiple armed groups operate alongside government forces and regional actors in a complex and protracted conflict environment.

title: AFC/M23 to Participate in Expanded International Ceasefire Monitoring Mechanism for Eastern DRC
excerpt: April 16, 2026 ; The AFC/M23 armed group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is set to be included in a restructured international mechanism tasked with monitoring the implementation of a ceasefire agreement, according to developments emerging from ongoing pea
title_en: AFC/M23 to Participate in Expanded International Ceasefire Monitoring Mechanism for Eastern DRC
excerpt_en: April 16, 2026 ; The AFC/M23 armed group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is set to be included in a restructured international mechanism tasked with monitoring the implementation of a ceasefire agreement, according to developments emerging from ongoing pea
body_en:
April 16, 2026 ; The AFC/M23 armed group operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is set to be included in a restructured international mechanism tasked with monitoring the implementation of a ceasefire agreement, according to developments emerging from ongoing peace negotiations.
The arrangement forms part of progress reported in talks between the DRC government and AFC/M23, facilitated by Qatar and supported by the United States and the African Union (AU), within broader efforts to stabilize the Great Lakes region.
The existing regional monitoring framework, known as the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism (EJVM), currently oversees security incidents along borders in the region and investigates violations when clashes occur between states.
Under the proposed reform, the mechanism would be upgraded into an expanded structure referred to as EJVM+, extending its mandate beyond state borders to include areas controlled by armed groups and their alliances.
New composition and mandate
According to the agreement discussed on April 14, 2026, during ongoing peace talks in Switzerland, the restructured body would include representatives from both the DRC government and AFC/M23, alongside international support from United Nations peacekeeping forces (MONUSCO).
The proposed composition includes three representatives from AFC/M23, three from the DRC government, and coordination support from MONUSCO personnel.
The expanded mandate would include monitoring compliance with the ceasefire agreement reached between the two parties, in addition to broader security verification functions.
Delayed implementation
The reform process was initially launched last year but has faced delays in implementation. While both parties have reportedly agreed in principle to the establishment of EJVM+, a formal launch date has not yet been announced.
Ongoing tensions despite negotiations
The discussions in Switzerland continue alongside reports of renewed violence in parts of eastern Congo, including areas under the control of AFC/M23 and allied armed groups such as MRDP-Twirwaneho in Minembwe.
AFC/M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka has accused the DRC government of maintaining military operations despite participating in peace talks, arguing that this undermines the negotiation process.
He stated that while the group remains committed to a political solution, it will continue to act in defense of civilians in areas affected by ongoing clashes.
The evolving monitoring framework is seen as a key test of confidence-building measures between the parties, as mediators push for a durable ceasefire and long-term political settlement.
