title_en: Reports of Suspicious Weapons Convoy Spark Confusion in Burundi Amid Regional TensionsApril 17, 2026 - Confusion and concern have emerged in Burundi following reports of a long convoy of trucks allegedly transporting weapons across the country, raising questions about their destination and purpose amid heightened regional tensions.
excerpt_en: Human rights activist Pacifique Nininahazwe stated that the trucks entered Burundi via a supply route passing through Kenya’s Port of Mombasa and Tanzania before crossing into Burundi at the Kobero border post. According to his account, the convoys were initially believed to be l
body_en:
Human rights activist Pacifique Nininahazwe stated that the trucks entered Burundi via a supply route passing through Kenya’s Port of Mombasa and Tanzania before crossing into Burundi at the Kobero border post.
According to his account, the convoys were initially believed to be linked to Burundi’s military operations in South Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where Burundian forces are engaged in ongoing combat operations.
However, recent movements of the trucks have generated uncertainty after several convoys reportedly changed direction or were returned to the border area under unclear circumstances.
Convoy movements and military escort claims
Nininahazwe, who leads the civil society organization FOCODE, claimed that on April 10, 2026, approximately 23 trucks carrying military cargo entered Burundi under escort from regional security forces along the transit route. He further alleged that additional convoys had entered earlier, bringing the total to more than 80 trucks observed in circulation.
He stated that the vehicles were escorted from the border to military facilities but were later redirected back toward the Tanzanian border, where they were reportedly held in the Kinazi area of Muyinga Province.
Images shared by the activist show a long line of stationary trucks, which he claims are part of the same convoy, though their exact cargo has not been independently verified.
Uncertainty over destination and purpose
Local reports suggest the trucks have remained stationary for several days while awaiting further instructions. Some sources claim they may be intended for transfer back to Tanzania or onward transport via the Port of Tanga, though no official confirmation has been provided.
Authorities in Burundi have not publicly clarified the nature of the cargo or the reasons behind the reported convoy movements.

title: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Agree on Prisoner Release and Ceasefire Monitoring Mechanism
excerpt: Kinshasa April 18, 2026 - The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebel group have agreed to release more than 400 prisoners within the next 10 days, in a confidence-building measure aimed at strengthening ongoing peace efforts. The agreement was reache
title_en: DRC Government and AFC/M23 Agree on Prisoner Release and Ceasefire Monitoring Mechanism
excerpt_en: Kinshasa April 18, 2026 - The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebel group have agreed to release more than 400 prisoners within the next 10 days, in a confidence-building measure aimed at strengthening ongoing peace efforts. The agreement was reache
body_en:
Kinshasa April 18, 2026 - The government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebel group have agreed to release more than 400 prisoners within the next 10 days, in a confidence-building measure aimed at strengthening ongoing peace efforts.
The agreement was reached during talks held in Switzerland from April 13 to 17, 2026, with support from Qatar and the United States. Under the deal, the Congolese government is expected to release 311 detainees linked to AFC/M23, while the armed group will free 166 individuals held in its custody.
Both parties confirmed that the lists of prisoners were compiled with the assistance of the International Committee of the Red Cross, in line with a prior agreement signed on September 14, 2025.
In a parallel development, the two sides also agreed on April 14 to establish a new international ceasefire monitoring mechanism, known as EJVM+, composed of three representatives from each side. The structure had initially been proposed during earlier peace talks in Doha, Qatar, but its implementation was delayed amid continued tensions between the parties.
According to the agreement, EJVM+ is expected to become operational within one week and will oversee compliance with the ceasefire arrangements. The United Nations peacekeeping mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) is also expected to support monitoring activities.
The latest agreements are being presented as part of broader efforts to reduce hostilities and rebuild trust between the government and armed groups operating in eastern DRC, where conflict has persisted for years despite multiple mediation initiatives.

title: Ndayishimiye Denies Attacks on Rwanda as Cross-Border Security Tensions Persist
excerpt: Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy. In an interview with Yaga Burund
title_en: Ndayishimiye Denies Attacks on Rwanda as Cross-Border Security Tensions Persist
excerpt_en: Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy. In an interview with Yaga Burund
body_en:
Bujumbura April 19, 2026 - Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye has reiterated that no armed attacks have been launched against Rwanda from Burundian territory, rejecting long-standing accusations from Kigali regarding cross-border militancy.
In an interview with Yaga Burundi, Ndayishimiye accused Rwanda of tolerating elements that he claims seek to destabilize Burundi, while insisting that Burundi does not permit its territory to be used for attacks against its neighbor.
“Rwanda does not agree with the criminals and bad people who come to attack Burundi. In other words, Rwanda opens the door for them, and they come to attack Burundi. Burundi never opens the door for someone who goes to attack Rwanda,” he said.
The Burundian leader suggested that greater border restrictions would be necessary to prevent infiltration, arguing that open movement across the frontier creates security risks. He questioned the effectiveness of current border controls, saying that individuals can sometimes evade security agencies and carry out attacks.
“If we opened them, you would find that they were attacking you right here,” he added, referring to the possibility of unrestricted movement between the two countries.
Since late 2023, Rwanda has repeatedly rejected allegations of supporting armed groups targeting Burundi, maintaining that it does not collaborate with organizations opposed to the Burundian government.
However, multiple armed incidents over the past years have been attributed by Rwandan authorities to groups such as the FLN, which Kigali says have operated from the Kibira forest area in Burundi. These include attacks in 2018 and 2019 in Nyaruguru and Nyamagabe districts, as well as an incident in May 2021 in Bweyeye Sector, Rusizi District.
Rwandan military officials have previously stated that FLN fighters involved in cross-border attacks were pushed back into Burundi through the Ruhwa River area, and that some of their equipment carried markings associated with Burundian military structures-an allegation Bujumbura has consistently denied.
Further incidents have also been reported in subsequent years, including an attack in Nyungwe Park in May 2022 that left civilians dead, according to Rwandan authorities.
The FLN and other armed groups, including RED-Tabara, have also been linked to operations in the wider Great Lakes region. In 2020, RED-Tabara fighters were captured in Rwanda after crossing from the Democratic Republic of Congo and later handed over to Burundi in 2021.
United Nations expert reports have previously indicated that relations between Rwanda and Burundi deteriorated further in late 2023, with allegations of indirect cooperation between Burundi and certain armed groups hostile to Rwanda, including the FLN and FDLR. Both Kigali and Bujumbura have denied supporting destabilization efforts against each other.
As tensions persist, both governments continue to publicly affirm their commitment to national security while exchanging accusations over the activities of armed groups operating in border regions.
Conclusion
The period from April 6 to 19, 2026, highlights a region shaped by a complex interplay of diplomatic engagement, historical remembrance, and persistent security challenges across East and Central Africa. Rwanda emerged as an active diplomatic actor, advancing bilateral cooperation through new agreements with partners such as Chad and Oman, reinforcing its strategic positioning on both the African and global stage.
However, these gains were tempered by continued instability in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, which remains a central concern for regional security. The launch of peace talks in Switzerland between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 coalition marked a cautious step forward, but negotiations were overshadowed by mutual accusations of renewed hostilities, including drone strikes and civilian casualties. While confidence-building measures-such as the release of more than 400 detainees and the establishment of a ceasefire monitoring mechanism-offer tentative progress, deep divisions over territorial control, governance, and humanitarian access continue to undermine prospects for a durable settlement.
At the same time, Rwanda commemorated the 32nd anniversary of the Genocide against the Tutsi, a solemn moment that underscored the enduring importance of remembrance, national unity, and vigilance against hate speech and genocide ideology. These commemorations, observed both domestically and internationally, reaffirmed a collective commitment to preventing future atrocities. Nonetheless, reports of continued mobilization and ideological influence by the FDLR near border areas highlight the persistence of extremist narratives that threaten long-term stability.
Beyond the Great Lakes region, broader continental dynamics reflected a growing call for reform and self-determination. Advocacy for a more effective African Union, alongside debates on global representation and structural inequalities, signals renewed momentum toward strengthening Africa’s voice in international affairs. Yet, political developments such as constitutional reforms in Zimbabwe and leadership disruptions in Burundi illustrate the ongoing volatility that continues to shape governance across the continent.
In sum, the first half of April 2026 presents a region at a crossroads-marked by meaningful diplomatic and institutional progress, yet still constrained by entrenched conflicts and fragile political transitions. Rwanda’s trajectory reflects both the opportunities and limitations of this broader context, as sustained peace and stability will depend on continued regional cooperation, credible governance frameworks, and the ability to address the root causes of conflict.
By Jeff Buleli

body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - Rwanda’s national football team, Rwanda national football team, has won the FIFA Series 2026 Group A title after a 2-0 victory over Estonia in the final held at Amahoro Stadium.
The tournament, hosted in Rwanda for the first time, was attended by President Paul Kagame and marked a historic achievement for the national side.
Captain Bizimana Djihad praised the team’s discipline and tactical execution, saying the squad’s unity and preparation were key to their success.
Newly introduced players, including Leroy-Jacques Mickels, were highlighted for their impact during the competition, with Mickels being named player of the tournament.
Team officials described the victory as a sign of growing confidence and a foundation for future competitions, including qualification campaigns for the Africa Cup of Nations.
Former international Haruna Niyonzima, now serving in a managerial role, said the result reflects a broader transformation within Rwandan football and signaled that the team could achieve further surprises in upcoming tournaments.

title_en: Rwanda participates in UK International Food & Drink Event to boost exports
excerpt_en: London, March 31, 2026 - Rwanda’s National Agricultural Export Board (NAEB) and partner agencies are participating in the International Food & Drink Event (IFE) 2026, currently underway in London at ExCeL London. The exhibition, which runs from March 30 to April 1, brings togethe
body_en:
London, March 31, 2026 - Rwanda’s National Agricultural Export Board (NAEB) and partner agencies are participating in the International Food & Drink Event (IFE) 2026, currently underway in London at ExCeL London.
The exhibition, which runs from March 30 to April 1, brings together global food, beverage, and agriculture stakeholders from across all continents, with more than 25,000 expected participants.
Rwanda’s delegation is attending the event to strengthen existing export markets and explore new opportunities, particularly in Europe and the Middle East, amid ongoing regional disruptions affecting trade routes.
Officials say the country is positioning itself as a growing hub for processed agricultural products and aims to increase international visibility for Rwandan exports.
The participation aligns with Rwanda’s broader export strategy, following strong performance in 2025 when agricultural and livestock exports generated over $893 million, with projections exceeding $1 billion for the 2025/26 fiscal year.
The government views events like IFE as key platforms to expand market access and attract international buyers for Rwandan products.

title: Rwanda to host international blood transfusion experts conference in 2026
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - Rwanda is set to host an international conference bringing together global experts in blood transfusion and blood-based medicine, marking a return of the high-level meeting after 12 years. The conference is organized in partnership with the Africa
title_en: Rwanda to host international blood transfusion experts conference in 2026
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - Rwanda is set to host an international conference bringing together global experts in blood transfusion and blood-based medicine, marking a return of the high-level meeting after 12 years. The conference is organized in partnership with the Africa
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - Rwanda is set to host an international conference bringing together global experts in blood transfusion and blood-based medicine, marking a return of the high-level meeting after 12 years.
The conference is organized in partnership with the Africa Society for Blood Transfusion (AfSBT) and is expected to gather specialists, blood bank professionals, and healthcare experts from across Africa and beyond.
The announcement was made during the 12th AfSBT conference held in Namibia from March 21-26, 2026, where Rwanda presented its advancements in blood transfusion systems, including the use of drones for rapid blood delivery to remote areas.
Rwanda was represented by Dr. Thomas Muyombo, who highlighted the country’s progress in ensuring efficient and timely access to blood supplies.
The country last hosted the AfSBT conference in 2016, and the upcoming edition is expected to further strengthen Rwanda’s role in regional and global blood safety initiatives.
AfSBT, founded in 1997 in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, works to promote safe and effective blood transfusion practices across African countries.
Rwanda has recorded significant improvements in its national blood program, with more than 84,000 units of blood collected in 2024 and a reported 99.72% supply fulfillment rate in hospitals.
Health data shows that O positive remains the most donated blood type, while AB negative is the least common. A total of over 58,000 people donated blood during the year, with men representing the majority of donors.
The upcoming conference is expected to reinforce collaboration among African health systems and advance innovations in blood transfusion services.

title: Minister Habimana says revised electoral law should not raise concerns
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - The Minister of Local Government Dominique Habimana has stated that the ongoing revision of the electoral law should not cause public concern, describing it instead as a reform aimed at improving the country’s local electoral system. He made the r
title_en: Minister Habimana says revised electoral law should not raise concerns
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - The Minister of Local Government Dominique Habimana has stated that the ongoing revision of the electoral law should not cause public concern, describing it instead as a reform aimed at improving the country’s local electoral system. He made the r
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - The Minister of Local Government Dominique Habimana has stated that the ongoing revision of the electoral law should not cause public concern, describing it instead as a reform aimed at improving the country’s local electoral system.
He made the remarks while appearing before the Chamber of Deputies, where lawmakers were examining the draft Organic Law on elections article by article.
The proposed changes include a shift in how district councilors are elected. Under the new framework, the eight general councilors at district level would be chosen indirectly by an electoral college composed of representatives elected from the cell level and representatives of different social categories at district level.
Officials explained that the reform is intended to streamline representation following the reduction of district council seats to eight, requiring an adjusted selection process.
Minister Habimana assured lawmakers that the changes remain within international legal standards and are consistent with Rwanda’s existing electoral practices.
The Chairperson of the National Electoral Commission Oda Gasinzigwa said the reforms are part of efforts to improve electoral processes and strengthen democratic participation.
She noted that the revised law is urgent, as it will be applied in local elections scheduled between October and November 2026, and urged Parliament to expedite its approval to allow adequate time for voter education.
The Executive Secretary of the National Electoral Commission Jean Claude Musabyimana added that the changes aim to broaden participation in the electoral college, ensuring stronger representation of citizens in decision-making structures.
Parliament’s Committee on Governance and Gender Equality confirmed that it will carefully review the draft law before forwarding it to the full Chamber of Deputies and subsequently to the Senate for further consideration.

title: Rwanda’s Education Ministry moves to strengthen counseling support after student suicide cases
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, March 27, 2026 - The Ministry of Education (MINEDUC) says it is working on introducing enhanced psychological counseling services in schools following recent cases of student deaths suspected to be linked to suicide. The announcement comes after the death of a stu
title_en: Rwanda’s Education Ministry moves to strengthen counseling support after student suicide cases
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 27, 2026 - The Ministry of Education (MINEDUC) says it is working on introducing enhanced psychological counseling services in schools following recent cases of student deaths suspected to be linked to suicide. The announcement comes after the death of a stu
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 27, 2026 - The Ministry of Education (MINEDUC) says it is working on introducing enhanced psychological counseling services in schools following recent cases of student deaths suspected to be linked to suicide.
The announcement comes after the death of a student at RP Tumba College of Vocational Education in Rulindo District on March 24, 2026. Authorities are investigating circumstances surrounding the incident, which also involved the death of a visiting student.
Education Minister Joseph Nsengimana said the government is considering new measures to strengthen mental health and psychosocial support systems within schools and higher learning institutions.
He noted that the initiative aims to complement existing student support programs, particularly for learners in secondary schools and public higher education institutions, where government assistance is already provided.
The minister emphasized that early identification of psychological distress among students is a key priority, adding that counseling services could play a critical role in prevention efforts.
He also urged parents and guardians to remain actively involved in the lives of their children, stressing that education is a shared responsibility between schools and families.
Authorities continue to investigate the recent incident, with findings expected to clarify the circumstances surrounding the deaths.
According to national health data, hundreds of suicide attempts are recorded annually in Rwanda, with young people aged 19 to 35 representing the largest proportion of cases. Officials say the figures highlight the need for stronger mental health awareness and intervention strategies in schools and communities.

title: Rwanda reports sharp decline in dental disease cases following nationwide awareness campaigns
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, March 28, 2026 - Health officials in Rwanda say cases of dental disease have significantly decreased following sustained public awareness campaigns, particularly in schools. According to the National Health Institute (RBC), reductions have been recorded in tooth d
title_en: Rwanda reports sharp decline in dental disease cases following nationwide awareness campaigns
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 28, 2026 - Health officials in Rwanda say cases of dental disease have significantly decreased following sustained public awareness campaigns, particularly in schools. According to the National Health Institute (RBC), reductions have been recorded in tooth d
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 28, 2026 - Health officials in Rwanda say cases of dental disease have significantly decreased following sustained public awareness campaigns, particularly in schools.
According to the National Health Institute (RBC), reductions have been recorded in tooth decay and hygiene-related oral conditions, following intensified education programs on oral health.
Bagahirwa Irène, a specialist in non-communicable diseases at RBC, said cases of tooth decay have dropped from 45% to 16%, while pain linked to poor oral hygiene has fallen from 44% to 7%.
She attributed the progress to school-based awareness campaigns aimed at encouraging children to adopt regular dental hygiene practices.
The head of the Association of Dentists and Oral Surgeons, Niyibizi Fabrice, said most patients treated are young children suffering from preventable dental conditions, but noted that awareness efforts are beginning to show results.
The Secretary of State in the Ministry of Education, Irere Claudette, stressed the importance of combining school feeding programs with hygiene education, urging students to adopt consistent oral care habits.
Despite the improvement, health data still indicates that dental care-seeking behavior remains largely reactive, with many patients only visiting clinics when pain becomes severe, highlighting ongoing gaps in preventive care awareness.

title: Rwanda banks finance major telecom infrastructure deal involving 1,400 towers

title_en: Rwanda banks finance major telecom infrastructure deal involving 1,400 towers
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 28, 2026 - A consortium of six commercial banks in Rwanda has provided financing to support a large-scale telecommunications infrastructure transaction involving more than 1,400 mobile network towers. The deal, led by the Bank of Kigali alongside BPR Bank Rw
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 28, 2026 - A consortium of six commercial banks in Rwanda has provided financing to support a large-scale telecommunications infrastructure transaction involving more than 1,400 mobile network towers.
The deal, led by the Bank of Kigali alongside BPR Bank Rwanda, the Development Bank of Rwanda (BRD), I&M Bank Rwanda, Ecobank Rwanda, and Access Bank Rwanda, is part of a syndicated loan arrangement backing the acquisition and management of critical telecom assets.
The towers, originally owned by IHS Holdings Rwanda, were sold in October 2025 to Paradigm Tower Ventures for an estimated $274.5 million and later transferred to its local subsidiary, Ishara Towers Rwanda, which will oversee operations in the country.
Bank of Kigali CEO Diane Karusisi said the transaction demonstrates the growing capacity of Rwanda’s financial sector to support large-scale infrastructure investments essential for digital connectivity and economic growth.
Paradigm Tower Ventures CEO Gordon Porter welcomed the agreement, describing it as a strong example of partnership between international investors and Rwandan financial institutions.
The telecom towers are considered critical infrastructure, supporting mobile communications, internet access, and digital financial services across the country.

excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 29, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Gender and Family Promotion, Consolée Uwimana, has called on members of the Liberal Party (PL) to play an active role in addressing pressing social challenges affecting families. Speaking at the party’s National Council meetin
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 29, 2026 - Rwanda’s Minister of Gender and Family Promotion, Consolée Uwimana, has called on members of the Liberal Party (PL) to play an active role in addressing pressing social challenges affecting families.
Speaking at the party’s National Council meeting, Uwimana highlighted key issues including domestic violence, teenage pregnancy, child abuse, trafficking, and drug use, warning that these problems continue to undermine family stability.
She stressed that building a secure and capable society begins at the family level, urging parents, communities, and institutions to take responsibility for child upbringing and social cohesion.
Uwimana emphasized that resolving family conflicts and strengthening parental roles could significantly reduce many of the country’s social challenges.
Liberal Party President Donatille Mukabalisa reaffirmed the party’s commitment to supporting national efforts, calling on members at all levels to contribute to building a stable and resilient society.
Authorities say collective action will be key to improving social well-being and supporting Rwanda’s long-term development goals.

body_en:
Kigali, April 3, 2026 - President Paul Kagame has dismissed speculation about his health following a period in 2025 when he spent several weeks away from public engagements.
In an interview with Jeune Afrique, President Kagame explained that his absence was due to personal time off, which he spent with his grandchildren, emphasizing that it should not be interpreted as a health concern.
He said he had taken around three weeks to a month of leave and noted that public reactions reflected unfamiliarity with leaders taking extended personal time.
Kagame added that his current health is strong, stating that he remains in good condition compared to many people of similar age, while acknowledging the natural uncertainties of aging.
The president’s remarks follow earlier public speculation during his 2025 absence, which prompted clarification from government officials at the time.
He also used the interview to reflect on privacy expectations for public officials and the need to normalize periods of rest away from official duties.

title: Over 31,000 cases resolved through plea bargains in Rwanda since 2022
excerpt: Kigali, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - The Ministry of Justice reports that more than 31,000 criminal and civil cases have been resolved through plea bargaining since 2022, as Rwanda continues efforts to reduce court congestion and prison overcrowding. According to official figures, 31
title_en: Over 31,000 cases resolved through plea bargains in Rwanda since 2022
excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - The Ministry of Justice reports that more than 31,000 criminal and civil cases have been resolved through plea bargaining since 2022, as Rwanda continues efforts to reduce court congestion and prison overcrowding. According to official figures, 31
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - The Ministry of Justice reports that more than 31,000 criminal and civil cases have been resolved through plea bargaining since 2022, as Rwanda continues efforts to reduce court congestion and prison overcrowding.
According to official figures, 31,143 cases have been concluded through plea bargains over the period, including 8,532 cases between July 2025 and March 2026 alone.
Authorities say these reforms have contributed to a 24.4% decline in the prison population during the 2024/2025 fiscal year.
The justice system has also expanded the use of mediation, with 9,559 cases resolved through alternative dispute mechanisms since 2022.
Legal reforms, including Law No. 22/2018 on civil and administrative procedures, have strengthened the role of mediation at different stages of judicial proceedings, encouraging settlement before trial.
The Ministry of Justice has also promoted training programs for professional mediators and launched an Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) center to institutionalize out-of-court settlements.
Officials say these initiatives have helped reduce the court case backlog from 62% in 2022/2023 to 45% as of March 2026.
Judicial authorities and law educators continue to promote ADR clubs in universities and secondary schools to further embed mediation culture among young people and future legal professionals.

excerpt_en: Kigali, Rwanda, April 2, 2026 - Journalists in Rwanda have outlined key challenges affecting their ability to work effectively, during discussions held on March 31 organized by the Legal Aid Forum (LAF). The dialogue brought together media professionals to reflect on the state of
body_en:
Kigali, Rwanda, April 2, 2026 - Journalists in Rwanda have outlined key challenges affecting their ability to work effectively, during discussions held on March 31 organized by the Legal Aid Forum (LAF).
The dialogue brought together media professionals to reflect on the state of journalism following Rwanda’s participation in the UN Human Rights Council’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which issued 286 recommendations, including 29 related to media freedom and development.
Participants highlighted several major concerns, including the rise of unqualified individuals presenting themselves as journalists, which they say is undermining professional standards in the sector.
Media practitioners also cited financial constraints as a major issue, noting that limited advertising revenue and weak media markets make it difficult for institutions to properly pay journalists, leading some professionals to leave traditional media for independent platforms such as YouTube.
Outdated media policies and regulatory frameworks were also raised as a barrier to adapting journalism standards to the digital age, with calls for legal reforms to better align with modern media practices.
Gender-based violence and limited participation of women in media were also identified as ongoing concerns affecting inclusivity in the sector.
The Legal Aid Forum said it will continue supporting efforts to strengthen journalism capacity, improve working conditions, and promote professional standards across the industry.

excerpt: Kinshasa, April 2, 2026 - A British citizen, Youssouf Ezangi, has been transferred from the Democratic Republic of Congo to the United Kingdom following his conviction in a high-profile coup plot case. Ezangi was among 37 individuals convicted for their alleged role in an attempt

excerpt_en: Kinshasa, April 2, 2026 - A British citizen, Youssouf Ezangi, has been transferred from the Democratic Republic of Congo to the United Kingdom following his conviction in a high-profile coup plot case. Ezangi was among 37 individuals convicted for their alleged role in an attempt
body_en:
Kinshasa, April 2, 2026 - A British citizen, Youssouf Ezangi, has been transferred from the Democratic Republic of Congo to the United Kingdom following his conviction in a high-profile coup plot case.
Ezangi was among 37 individuals convicted for their alleged role in an attempted overthrow of President Félix Tshisekedi linked to events in May 2024 involving Christian Malanga.
Initially sentenced to death alongside several foreign nationals, including U.S. citizens Tyler Thomson and Benjamin Zalman-Polun, his sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment following international diplomatic pressure.
Authorities in Kinshasa confirmed that Ezangi was transferred on March 31, 2026, under a judicial cooperation agreement between the DRC and the United Kingdom, with the presence of British Embassy officials during the handover.
Officials say the arrangement allows him to serve the remainder of his sentence in the UK.
The move follows earlier decisions in which other foreign convicts were pardoned or repatriated to their home countries after diplomatic negotiations.

title: Rwandan and Tanzanian armies hold 15th border security meeting
excerpt: Karagwe District, Tanzania, March 25, 2026 - Military leaders from Rwanda and Tanzania have convened for the 15th Border Military Leaders Meeting, aimed at addressing border security challenges and strengthening bilateral cooperation. The three-day meeting, which began on March 2
title_en: Rwandan and Tanzanian armies hold 15th border security meeting
excerpt_en: Karagwe District, Tanzania, March 25, 2026 - Military leaders from Rwanda and Tanzania have convened for the 15th Border Military Leaders Meeting, aimed at addressing border security challenges and strengthening bilateral cooperation. The three-day meeting, which began on March 2
body_en:
Karagwe District, Tanzania, March 25, 2026 - Military leaders from Rwanda and Tanzania have convened for the 15th Border Military Leaders Meeting, aimed at addressing border security challenges and strengthening bilateral cooperation.
The three-day meeting, which began on March 24 and runs through March 26, brings together units operating along the shared border, including Rwanda’s 5th Division and Tanzania’s 202nd Brigade.
The Rwandan delegation is led by Maj. Gen. Ruki Karusisi, commander of the 5th Division of the Rwanda Defence Force, while the Tanzanian side is headed by Brig. Gen. Gabriel Elias Kwiligwa, commander of the 202nd Brigade of the Tanzania People’s Defence Force.
The talks focus on enhancing coordination in tackling cross-border crime, with both sides emphasizing the importance of intelligence sharing and sustained collaboration.
Rwanda and Tanzania have maintained longstanding military and security cooperation, particularly along their common border, where joint efforts have helped address security threats and improve stability.
Beyond security, the two countries share strong economic ties. Tanzania remains a key trade partner for Rwanda, notably through the port of Dar es Salaam, which serves as a major gateway for imports.
A significant share of Rwanda’s petroleum products transits through Tanzania, with an estimated 60 million liters imported monthly. The accessibility and logistical advantages of Dar es Salaam have made it a preferred route compared to alternative corridors.
Trade between the two nations continues to grow, with Rwanda importing goods worth over $228 million from Tanzania as of late 2023.
The two countries have also expanded cooperation into other sectors, including agriculture, following a bilateral agreement signed in November 2025 aimed at boosting joint development initiatives.

title: Mass grave containing 32 bodies, mostly children, discovered in Kericho
excerpt: Kericho, Kenya, March 25, 2026 - Authorities in Kenya have launched an investigation after 32 bodies, mostly children, were discovered in a mass grave in the Kericho area. Police said the exhumation began following a court order directing them to recover 14 bodies suspected to ha
title_en: Mass grave containing 32 bodies, mostly children, discovered in Kericho
excerpt_en: Kericho, Kenya, March 25, 2026 - Authorities in Kenya have launched an investigation after 32 bodies, mostly children, were discovered in a mass grave in the Kericho area. Police said the exhumation began following a court order directing them to recover 14 bodies suspected to ha
body_en:
Kericho, Kenya, March 25, 2026 - Authorities in Kenya have launched an investigation after 32 bodies, mostly children, were discovered in a mass grave in the Kericho area.
Police said the exhumation began following a court order directing them to recover 14 bodies suspected to have been buried in the area. The operation later uncovered additional remains, bringing the total to 32 bodies.
According to officials, the victims include seven adults and 25 children. A Kenyan medical officer said post-mortem examinations are underway to establish the identities of the deceased and determine the exact causes of death.
Preliminary findings suggest that some of the bodies were transferred from a hospital in Nyamira to Kericho for burial without proper authorization, raising questions over procedural and legal compliance.
Authorities stated that some remains appeared to have been removed from a hospital before burial, but emphasized that forensic analysis is ongoing to clarify circumstances surrounding the deaths.
The discovery has prompted widespread concern, with investigators continuing efforts to determine whether the burials were conducted in violation of legal procedures or involve additional criminal elements.

title: Gen Muhoozi signals possible Uganda troop withdrawal from eastern DRC amid political conditions
excerpt: Kampala, Uganda, March 25, 2026 - Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces Muhoozi Kainerugaba has announced that Ugandan troops deployed in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo could be withdrawn from several positions, depending on political developments in Ituri Province. Ugandan forc
title_en: Gen Muhoozi signals possible Uganda troop withdrawal from eastern DRC amid political conditions
excerpt_en: Kampala, Uganda, March 25, 2026 - Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces Muhoozi Kainerugaba has announced that Ugandan troops deployed in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo could be withdrawn from several positions, depending on political developments in Ituri Province. Ugandan forc
body_en:
Kampala, Uganda, March 25, 2026 - Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces Muhoozi Kainerugaba has announced that Ugandan troops deployed in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo could be withdrawn from several positions, depending on political developments in Ituri Province.
Ugandan forces are currently deployed in joint operations with the Armed Forces of the DRC to combat armed groups, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), which are linked to the Islamic State network.
Gen. Muhoozi said Uganda is prepared to withdraw troops from areas stretching from Lubero to Mahagi in coordination with the Congolese government, emphasizing the goal of achieving lasting stability in eastern DRC.
However, he stated that the withdrawal from Lubero would depend on whether changes are made to the leadership of Ituri Province, indicating that all Ugandan troops could leave the area if the current governor remains in office.
Eastern DRC continues to face complex insecurity, with more than 250 armed groups operating in the region, many of which are involved in violence against civilians, according to regional security assessments.
The announcement comes amid ongoing military cooperation between Uganda and the DRC, which has focused on joint operations against insurgent groups and improving security along shared border regions.

body_en:
Rusizi District, Rwanda, March 26, 2026 - Rwanda has received 222 citizens who were previously held in areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo under the control of the FDLR armed group.
The returnees, including 149 children, 58 women, and 15 men, crossed into Rwanda through the La Corniche border post, which connects Rwanda and the DRC.
Upon arrival, they were transported to the Nyarushishi transit camp in Rusizi District, where they will undergo temporary reception and support procedures before reintegration into their communities.
Officials said the group had been living in a temporary camp in Goma after leaving various locations in eastern DRC where they had reportedly been under the influence or control of the FDLR.
Local authorities welcomed the returnees, urging them to actively participate in rebuilding their lives and contributing to national development.
The Deputy Mayor of Rubavu District in charge of economic development Nzabonimpa Déogratias encouraged them to reunite with their families, resume education for children, and access available social and health services.
He emphasized that reintegration support includes financial assistance and basic supplies intended to help returnees restart their lives, with adults receiving 188 USD, minors receiving 113 USD, and each individual provided with food assistance valued at 45,000 Rwandan francs.
Authorities stated that the return process is part of ongoing efforts to assist nationals coming back from conflict-affected areas and to facilitate their reintegration into normal civilian life.

body_en:
Musanze, Rwanda, March 29, 2026 - A group of 28 postgraduate students from SOAS University of London has visited the Mutobo Demobilization and Reintegration Centre in northern Rwanda to study the country’s approach to rehabilitating former armed group members.
The visit focused on understanding how Rwanda receives and reintegrates former fighters from groups such as the FDLR, many of whom return from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo after years in armed movements.
The delegation was received by Jacques Nziza, Vice President of the Rwanda Demobilization and Reintegration Commission, who outlined ongoing efforts to support ex-combatants in transitioning back into civilian life.
Students also held discussions with former fighters, who shared testimonies about their experiences in the bush and their decision to return and reintegrate into Rwandan society.
Professor Phil Clark, speaking on behalf of the group, praised the initiative, highlighting its role in promoting peace, reconciliation, and long-term stability in the Great Lakes region.

North Kivu, DR Congo, March 29, 2026 - The AFC/M23 rebel group has denied reports that it is withdrawing fighters from areas under its control in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The claims, circulated in local media over the weekend, suggested that M23 forces were redeploying from several locations in Lubero territory to other positions, allegedly under international pressure.
In a statement, North Kivu Governor Erasto Bahati dismissed the reports, describing ongoing movements as routine military rotations rather than a withdrawal.
Authorities said the information circulating on social media was intended to create confusion among the population, urging residents to remain calm and continue their daily activities.
The situation in eastern DRC remains tense, with ongoing military operations and competing narratives surrounding developments on the ground.

Nakuru County, Kenya, March 29, 2026 - Kenyan police have rescued 67 girls believed to be victims of a suspected human trafficking network in Njoro, Nakuru County.
According to local police commander Nelson Koech, the victims were found confined in a house where they had reportedly been lured with promises of employment opportunities.
Survivors told authorities they had been held for months in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions, alleging abuse and punishment for those who questioned their situation.
Police said the premises were being used by an agency that recruits individuals for work abroad, though its operating license had expired in December 2025. Authorities had previously ordered its closure.

The Kenyan government has repeatedly warned citizens against using unverified recruitment channels, citing growing cases of fraud and trafficking linked to illegal job placement schemes.

excerpt_en: South Kivu, DR Congo, March 30, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and allied groups of carrying out drone strikes on civilian areas in the Minembwe highlands, resulting in at least seven deaths. According to M23
body_en:
South Kivu, DR Congo, March 30, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and allied groups of carrying out drone strikes on civilian areas in the Minembwe highlands, resulting in at least seven deaths.
According to M23 spokesperson Lawrence Kanyuka, the attacks took place between late March 29 and early March 30, targeting densely populated areas including Mikenke and Gakenke.
He alleged that suicide drones were used in what he described as indiscriminate strikes against civilian populations, also reporting additional casualties in Shanji, Kalehe Territory, where at least seven civilians were killed and around 20 others injured.
The group claims the attacks violate international humanitarian standards and accuses the Congolese government of continuing military operations despite prior ceasefire understandings linked to postponed talks in Doha.
Kinshasa has not immediately responded to the allegations.

title: DRC announces plan to begin disarming FDLR under regional peace commitments
excerpt: Kinshasa, DR Congo, March 30, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have announced plans to begin disarming the FDLR armed group as part of ongoing regional peace and security arrangements. The group, composed of remnants of former FAR soldiers and I
title_en: DRC announces plan to begin disarming FDLR under regional peace commitments
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, DR Congo, March 30, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have announced plans to begin disarming the FDLR armed group as part of ongoing regional peace and security arrangements. The group, composed of remnants of former FAR soldiers and I
body_en:
Kinshasa, DR Congo, March 30, 2026 - The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) have announced plans to begin disarming the FDLR armed group as part of ongoing regional peace and security arrangements.
The group, composed of remnants of former FAR soldiers and Interahamwe militia linked to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, has long been cited by Rwanda as a persistent security threat operating in eastern DRC.
Military officials say the disarmament operation will start with calls for voluntary surrender, followed by enforced disarmament if necessary, with designated reception sites reportedly being prepared in Kisangani.
Deputy Chief of Staff Jacques Ychaligonza Nduru said the army’s objective is to avoid bloodshed while ensuring all fighters lay down their weapons.
The move aligns with provisions of the Washington peace agreement signed in December 2025, which links security normalization steps to the dismantling of armed groups in the region.
Rwanda’s ambassador to the United Nations, Martin Ngoga, has previously reiterated that the FDLR remains a serious security concern due to its ideological roots and continued activity in eastern DRC.
Analysts warn that implementation may be complex, citing longstanding accusations of infiltration and integration of armed elements into local security structures.
Authorities in the region say successful disarmament could mark a significant step toward reducing tensions in the Great Lakes region, though challenges remain over verification and coordination.

title: Over 200 ex-FDLR combatants repatriated and reintegrated in Rwanda
excerpt: Northern Province, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - The Rwandan Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) has announced the reintegration of 214 former fighters from armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including the FDLR. The group represents the 76t
title_en: Over 200 ex-FDLR combatants repatriated and reintegrated in Rwanda
excerpt_en: Northern Province, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - The Rwandan Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) has announced the reintegration of 214 former fighters from armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including the FDLR. The group represents the 76t
body_en:
Northern Province, Rwanda, March 31, 2026 - The Rwandan Demobilization and Rehabilitation Commission (RDRC) has announced the reintegration of 214 former fighters from armed groups operating in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including the FDLR.
The group represents the 76th batch processed through Rwanda’s demobilization program, with officials also confirming that about 400 more ex-combatants are expected in the next intake.
According to the commission, since the program began, a total of 12,686 former combatants have passed through the Mutobo Reintegration Centre.
RDRC head Valerie Nyirahabineza said many of the returnees come from border districts such as Rubavu, highlighting ongoing cross-border movement between Rwanda and eastern DRC.
Officials used the occasion to call for stronger community vigilance against recruitment by armed groups and to encourage continued repatriation efforts.
Returnees also shared testimonies about conditions inside armed groups and described previous recruitment and propaganda practices used in the forests of eastern DRC.
Authorities urged the reintegrated ex-combatants to promote unity, reject divisive ideology, and support efforts to encourage remaining fighters to return home peacefully.
Government spokespersons emphasized that reintegration remains a key part of Rwanda’s broader stability and reconciliation strategy.

title: AFC/M23 claims FARDC seen fighting alongside FDLR despite disarmament pledge
excerpt: Eastern DRC, April 1, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Congolese army (FARDC) of operating alongside FDLR fighters just days after government announcements that operations had begun to dismantle the armed group. The allegations come shortly after the DRC military decl
title_en: AFC/M23 claims FARDC seen fighting alongside FDLR despite disarmament pledge
excerpt_en: Eastern DRC, April 1, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Congolese army (FARDC) of operating alongside FDLR fighters just days after government announcements that operations had begun to dismantle the armed group. The allegations come shortly after the DRC military decl
body_en:
Eastern DRC, April 1, 2026 - The AFC/M23 coalition has accused the Congolese army (FARDC) of operating alongside FDLR fighters just days after government announcements that operations had begun to dismantle the armed group.
The allegations come shortly after the DRC military declared on March 29, 2026, that it had launched efforts to disarm the FDLR and compel its fighters to surrender voluntarily or by force.
Deputy Chief of Staff of the FARDC, Lt. Gen. Nduru Jacques Ychaligonza, had stated that troops deployed in eastern regions would prioritize disarmament operations while aiming to avoid bloodshed.
However, AFC/M23 later alleged that government forces were seen collaborating with FDLR units on active front lines, calling it a violation of ceasefire commitments and recent peace understandings.
The group further claimed that joint FARDC-FDLR activity has contributed to civilian casualties in ongoing clashes, and accused Kinshasa of failing to implement agreed security measures.
The Congolese government has not independently confirmed these allegations.
The dispute highlights ongoing tensions surrounding implementation of the Washington D.C. peace agreement, which includes provisions requiring the dismantling of the FDLR as part of broader regional security commitments.

body_en:
Bujumbura, April 1, 2026 - Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye has confirmed that fatalities occurred following a weapons explosion at a military base in the Musaga area of Bujumbura.
In a statement shared on social media, President Ndayishimiye expressed condolences to families of those killed and wished a swift recovery to the injured.
He said the government remains confident in its capacity to defend national sovereignty despite the incident.
The explosion, which occurred on the night of March 31, reportedly affected an arms depot inside a military facility in the Musaga zone. Authorities have attributed the fire to an electrical fault.
However, security sources cited by AFP indicated that the incident may have resulted in more than 10 deaths, although official figures have not been fully confirmed.
The Burundian military and Ministry of Internal Security have launched further assessments to determine the exact cause and full extent of the damage.

title: Over 130 Rwandans return home from DRC after years held by armed group
excerpt: Rusizi, Rwanda, April 2, 2026 - A total of 133 Rwandans have returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo after years of displacement and alleged captivity under the FDLR armed group. The group crossed into Rwanda through the Grande Barrière border post and was received by auth
title_en: Over 130 Rwandans return home from DRC after years held by armed group
excerpt_en: Rusizi, Rwanda, April 2, 2026 - A total of 133 Rwandans have returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo after years of displacement and alleged captivity under the FDLR armed group. The group crossed into Rwanda through the Grande Barrière border post and was received by auth
body_en:
Rusizi, Rwanda, April 2, 2026 - A total of 133 Rwandans have returned from the Democratic Republic of Congo after years of displacement and alleged captivity under the FDLR armed group.
The group crossed into Rwanda through the Grande Barrière border post and was received by authorities before being transferred to the Nyarushishi transit center in Rusizi District for reintegration support.
Among the returnees were women, men, and children, many of whom say they had been influenced by fear-based messages warning them not to return to Rwanda.
One returnee, Nyirakaromba, said they were told they would be killed if they went back to Rwanda, but later learned from others who had returned that conditions were safe and peaceful.
Others described difficult living conditions in eastern DRC, including forced labor, insecurity, and exploitation by armed groups.
The return operation was coordinated under agreements involving Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), reached during a meeting in Addis Ababa in 2025.
Local authorities in Rubavu District welcomed the returnees and encouraged them to reintegrate into their communities, resume normal life, and ensure children return to school.
The government also provided reintegration assistance, including cash support and basic supplies to help families restart their lives.

Kigali, Rwanda, April 2, 2026 - The Cabinet has appointed CP Theos Badege as the Deputy Commissioner General of the Rwanda Correctional Service (RCS), following a meeting held at Village Urugwiro and chaired by President Paul Kagame.
Badege, a senior police officer with extensive experience in law enforcement and international policing cooperation, previously served as spokesperson of the Rwanda National Police and worked with Interpol.

title_en: Rwanda and DRC exchange accusations over Banyamulenge attacks amid ongoing tensions
excerpt_en: Kigali, April 3, 2026 - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have traded accusations over recent violence in eastern DRC, particularly in areas inhabited by the Banyamulenge community. Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo criticized statements from the DRC
body_en:
Kigali, April 3, 2026 - Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have traded accusations over recent violence in eastern DRC, particularly in areas inhabited by the Banyamulenge community.
Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo criticized statements from the DRC government accusing AFC/M23 of responsibility for attacks in Minembwe, arguing instead that Congolese forces and their allies are the ones carrying out abuses.
Makolo accused Kinshasa of “distorting the truth” and attempting to shift blame for actions committed by government forces and allied groups, including Burundian troops and Wazalendo militias.
The allegations come amid continued instability in eastern DRC, where multiple armed actors remain active despite ongoing peace talks in Doha.
Rwanda maintains that lasting peace in the region depends on the dismantling of the FDLR, which Kigali accuses of spreading genocidal ideology and fueling insecurity in the area.
The DRC government has not publicly responded to the latest statements.

Ituri Province, April 3, 2026 - At least 43 people have been killed in a new attack attributed to the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in the Bafwako area of Mambasa Territory, according to local military officials in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Lieutenant Jules Tshikudi Ngongo, a spokesperson for the Congolese army in the region, said the attackers also burned 44 homes during the assault, which occurred on April 2, 2026.
Local authorities report that search operations are ongoing, with fears the death toll could rise as more information becomes available from remote areas.
Residents described scenes of extreme violence, including killings with machetes, arson attacks, and kidnappings.
The ADF, an armed group operating in eastern Congo, has been blamed for a series of deadly civilian attacks in Ituri Province in recent months, including another incident in March 2026 that left around 50 people dead in the same territory.

title: Alleged 1994 letter denying the Genocide against the Tutsi linked to Rusesabagina case surfaces
excerpt: Kigali, April 3, 2026 - New claims have emerged regarding the contents of a letter reportedly found at the home of Paul Rusesabagina during the post-1994 period, which is alleged to contain narratives denying or distorting the Genocide against the Tutsi. According to author Mukag
title_en: Alleged 1994 letter denying the Genocide against the Tutsi linked to Rusesabagina case surfaces
excerpt_en: Kigali, April 3, 2026 - New claims have emerged regarding the contents of a letter reportedly found at the home of Paul Rusesabagina during the post-1994 period, which is alleged to contain narratives denying or distorting the Genocide against the Tutsi. According to author Mukag
body_en:
Kigali, April 3, 2026 - New claims have emerged regarding the contents of a letter reportedly found at the home of Paul Rusesabagina during the post-1994 period, which is alleged to contain narratives denying or distorting the Genocide against the Tutsi.
According to author Mukagasana Yolande, the letter-said to have been written in August 1994 by clergy who had fled to Goma and addressed to Pope John Paul II-contained statements attributing responsibility for the violence to political actors rather than acknowledging the genocide.
Mukagasana, who shared her account during a book presentation in Mageragere, said she discovered the document while visiting Rusesabagina’s home shortly after the end of the genocide. She later referenced the alleged contents in her published work, stating that it reflected harmful narratives about the 1994 events.
She also said the letter influenced her personal relationship with the household at the time.
The claims have not been independently verified.
Paul Rusesabagina, known internationally for his role during the 1994 genocide and later legal controversies in Rwanda, was convicted in 2021 on terrorism-related charges linked to the MRCD/FLN group. He was released in March 2023 after receiving a presidential pardon and later returned to the United States.
Rusesabagina has previously acknowledged writing a letter expressing remorse, but later disputed interpretations of its meaning in a 2024 interview.
The latest allegations add to ongoing historical and political disputes surrounding narratives of the 1994 genocide and related figures.
body_fr:

title: DRC and Burundi launch talks to repatriate Congolese refugees displaced by Uvira conflict
excerpt: Kalemie, April 4, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi have begun discussions aimed at facilitating the voluntary return of Congolese refugees displaced by last year’s fighting in Uvira, South Kivu Province. The talks, which also include the United Nations High Com
title_en: DRC and Burundi launch talks to repatriate Congolese refugees displaced by Uvira conflict
excerpt_en: Kalemie, April 4, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi have begun discussions aimed at facilitating the voluntary return of Congolese refugees displaced by last year’s fighting in Uvira, South Kivu Province. The talks, which also include the United Nations High Com
body_en:
Kalemie, April 4, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi have begun discussions aimed at facilitating the voluntary return of Congolese refugees displaced by last year’s fighting in Uvira, South Kivu Province.
The talks, which also include the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), are taking place in Kalemie, Tanganyika Province, according to South Kivu Governor Jean-Jacques Purusi.
Authorities estimate that the December 2025 clashes in and around Uvira and nearby areas displaced large populations internally, while hundreds of thousands sought refuge in Burundi and Tanzania.
The discussions are expected to define procedures and timelines for repatriation of refugees currently hosted in Burundi and Tanzania.
Officials in Kinshasa say the initiative is part of broader efforts to stabilize return areas and coordinate humanitarian assistance for displaced populations.
The situation in Uvira remains sensitive following months of conflict involving armed groups and government forces, which led to large-scale population movements across the region.

title: Tibor Nagy urges focus on FDLR dismantling as key to resolving eastern DRC conflict
excerpt: Washington, April 4, 2026 - Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Tibor Nagy has said that dismantling the FDLR armed group in the Democratic Republic of Congo is essential to ending long-standing insecurity in the country’s east. In comments following a re

body_en:
Washington, April 4, 2026 - Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Tibor Nagy has said that dismantling the FDLR armed group in the Democratic Republic of Congo is essential to ending long-standing insecurity in the country’s east.
In comments following a recent interview with Rwandan President Paul Kagame published in Jeune Afrique, Nagy argued that international actors should apply consistent expectations on all armed groups operating in the region.
He stated that if pressure is placed on Rwanda regarding its alleged links to armed actors, similar scrutiny should be applied to the DRC concerning groups it is accused of tolerating or failing to dismantle.
Nagy has previously questioned the Congolese government’s commitment to eliminating the FDLR, a group widely described by regional and international stakeholders as a destabilizing armed force in the Great Lakes region.
In the referenced interview, President Kagame reiterated Rwanda’s security concerns along its border and defended what he described as defensive measures aimed at preventing cross-border threats. He also argued that regional security dynamics require broader attention to multiple armed actors rather than focusing on a single party.
The remarks come amid continued diplomatic debate over security arrangements, armed group activity, and peace implementation efforts in eastern DRC.

title: DRC-AFC/M23 peace talks may be relocated from Doha to Switzerland
excerpt: April 4, 2026 - Ongoing peace talks between the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebel group, currently held in Doha, Qatar, could be moved to Switzerland, according to diplomatic and institutional sources. The negotiations, which began early last ye
title_en: DRC-AFC/M23 peace talks may be relocated from Doha to Switzerland
excerpt_en: April 4, 2026 - Ongoing peace talks between the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebel group, currently held in Doha, Qatar, could be moved to Switzerland, according to diplomatic and institutional sources. The negotiations, which began early last ye
body_en:
April 4, 2026 - Ongoing peace talks between the Government of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the AFC/M23 rebel group, currently held in Doha, Qatar, could be moved to Switzerland, according to diplomatic and institutional sources.
The negotiations, which began early last year under Qatari mediation, aim to address the root causes of the conflict in eastern DRC.
Reports indicate that renewed instability in the region, alongside broader international developments affecting Qatar, have contributed to discussions about relocating the talks.
The Center on International Cooperation at New York University has suggested that Switzerland could host the next phase of negotiations, with possible dates mentioned around mid-April 2026, though no formal agreement has been confirmed by either party.
Mediators continue to push for the resumption of dialogue, but both sides remain divided over allegations of ceasefire violations and ongoing security incidents in eastern DRC.
The AFC/M23 movement has accused the government in Kinshasa of continuing military operations in civilian-populated areas, while the government maintains its position on restoring state authority and security in conflict zones.
Conclusion
The period from March 23 to April 4, 2026 reflects a region shaped by a combination of persistent insecurity, active diplomacy, and ongoing modernization, with Rwanda playing a notable role in several developments across East Africa.
Eastern DR Congo remained highly unstable, marked by deadly ADF attacks and continued tensions between the DRC government and the AFC/M23 coalition. Although the DRC announced plans to disarm the FDLR, mistrust persists, as M23 continues to allege collaboration between the DRC forces and armed groups. Uganda’s military leadership has also suggested a possible conditional withdrawal from the region, adding further uncertainty to an already fragile security environment.
At the diplomatic and governance level, Rwanda expanded its international engagement through new ambassadorial appointments and strengthened cooperation with regional partners, including the export of digital tax systems to other African countries. Across the continent, broader political developments such as African Union procedural disputes and constitutional adjustments in Cameroon reflect ongoing institutional and governance transitions.
Economically, the region continues to attract investment, particularly in Rwanda’s industrial and infrastructure sectors, supported in part by international partners including China. The growth of digital financial services, including mobile lending platforms, highlights a wider regional shift toward financial inclusion, innovation, and modernization. Rwanda is also increasingly positioning itself in emerging discussions on digital governance and technologies such as artificial intelligence.
At the same time, Rwanda continues institutional reforms aimed at improving governance and efficiency, including updates to electoral frameworks and the expansion of plea bargaining within the justice system. Social policy efforts are also focused on issues such as student mental health and addressing long-standing challenges related to genocide memory and ideology.
Overall, while the region shows clear progress in economic development, governance reform, and digital transformation, long-term stability remains dependent on resolving armed conflicts in eastern DR Congo and strengthening trust and cooperation among regional actors.
By Jeff Buleli

title: Hundreds Killed as Drone Strikes Escalate Across Sudan, Targeting Civilian Infrastructure
excerpt: Sudan April 7, 2026 ; Intensifying drone warfare by Sudan’s warring parties has resulted in hundreds of civilian deaths and widespread destruction of critical infrastructure in the first quarter of 2026, according to conflict monitoring data and humanitarian sources. Analysis fro
title_en: Hundreds Killed as Drone Strikes Escalate Across Sudan, Targeting Civilian Infrastructure
excerpt_en: Sudan April 7, 2026 ; Intensifying drone warfare by Sudan’s warring parties has resulted in hundreds of civilian deaths and widespread destruction of critical infrastructure in the first quarter of 2026, according to conflict monitoring data and humanitarian sources. Analysis fro
body_en:
Sudan April 7, 2026 ; Intensifying drone warfare by Sudan’s warring parties has resulted in hundreds of civilian deaths and widespread destruction of critical infrastructure in the first quarter of 2026, according to conflict monitoring data and humanitarian sources.
Analysis from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project and local emergency response networks indicates a sharp rise in the use of suicide and loitering munitions since the start of the year, turning several cities across Darfur and Kordofan into active combat zones.
Estimates compiled from local and international reporting suggest that between 480 and 500 civilians have been killed in direct drone strikes on civilian targets since January, with more than 1,200 others injured.
The United Nations reported in late March that a drone strike on the Ed Daein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur killed more than 70 people, including patients, children, women, and medical personnel. The UN further estimated that over 500 civilians have been killed in similar strikes nationwide since the beginning of the year.
Medical staff at the Ed Daein facility described narrowly surviving the attack, which occurred during the first day of Eid, when multiple missiles struck the hospital in quick succession, causing panic and heavy casualties among patients and staff.
East Darfur has recorded the highest number of drone strikes, with local authorities reporting more than 250 raids in the past six months. South and West Darfur have also been heavily affected, with strikes hitting hospitals, religious sites, and marketplaces.
In North Kordofan, the city of El Obeid has been repeatedly targeted in attacks attributed to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In South Kordofan, the cities of Dilling and Kadugli have also experienced sustained aerial bombardment.
Elsewhere, reciprocal strikes have expanded the geographic scope of the conflict. The RSF has carried out attacks in White Nile, Al Jazirah, River Nile, and Red Sea states, while government forces have targeted RSF positions in Blue Nile, Darfur, and Kordofan regions.
At least 18 health and essential service facilities were hit by drone strikes during the first quarter of the year, forcing four major hospitals out of operation. The World Health Organization documented at least five attacks on medical facilities within the first 50 days of 2026, resulting in 69 deaths.
In West Kordofan, drone strikes on residential areas in Lagawa killed five civilians and injured 15 others, triggering new waves of displacement as residents fled intensified bombardments.

title: Legal Group Warns of Systematic Attacks on Aid Convoys and Drone Strikes in Sudan
excerpt: Sudan April 7, 2026 ; A Sudanese legal monitoring organization has raised alarm over what it describes as a sustained and systematic pattern of attacks targeting humanitarian operations amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
title_en: Legal Group Warns of Systematic Attacks on Aid Convoys and Drone Strikes in Sudan
excerpt_en: Sudan April 7, 2026 ; A Sudanese legal monitoring organization has raised alarm over what it describes as a sustained and systematic pattern of attacks targeting humanitarian operations amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
body_en:
Sudan April 7, 2026 ; A Sudanese legal monitoring organization has raised alarm over what it describes as a sustained and systematic pattern of attacks targeting humanitarian operations amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In a report released Tuesday, the group Emergency Lawyers said incidents involving aid convoys, warehouses, and relief workers have sharply increased since the war began in April 2023, severely undermining humanitarian access across Darfur and Kordofan.
The report documents more than 15 attacks on humanitarian convoys as of February 2026, alongside repeated cases of looting and destruction of logistics facilities. It describes the pattern as coordinated rather than isolated, pointing to a broader collapse in protections for humanitarian operations.
At least 10 aid workers have been killed and 11 others injured, according to the findings. In addition, around 20 aid trucks have been destroyed or burned, while some convoys were completely looted. The group also reported that more than 50 World Food Programme warehouses and 87 humanitarian offices have been seized, looted, or destroyed, resulting in significant losses of food and medical supplies.
The report further highlights what it calls a qualitative escalation in attacks, including the reported use of drones against aid convoys during 2025 and 2026.
The organization said these actions constitute serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes, particularly where humanitarian assistance is deliberately obstructed or starvation is used as a method of warfare.
It also outlined additional methods used to restrict aid delivery, including administrative obstruction, criminalization of humanitarian work, and politicization of relief efforts by warring parties.
Emergency Lawyers called for urgent international intervention to strengthen accountability mechanisms and ensure protection for humanitarian workers, warning that continued attacks risk deepening the country’s humanitarian crisis.

It also outlined additional methods used to restrict aid delivery, including administrative obstruction, criminalization of humanitarian work, and politicization of relief efforts by warring parties.
Emergency Lawyers called for urgent international intervention to strengthen accountability mechanisms and ensure protection for humanitarian workers, warning that continued attacks risk deepening the country’s humanitarian crisis.

title: UN Reports 28,000 Displaced in Blue Nile as Fighting Expands in Sudan
excerpt: Sudan April 7, 2026 ; Escalating violence in Sudan’s Blue Nile State has displaced more than 28,000 people since mid-January, according to the United Nations, as ongoing clashes and disrupted supply routes continue to hinder humanitarian operations. The UN said displacement surge
title_en: UN Reports 28,000 Displaced in Blue Nile as Fighting Expands in Sudan
excerpt_en: Sudan April 7, 2026 ; Escalating violence in Sudan’s Blue Nile State has displaced more than 28,000 people since mid-January, according to the United Nations, as ongoing clashes and disrupted supply routes continue to hinder humanitarian operations. The UN said displacement surge
body_en:
Sudan April 7, 2026 ; Escalating violence in Sudan’s Blue Nile State has displaced more than 28,000 people since mid-January, according to the United Nations, as ongoing clashes and disrupted supply routes continue to hinder humanitarian operations.
The UN said displacement surged following an offensive in Baw launched in January by an alliance involving the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N). Additional attacks on Al Kurmuk and areas near Geisan in March further accelerated civilian flight.
UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric reported that more than 4,000 people were displaced in the last 10 days alone. Data from the International Organization for Migration indicates that 87% of newly displaced people are sheltering in informal sites, while 9% are staying in schools and other public buildings.
The influx of displaced populations into Ed Damazin has placed severe pressure on food and water supplies. According to IOM assessments, 64% of displaced households lack access to clean drinking water, with many reporting long distances or non-functional water points. In addition, 73% face critical sanitation challenges, including a lack of gender-segregated facilities.
Humanitarian conditions have worsened due to continued attacks on infrastructure. In White Nile State, a drone strike on Al-Jabalain Hospital reportedly killed 10 health workers, while the destruction of a medical warehouse has disrupted the supply of essential medicines. Fuel shortages in South Kordofan have further slowed relief efforts and increased operational costs.
Insecurity continues to obstruct key transport routes, including the road between Rahad and Dilling. While some reports indicated partial reopening of the Dilling-North Kordofan corridor, the UN warned that the situation remains unstable, with ongoing fighting reported.
Despite the security risks, the United Nations Children's Fund and the World Health Organization are continuing vaccination campaigns in parts of Kordofan to address rising measles outbreaks in overcrowded displacement sites.
However, humanitarian agencies report that 65% of people in need are unable to access healthcare due to cost barriers and limited service availability.
The United Nations has reiterated its call for an immediate cessation of hostilities and unimpeded humanitarian access. The Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, is currently in Nairobi holding consultations aimed at addressing the worsening conflict and humanitarian crisis.
