title: Over 850 Foreign Fighters Backing RSF in Sudan Conflict, Military Sources Say
excerpt: Sudan April 5, 2026 ; More than 850 foreign nationals are fighting alongside Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), according to military sources, underscoring the growing international dimension of the country’s ongoing conflict. The development follows warnings from the United Nat
title_en: Over 850 Foreign Fighters Backing RSF in Sudan Conflict, Military Sources Say
excerpt_en: Sudan April 5, 2026 ; More than 850 foreign nationals are fighting alongside Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), according to military sources, underscoring the growing international dimension of the country’s ongoing conflict. The development follows warnings from the United Nat
body_en:
Sudan April 5, 2026 ; More than 850 foreign nationals are fighting alongside Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), according to military sources, underscoring the growing international dimension of the country’s ongoing conflict.
The development follows warnings from the United Nations Security Council that Sudan is increasingly serving as a “logistical hub” for armed groups, raising concerns about wider regional destabilization across the Sahel and East Africa.
Sources indicate that the foreign contingent includes both highly trained mercenaries-such as former soldiers and technical specialists-and irregular fighters from neighboring countries, many of whom are mobilized through traditional networks.
Investigations into RSF operations point to a notable reliance on Latin American personnel for advanced military functions. Colombian contractors are reportedly involved in operating unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), managing artillery systems, and overseeing aviation logistics at RSF-controlled airfields.
Intercepted communications in Spanish and Portuguese have been cited as evidence of foreign involvement. A group of Colombian fighters, reportedly composed of former security personnel, has been identified within RSF ranks and is believed to have played a role in coordinating combat operations.
Colombian authorities have previously confirmed that dozens of their nationals were killed in Sudan during 2025, including in airstrikes targeting strategic locations in Darfur.
Foreign involvement in RSF activities is not new. Prior to the outbreak of war in April 2023, Russian specialists were reportedly embedded in RSF-linked operations, particularly in gold mining and technical infrastructure. Sources suggest that some foreign contractors may still be providing operational support in western Sudan.
The movement of fighters and equipment is believed to rely on a complex regional network. Routes reportedly pass through cities such as Bosaso in Somalia and Benghazi in Libya, before crossing into Sudan through Chad or Libya.
Satellite imagery from late 2025 and early 2026 has shown increased activity at remote airstrips in Darfur, with unidentified cargo flights suspected of transporting personnel and advanced weaponry.
The International Organization for Migration has warned that Sudan’s porous borders, particularly in the west, are contributing to a cycle of instability. Armed groups from countries including Chad, Niger, and Mali are reportedly using RSF-controlled areas as staging grounds for recruitment and resupply before returning to their home regions.
Analysts say the growing presence of foreign fighters risks further complicating the conflict and undermining efforts to reach a political resolution.

title: Sudan, Libya Military Officials Hold Talks on Security Cooperation in Tripoli
excerpt: April 5, 2026 ; A Sudanese military delegation held high-level talks in Tripoli with senior Libyan officials, agreeing to strengthen intelligence sharing and security coordination between the two countries. The discussions brought together representatives of the Sudanese Armed Fo
title_en: Sudan, Libya Military Officials Hold Talks on Security Cooperation in Tripoli
excerpt_en: April 5, 2026 ; A Sudanese military delegation held high-level talks in Tripoli with senior Libyan officials, agreeing to strengthen intelligence sharing and security coordination between the two countries. The discussions brought together representatives of the Sudanese Armed Fo
body_en:
April 5, 2026 ; A Sudanese military delegation held high-level talks in Tripoli with senior Libyan officials, agreeing to strengthen intelligence sharing and security coordination between the two countries.
The discussions brought together representatives of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Libya’s internationally recognized government based in Tripoli, which controls large parts of western and southern Libya.
According to a statement from the Libyan General Staff, Lieutenant General Salahuddin al-Namroush met with Sudan’s Director of Military Intelligence, Lieutenant General Mohamed Ali Sabir, to explore avenues for expanding bilateral military cooperation.
The meeting focused on enhancing coordination in security matters, with both sides emphasizing the importance of closer collaboration to address shared regional challenges.
Libyan officials highlighted the longstanding ties between Sudan and Libya, noting that strengthened cooperation would contribute to broader regional stability. The two sides also agreed to expand joint training programs and increase the exchange of military expertise to improve operational readiness.
The talks come amid ongoing tensions involving eastern Libyan commander Khalifa Haftar, whom Sudanese authorities have accused of supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Sudanese officials allege that weapons have been transferred through eastern Libya and that RSF elements have received logistical and training support at bases under Haftar’s control, including facilities in southern Libya.
In June 2025, the Sudanese army also accused Haftar-aligned forces of participating alongside RSF fighters in an attack on a border area in Sudan’s Northern State.
The latest engagement in Tripoli reflects ongoing efforts by Sudan’s military leadership to reinforce regional alliances while addressing cross-border security concerns linked to the conflict.

title: Medical Group Accuses RSF of Storming Hospital in East Darfur
excerpt: East Darfur April 2, 2026 ; A Sudanese medical organization has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of storming a hospital in Ed Daein and assaulting healthcare workers, amid worsening insecurity in the region. In a statement released Thursday, the Sudan Doctors Network said a
title_en: Medical Group Accuses RSF of Storming Hospital in East Darfur
excerpt_en: East Darfur April 2, 2026 ; A Sudanese medical organization has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of storming a hospital in Ed Daein and assaulting healthcare workers, amid worsening insecurity in the region. In a statement released Thursday, the Sudan Doctors Network said a
body_en:
East Darfur April 2, 2026 ; A Sudanese medical organization has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of storming a hospital in Ed Daein and assaulting healthcare workers, amid worsening insecurity in the region.
In a statement released Thursday, the Sudan Doctors Network said an RSF unit raided Al-Usra Hospital in the Al-Nazir neighborhood, where medical staff were reportedly beaten during the incident.
The group said the attackers caused extensive damage to the facility and destroyed critical medical equipment, severely disrupting healthcare services in the city.
Ed Daein, which is under RSF control, has experienced a sharp deterioration in security conditions, with increasing reports of violent crime, including killings, looting, and kidnappings for ransom.
According to the statement, the attack occurred without any response from local authorities, raising concerns about the safety of civilians and the ability of medical facilities to operate under current conditions.
The Sudan Doctors Network also alleged that the group responsible for the raid is protected by local administrative leadership, and described the incident as a serious violation of international law prohibiting attacks on healthcare infrastructure and personnel.
The report comes amid a broader escalation of violence against medical workers in Darfur. In a separate incident on March 30, a doctor was killed in Nyala following an assault by RSF personnel at his residence.
The organization warned that continued attacks on healthcare facilities risk further collapsing already fragile medical services in conflict-affected areas.

title: Drone Strike on Al-Jabalain Hospital Kills 12 in Sudan’s White Nile State
excerpt: Sudan April 2, 2026 ; A drone strike on a hospital in southern Sudan has killed at least 12 people, including two doctors, according to medical sources, in the latest attack on healthcare infrastructure amid the country’s ongoing conflict. The strike targeted Al-Jabalain Hospital
title_en: Drone Strike on Al-Jabalain Hospital Kills 12 in Sudan’s White Nile State
excerpt_en: Sudan April 2, 2026 ; A drone strike on a hospital in southern Sudan has killed at least 12 people, including two doctors, according to medical sources, in the latest attack on healthcare infrastructure amid the country’s ongoing conflict. The strike targeted Al-Jabalain Hospital
body_en:
Sudan April 2, 2026 ; A drone strike on a hospital in southern Sudan has killed at least 12 people, including two doctors, according to medical sources, in the latest attack on healthcare infrastructure amid the country’s ongoing conflict.
The strike targeted Al-Jabalain Hospital in Al-Jabalain, near the border with South Sudan. Victims reportedly included patients and medical staff present at the facility at the time of the attack.
The incident follows another drone strike a day earlier on a medical warehouse in Kosti, also in White Nile State, which left three people injured, including a pharmacist.
Local sources attributed the hospital attack to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), though casualty figures varied, with some reports indicating slightly lower death tolls, including senior hospital personnel.
The attack is part of a broader pattern of violence targeting healthcare services. The World Health Organization has previously reported hundreds of attacks on medical facilities since the start of the war, resulting in significant loss of life and widespread damage to health infrastructure.
Other monitoring groups have also documented extensive violence against healthcare workers and facilities, citing hundreds of incidents ranging from direct attacks to obstruction of medical services.
Rights observers have condemned the continued targeting of hospitals and medical personnel, warning that such actions constitute violations of international humanitarian law.
White Nile State has seen a recent surge in drone strikes, with attacks hitting fuel stations, supply depots, and other civilian infrastructure in addition to healthcare facilities.
Regional authorities have visited affected sites in Kosti, Rabak, and Al-Jabalain, stating that such attacks would not deter efforts to maintain control and restore stability.
The increasing use of drones in the conflict has intensified concerns, as strikes increasingly affect civilian areas, including hospitals, energy infrastructure, and humanitarian assets.

title: Foreign Fighters and Mercenaries Emerge as Key Factor in Sudan’s War
excerpt: Sudan April 5, 2026 ; Sudanese military sources say that more than 850 foreign fighters are currently operating alongside the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), underscoring what officials describe as a growing internationalization of the country’s ongoing conflict. The claims align wit
title_en: Foreign Fighters and Mercenaries Emerge as Key Factor in Sudan’s War
excerpt_en: Sudan April 5, 2026 ; Sudanese military sources say that more than 850 foreign fighters are currently operating alongside the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), underscoring what officials describe as a growing internationalization of the country’s ongoing conflict. The claims align wit
body_en:
Sudan April 5, 2026 ; Sudanese military sources say that more than 850 foreign fighters are currently operating alongside the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), underscoring what officials describe as a growing internationalization of the country’s ongoing conflict.
The claims align with earlier warnings from the United Nations Security Council that Sudan has evolved into a logistical hub for armed groups, with implications for regional stability across the Sahel and East Africa.
According to military sources, the foreign presence is divided into two main categories: experienced mercenaries with prior military training, and less organized fighters with limited battlefield experience who rely on irregular combat tactics.
Officials say these individuals are involved in a wide range of operations, including drone warfare, artillery coordination, technical support, communications, and airfield management.
Reports indicate that some Colombian nationals are among the most prominent foreign participants, allegedly specializing in drone operations and artillery systems. Military sources claim that communications in Spanish and Portuguese have been intercepted in conflict zones, particularly in Darfur.
The presence of additional fighters from Chad, Libya, Niger, and South Sudan has also been reported, with Libyan-linked networks allegedly facilitating logistics, arms transfers, and movement of personnel across borders.
Military and intelligence assessments suggest that foreign support networks extend beyond Africa, with unverified reports pointing to possible involvement of Russian technical specialists in areas such as communications, logistics, and resource management prior to and during the conflict.
Investigative findings and UN-related reporting have further pointed to structured recruitment and transit routes that move fighters through regional hubs such as Somalia and Libya before they enter Sudan via its western borders.

Analysts say the growing presence of foreign fighters is contributing to the complexity and intensity of the war, complicating efforts to reach a political settlement and further destabilizing already fragile border regions.
Conclusion
The situation in Sudan as of April 10, 2026 is defined by a stark contradiction: cautious diplomatic re-engagement on one hand, and escalating, increasingly technologized warfare alongside a deepening humanitarian collapse on the other.
While the reopening of the United Nations headquarters in Khartoum signals a symbolic return of international presence and renewed engagement, and while regional consultations and emerging political coalitions suggest attempts to shape a post-conflict trajectory, these developments remain largely disconnected from conditions on the ground.
Diplomatic re-engagement amid political fragmentation
The UN’s return to Khartoum marks a notable shift toward in-country coordination after nearly three years of remote operations from Port Sudan. At the political level, new civilian-oriented alliances continue to emerge, including coalitions advocating for transitional governance and civilian rule. However, these efforts are fragmented, often competing, and shaped by internal divisions-such as disputes over institutional reforms and the reactivation of legacy anti-corruption bodies.
At the same time, Sudan’s rival power centers remain entrenched. The military leadership publicly reiterates commitments to a democratic transition, while the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) seek parallel legitimacy, including proposals for independent UN humanitarian offices in territories under their control-an approach that highlights the ongoing contest over sovereignty and recognition.
Escalation of drone warfare and foreign involvement
The conflict has increasingly shifted toward high-intensity, technology-driven warfare. Drone strikes and loitering munitions have become central instruments of combat, with hundreds of civilian deaths reported in the first months of 2026 alone.
Civilian infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted, including hospitals, energy facilities, markets, and residential areas. Notable incidents include strikes on medical facilities in White Nile State and mass casualty attacks in civilian gatherings, underscoring a pattern of attacks that continues to erode basic protections for non-combatants.
This escalation is further complicated by the growing internationalization of the conflict. Military sources and investigations indicate the presence of hundreds of foreign fighters supporting the RSF in roles involving drone operations, artillery systems, logistics, and technical command functions. These transnational networks have expanded the operational capacity of armed groups and widened the geographic footprint of the war.
Humanitarian and economic collapse
At the humanitarian level, Sudan faces a rapidly deteriorating emergency. The 2026 response plan remains severely underfunded despite tens of millions in need, while neighboring countries such as Chad are hosting over a million Sudanese refugees under increasingly unsustainable conditions.
Reports from humanitarian and human rights organizations document widespread abuses, including mass displacement, sexual violence, attacks on healthcare systems, and arbitrary detention. In parallel, the economic situation continues to deteriorate sharply, with the national currency collapsing and authorities introducing emergency stabilization measures aimed at containing inflation and restoring basic fiscal control.
Overall trajectory
Sudan is increasingly trapped in a cycle where diplomatic initiatives and political restructuring efforts are outpaced by the intensity and sophistication of ongoing conflict. The expansion of drone warfare, the involvement of foreign fighters, and the systematic targeting of civilian infrastructure point to a conflict that is becoming both more complex and more difficult to contain.
Without a sustained and enforceable international framework to protect humanitarian corridors, restrict attacks on civilian infrastructure, and support a credible political settlement, the risk of long-term state fragmentation and social collapse continues to rise.

title: Sudan Mining Revenues Surge as Gold Production Nears Targets
excerpt: Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - Sudan’s mineral resources regulator has reported a sharp increase in artisanal mining revenues during the first quarter of 2026, with collections reaching 113% of projected targets, according to official figures released on Thursday. The Sudanese Minera
title_en: Sudan Mining Revenues Surge as Gold Production Nears Targets
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - Sudan’s mineral resources regulator has reported a sharp increase in artisanal mining revenues during the first quarter of 2026, with collections reaching 113% of projected targets, according to official figures released on Thursday. The Sudanese Minera
body_en:
Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - Sudan’s mineral resources regulator has reported a sharp increase in artisanal mining revenues during the first quarter of 2026, with collections reaching 113% of projected targets, according to official figures released on Thursday.
The Sudanese Mineral Resources Company (SMRC) said gold production over the same period achieved 89% of its planned target, underscoring the mining sector’s continued importance as the country’s primary economic driver amid ongoing conflict.
Officials noted that artisanal mining now accounts for approximately 80% of Sudan’s total gold output, with major activity concentrated in River Nile, Northern, and Red Sea states, while the organized corporate sector contributes the remaining share.
During an executive meeting in Khartoum, SMRC’s general manager, Mohamed Taher Omer, described the quarterly performance as strong and called for increased production to further support the national treasury. He also highlighted improvements in environmental safety measures and ongoing efforts to modernize operations through digital governance.
The director of the planning department, Al-Sadiq Al-Haj Taha, said surplus revenues have been directed toward social responsibility programs, including projects in healthcare, water access, and education. He added that environmental compliance currently stands at 70% in the formal mining sector and 57% in artisanal mining areas.
The company also announced plans to launch a digital platform and an artificial intelligence-based system for mineral transactions, as part of broader government-led digital transformation efforts in the sector.
Despite strong production figures, challenges persist in formal export channels. Authorities have previously noted a significant gap between total production and officially recorded exports, with large volumes of gold believed to circulate through informal networks.
Official data indicate that Sudan produced approximately 70 tonnes of gold in 2025, while exports through formal channels were significantly lower. Gold remains the country’s dominant export commodity, accounting for more than half of total export revenues.

title: Sudan Industrial Recovery Stalls as Only 10% of Factories Resume Operations
excerpt: Khartoum, April 26, 2026 - Sudan’s industrial recovery remains severely constrained, with only about 10% of factories back in operation three years after the outbreak of conflict, according to industry officials. A senior figure within the Industrial Chambers Union said the slow
title_en: Sudan Industrial Recovery Stalls as Only 10% of Factories Resume Operations
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 26, 2026 - Sudan’s industrial recovery remains severely constrained, with only about 10% of factories back in operation three years after the outbreak of conflict, according to industry officials. A senior figure within the Industrial Chambers Union said the slow
body_en:
Khartoum, April 26, 2026 - Sudan’s industrial recovery remains severely constrained, with only about 10% of factories back in operation three years after the outbreak of conflict, according to industry officials.
A senior figure within the Industrial Chambers Union said the slow pace of recovery reflects deep structural challenges, despite isolated signs of resilience within the sector.
He noted that his steel manufacturing plant recently resumed production with an initial monthly capacity of 7,000 tonnes, with plans to gradually increase output to 12,000 tonnes. However, he warned that broader industrial activity continues to face significant obstacles.
Key challenges include complex import procedures for spare parts, difficulties obtaining certificates of origin, high storage costs at ports, and ongoing shortages of raw materials. Regulatory requirements linked to import documentation have also been cited as a major bottleneck.
Some factories have reportedly taken more than 300 days to resume operations, far exceeding initial projections of around 50 days, due to extensive war-related damage and logistical constraints in sourcing equipment and conducting repairs.
Industry representatives are calling on authorities, including the central bank, to introduce exemptions and facilitate access to essential inputs in order to accelerate recovery and stabilize production.
Official data indicate that approximately 1,800 industrial facilities have been impacted by the conflict, including around 650 that were completely destroyed. Estimates suggest total losses in the industrial sector range between $50 billion and $58 billion, underscoring the scale of the economic damage.

title: Sudan’s Democratic Block Adopts New Statutes, Discusses Democratic Transition

title_en: Sudan’s Democratic Block Adopts New Statutes, Discusses Democratic Transition
excerpt_en: Port Sudan, April 26, 2026 - Sudan’s Democratic Block alliance has adopted new internal statutes and held discussions on the country’s path toward democratic transition during a two-day organizational meeting in Port Sudan. The meeting, held under the theme “A National Vision Tha
body_en:
Port Sudan, April 26, 2026 - Sudan’s Democratic Block alliance has adopted new internal statutes and held discussions on the country’s path toward democratic transition during a two-day organizational meeting in Port Sudan.
The meeting, held under the theme “A National Vision That Prioritizes Peace and Restores Stability,” brought together more than 19 political and armed groups aligned within the Forces for Freedom and Change - Democratic Block (FFC-DB).
A senior member of the Sovereign Council and leading figure in the alliance said discussions focused on shaping a roadmap for democratic transition while maintaining unity among political actors in the face of ongoing conflict. He emphasized the need to prioritize national interests and strengthen internal cohesion.
Participants described the current situation as a critical moment for the country, calling for a shift away from entrenched political approaches in order to address evolving challenges and plan for long-term stability.
The Democratic Block, formed in 2021 following a split within the broader Forces for Freedom and Change coalition, includes groups that later supported the military’s measures in October of that year.
During the meeting, member organizations formally endorsed the alliance’s new statutes, which leaders said aim to strengthen coordination and provide a unified political framework. Officials described the move as a step toward rebuilding state institutions and consolidating a common national vision.
The gathering included a wide range of political figures, armed movement leaders, and representatives of civil society, as well as delegates from displaced and refugee communities and groups from eastern Sudan.
Organizers said the adoption of the statutes reflects an effort to overcome fragmentation within the political landscape and establish a more cohesive front to address governance challenges and advance stability.

title: Dengue Fever Deaths Rise in Northern Sudan as Outbreak Spreads
excerpt: Khartoum, April 24, 2026 - Health authorities in Sudan’s Northern State have issued an urgent warning following a confirmed death linked to a growing dengue fever outbreak, as cases continue to rise across northern regions of the country. The Humanitarian Aid Commission in Northe
title_en: Dengue Fever Deaths Rise in Northern Sudan as Outbreak Spreads
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 24, 2026 - Health authorities in Sudan’s Northern State have issued an urgent warning following a confirmed death linked to a growing dengue fever outbreak, as cases continue to rise across northern regions of the country. The Humanitarian Aid Commission in Northe
body_en:
Khartoum, April 24, 2026 - Health authorities in Sudan’s Northern State have issued an urgent warning following a confirmed death linked to a growing dengue fever outbreak, as cases continue to rise across northern regions of the country.
The Humanitarian Aid Commission in Northern State called for immediate intervention from international humanitarian partners to help contain the spread of the disease, particularly in Merowe and the Alzuma area.
Officials confirmed that infections in the state have reached 173 cases, with the first recorded fatality prompting concerns that the outbreak could escalate rapidly without urgent preventive action.
Northern State is currently hosting large numbers of displaced people from conflict-affected areas in Darfur and Kordofan, many of whom are living in overcrowded conditions in camps east of Al Dabbah, further increasing health risks.
In neighbouring River Nile State, the Ministry of Health reported a continued rise in infections across multiple localities. Recent figures show 108 new cases, bringing the total number of dengue infections in the state to 6,304, with 12 recorded deaths.
National health authorities have already warned that dengue fever is spreading across at least seven states, alongside separate outbreaks of hepatitis in three regions.
The country’s healthcare system remains under severe strain due to the ongoing conflict, which has disrupted supply chains, restricted access to medical facilities, and significantly weakened primary healthcare services across affected areas.

Northern State is currently hosting large numbers of displaced people from conflict-affected areas in Darfur and Kordofan, many of whom are living in overcrowded conditions in camps east of Al Dabbah, further increasing health risks.
In neighbouring River Nile State, the Ministry of Health reported a continued rise in infections across multiple localities. Recent figures show 108 new cases, bringing the total number of dengue infections in the state to 6,304, with 12 recorded deaths.
National health authorities have already warned that dengue fever is spreading across at least seven states, alongside separate outbreaks of hepatitis in three regions.
The country’s healthcare system remains under severe strain due to the ongoing conflict, which has disrupted supply chains, restricted access to medical facilities, and significantly weakened primary healthcare services across affected areas.

title_en: Six Killed in Gold Mine Collapse in Red Sea State
excerpt_en: Port Sudan, April 14, 2026 - At least six people have died after the collapse of an informal gold mine in Sudan’s Red Sea State, underscoring persistent safety risks in the country’s largely unregulated artisanal mining sector. The incident occurred on Wednesday at a mining site
body_en:
Port Sudan, April 14, 2026 - At least six people have died after the collapse of an informal gold mine in Sudan’s Red Sea State, underscoring persistent safety risks in the country’s largely unregulated artisanal mining sector.
The incident occurred on Wednesday at a mining site in the Keliti area of the Ganab and Aulib locality, where the mine reportedly caved in while workers were underground, trapping several miners.
Local sources said rescue teams have recovered six bodies so far, but recovery operations are being hampered by a lack of heavy equipment, limited civil defense capacity, and inadequate emergency medical supplies. Eyewitnesses described the situation at the site as critical, with delays in access to ambulances and basic first aid resources.
The collapse adds to a growing number of similar accidents in Sudan’s informal mining industry, where safety regulations remain minimal or poorly enforced.
Since the outbreak of conflict in 2023, artisanal mining has expanded significantly across the country. The sector is now estimated to employ more than two million people and accounts for over 80% of Sudan’s gold production, making it both a crucial economic lifeline and a major source of occupational risk.

title: Measles Outbreak Kills Four in North Darfur as Health System Collapses
excerpt: Shangil Tobaya, April 25, 2026 - A measles outbreak has killed at least four people in North Darfur, as health authorities warn of a worsening epidemic amid a near-total breakdown of healthcare services in the region. The General Coordination for Displaced Persons and Refugees in
title_en: Measles Outbreak Kills Four in North Darfur as Health System Collapses
excerpt_en: Shangil Tobaya, April 25, 2026 - A measles outbreak has killed at least four people in North Darfur, as health authorities warn of a worsening epidemic amid a near-total breakdown of healthcare services in the region. The General Coordination for Displaced Persons and Refugees in
body_en:
Shangil Tobaya, April 25, 2026 - A measles outbreak has killed at least four people in North Darfur, as health authorities warn of a worsening epidemic amid a near-total breakdown of healthcare services in the region.
The General Coordination for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Darfur reported a sharp rise in suspected measles infections, citing more than 50 recorded cases in the Shangil Tobaya area alone. Officials warned that the number is likely to increase due to limited medical response capacity and shortages of essential medicines.
Additional cases have been reported in surrounding localities, including Dar al-Salam and Abu Hamra, with verification and case tracking still ongoing in some areas.
Health workers say the outbreak is occurring against the backdrop of widespread disruption to immunization campaigns and the closure of many health facilities due to ongoing conflict. The collapse of basic health services has significantly reduced access to treatment, particularly for children, who remain the most vulnerable.
A spokesperson for the coordination group said the situation reflects a broader humanitarian crisis in which deteriorating infrastructure and insecurity have severely weakened epidemic response mechanisms.
Humanitarian appeals have been directed to international health agencies for urgent intervention, including vaccination campaigns and emergency medical support to contain the spread of the disease.
The group also called for an end to hostilities, warning that continued fighting is worsening humanitarian conditions and increasing the risk of preventable deaths among women and children due to disease outbreaks and lack of care.

title: Doctors Report Ethnic Killings and Cholera Outbreak in RSF Detention Centres
excerpt: El Fasher, April 27, 2026 - Sudanese medical professionals have raised alarm over reports of ethnically targeted killings and a severe cholera outbreak inside detention facilities run by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in El Fasher, North Darfur. According to findings covering the
title_en: Doctors Report Ethnic Killings and Cholera Outbreak in RSF Detention Centres
excerpt_en: El Fasher, April 27, 2026 - Sudanese medical professionals have raised alarm over reports of ethnically targeted killings and a severe cholera outbreak inside detention facilities run by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in El Fasher, North Darfur. According to findings covering the
body_en:
El Fasher, April 27, 2026 - Sudanese medical professionals have raised alarm over reports of ethnically targeted killings and a severe cholera outbreak inside detention facilities run by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in El Fasher, North Darfur.
According to findings covering the period from January to April 2026, hundreds of civilians, including women and children, are being held in RSF-controlled detention sites under conditions described as inhumane. The report alleges that detainees are subjected to torture, interrogation, and, in some cases, execution based on ethnic identity.
Data compiled by medical networks indicate that approximately 907 military detainees and 1,470 civilians are currently in custody. Among the civilian detainees are 426 children and 370 women, held in various locations including Shala Prison, a pediatric hospital, the land port, and makeshift facilities such as shipping containers.
Health conditions within these centres are reported to be critical. A cholera outbreak that began in February has spread rapidly due to overcrowding, lack of clean water, poor sanitation, and widespread malnutrition. Medical sources estimate that between five and 10 people are dying each week due to inadequate access to treatment, with total deaths linked to the outbreak surpassing 300 over the past two months.
The report also describes grim conditions in which bodies are sometimes left for extended periods within detention areas before other detainees are compelled to bury them.
Healthcare services in El Fasher have largely collapsed amid ongoing conflict, with severe shortages of medical staff and supplies. At least 22 doctors, including four women, are reported to have been detained, further weakening the already strained health system.
The findings add to growing concerns over conditions in detention facilities and the broader humanitarian crisis in Darfur as the conflict continues.

title: First International Flight Lands at Khartoum Airport Since Start of War
excerpt: Khartoum, April 28, 2026 - The first direct international commercial flight in three years has landed at Khartoum International Airport, marking a significant step toward restoring air connectivity to Sudan’s capital. The Kuwait Airways flight arrived on Tuesday carrying around 3
title_en: First International Flight Lands at Khartoum Airport Since Start of War
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 28, 2026 - The first direct international commercial flight in three years has landed at Khartoum International Airport, marking a significant step toward restoring air connectivity to Sudan’s capital. The Kuwait Airways flight arrived on Tuesday carrying around 3
body_en:
Khartoum, April 28, 2026 - The first direct international commercial flight in three years has landed at Khartoum International Airport, marking a significant step toward restoring air connectivity to Sudan’s capital.
The Kuwait Airways flight arrived on Tuesday carrying around 300 Sudanese citizens returning from Kuwait, in what officials described as a milestone in the gradual reopening of the country’s main aviation hub.
Khartoum airport had been largely out of service since the outbreak of conflict in April 2023, when fighting and attacks caused extensive damage to infrastructure, terminals, and aircraft.
Airport authorities said the facility is now ready to resume international operations after meeting safety standards and securing the necessary clearances.
Officials overseeing expatriate affairs said the flight reflects ongoing government efforts to facilitate the return of Sudanese nationals from abroad. They added that the move could pave the way for the resumption of regular routes between Khartoum and regional destinations, potentially supporting trade, including agricultural and livestock exports.
Government representatives also highlighted the role of bilateral coordination in organizing the return, noting strengthened cooperation with partners involved in facilitating the operation.
Local officials said the flight follows a broader trend of returns to the capital, including arrivals by land from neighboring countries, attributing the movement to gradual improvements in basic services and relative stability in parts of Khartoum.
The reopening process has been gradual. Earlier this year, Sudan’s national carrier resumed limited domestic flights to the capital following rehabilitation work. However, the airport has faced setbacks, including damage from a drone strike that affected newly restored infrastructure.
Since the start of the conflict, most international and regional air traffic has been redirected to Port Sudan, where aviation operations were relocated as Khartoum remained largely inaccessible.

title: Sudanese Rights Group Says Army and RSF Detained Three Brothers
excerpt: Khartoum, April 20, 2026 - A Sudanese legal advocacy group, Emergency Lawyers, has reported the detention and enforced disappearance of three brothers by both the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), warning of what it describes as a growing pattern of serious violat
title_en: Sudanese Rights Group Says Army and RSF Detained Three Brothers
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 20, 2026 - A Sudanese legal advocacy group, Emergency Lawyers, has reported the detention and enforced disappearance of three brothers by both the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), warning of what it describes as a growing pattern of serious violat
body_en:
Khartoum, April 20, 2026 - A Sudanese legal advocacy group, Emergency Lawyers, has reported the detention and enforced disappearance of three brothers by both the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), warning of what it describes as a growing pattern of serious violations against civilians.
In a statement issued Monday, the group said the cases reflect an escalating climate of arbitrary detention, lack of accountability, and the collapse of legal protections amid the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
According to the report, the three brothers - Abdel Rahman, Mohammed, and Badri Ibrahim Badri - were detained separately in different parts of the country under varying circumstances.
Abdel Rahman Ibrahim was arrested by military intelligence on May 20 at his home in Omdurman. He was reportedly held incommunicado and moved between detention facilities in Omdurman and Soba on accusations of collaborating with the RSF. He was released after 11 months in detention in what the group described as poor physical and psychological condition.
The RSF detained the youngest brother, Mohammed Badri, on August 20, 2025, in Bara, North Kordofan. He was later transferred to Nyala in South Darfur and is believed to be held in Kober prison, though his exact status remains unconfirmed.
The eldest brother, Badri Ibrahim, was also detained by the RSF on August 25 in North Kordofan and transferred to the Dagris detention centre in Nyala, where he remains forcibly disappeared under conditions the group says lack transparency and basic dignity.
Emergency Lawyers further reported that the family has been subjected to financial extortion and fraud by individuals falsely claiming to have information about the detainees’ whereabouts.
The group called for the immediate and unconditional release of all arbitrarily detained individuals and urged both warring parties to shut down illegal detention facilities, stressing that detention is increasingly being used as a tool of war.

title: RSF Leader Sentences Defected General to Death in Absentia
excerpt: Nyala, April 23, 2026 - The commander of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemetti, has stripped defected Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as “Al-Qubba,” of his military rank and sentenced him to death in absentia. The decision follow
title_en: RSF Leader Sentences Defected General to Death in Absentia
excerpt_en: Nyala, April 23, 2026 - The commander of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemetti, has stripped defected Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as “Al-Qubba,” of his military rank and sentenced him to death in absentia. The decision follow
body_en:
Nyala, April 23, 2026 - The commander of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemetti, has stripped defected Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as “Al-Qubba,” of his military rank and sentenced him to death in absentia.
The decision follows accusations that the senior officer deserted his post and collaborated with the Sudanese army. Al-Qubba had recently defected amid internal tensions within the RSF leadership in North Darfur after disagreements over command appointments following the group’s takeover of El Fasher in October 2025.
Sources indicate that the officer’s defection was linked to disputes over his exclusion from key leadership roles, particularly the appointment of another commander in North Darfur. He is also reported to have raised concerns about discrimination against his forces and inadequate logistical support.
After fleeing North Darfur, Al-Qubba reportedly reached Dongola on April 19, where he surrendered to the Sudanese army. He later met with the head of Sudan’s Sovereign Council and commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
In an internal RSF decision, a field court reportedly approved charges against him, including desertion, abandonment of military positions, and communication with opposing forces. The ruling also cited rebellion against the group’s 2025 internal order framework.
A formal memo from the RSF administration confirmed that Hemetti ratified the court’s decision, demoting Al-Nour to the rank of private and formally dismissing him from service effective April 22. The death sentence was issued in absentia following his arrival in territory controlled by the army.
Al-Qubba is a founding member of the RSF and a prominent figure in the ongoing conflict that began in April 2023. He previously played a key role in battles for El Fasher alongside senior commanders, some of whom have since been killed or reassigned amid internal power struggles within the group.

title: Legal Group Says RSF Extorting Families for Release of Detainees
excerpt: Nyala, April 25, 2026 - A Sudanese legal advocacy group has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of extorting money from families in exchange for the release of civilian detainees held at Dagrees prison in Nyala, South Darfur, describing the practice as a pattern of systematic
title_en: Legal Group Says RSF Extorting Families for Release of Detainees
excerpt_en: Nyala, April 25, 2026 - A Sudanese legal advocacy group has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of extorting money from families in exchange for the release of civilian detainees held at Dagrees prison in Nyala, South Darfur, describing the practice as a pattern of systematic
body_en:
Nyala, April 25, 2026 - A Sudanese legal advocacy group has accused the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of extorting money from families in exchange for the release of civilian detainees held at Dagrees prison in Nyala, South Darfur, describing the practice as a pattern of systematic abuse.
The Emergency Lawyers group said that recent releases of detainees were carried out in return for cash payments, alleging that families were forced to provide ransom money under coercive conditions.
The RSF, which has established Nyala as the center of its parallel administrative authority in Darfur, has faced growing domestic and international criticism over its governance structures and detention practices.
Human rights monitors report a sharp increase in arbitrary arrests and enforced disappearances across Darfur since the outbreak of conflict in April 2023, with civilians held in conditions described as severely lacking legal oversight and humanitarian access.
Dagrees prison, located approximately 25 kilometres west of Nyala, has been cited in multiple reports as a site of serious abuse, including allegations of mistreatment of detainees and prolonged incommunicado detention.
According to the legal group, some detainees were permitted to contact relatives to request payment for their release, with arrests reportedly carried out in areas under current or former RSF control.
The statement said detainees have endured prolonged confinement in conditions that fall far below minimum international standards, calling the practice a serious violation of human rights and humanitarian law. It further warned that linking release to financial payment could constitute elements of trafficking and illicit profiteering.
The group stressed that such releases do not exempt perpetrators from future legal accountability and called for investigations into detention practices and conditions in RSF-run facilities.

title: Army Drone Strikes in Darfur Kill Dozens as Conflict Intensifies
excerpt: Ed Daein / Geneina, April 13, 2026 - Sudan’s armed forces have launched a series of drone strikes across the Darfur region, resulting in at least 20 civilian deaths and significant destruction, according to local officials and monitoring groups. The strikes, carried out over Sund
title_en: Army Drone Strikes in Darfur Kill Dozens as Conflict Intensifies
excerpt_en: Ed Daein / Geneina, April 13, 2026 - Sudan’s armed forces have launched a series of drone strikes across the Darfur region, resulting in at least 20 civilian deaths and significant destruction, according to local officials and monitoring groups. The strikes, carried out over Sund
body_en:
Ed Daein / Geneina, April 13, 2026 - Sudan’s armed forces have launched a series of drone strikes across the Darfur region, resulting in at least 20 civilian deaths and significant destruction, according to local officials and monitoring groups.
The strikes, carried out over Sunday and Monday, targeted areas in East, West, and North Darfur, marking one of the most extensive aerial campaigns in recent months as the military seeks to weaken the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which control large parts of the region.
In West Darfur, local authorities reported that drones struck multiple sites, including a crowded market area, where at least five people were killed and around 20 others injured. The attack caused extensive damage, with shops and infrastructure destroyed by fire.
Additional strikes reportedly hit a civilian vehicle in the Sisi area, along the road between Zalingei and Geneina, killing five more people. Local officials condemned the incidents, describing them as violations of international humanitarian law and calling for accountability.
In East Darfur, the city of Ed Daein was also heavily targeted. According to local administrative sources, at least 10 civilians were killed, including several environmental health workers. Some of the strikes reportedly hit buildings used by the RSF, including facilities previously associated with intelligence services.
Residents reported repeated drone activity in recent weeks, with attacks affecting both military-linked sites and civilian infrastructure, including health facilities.
In North Darfur, further strikes were reported in the Al-Sereif area, where a police station was destroyed along with vehicles believed to be used by RSF fighters.
Military sources indicated that part of the campaign aims to disrupt RSF supply lines, particularly fuel shipments entering from neighboring countries.
The escalation highlights the growing reliance on aerial warfare in Sudan’s conflict and its increasing toll on civilian populations, particularly in densely populated or contested urban areas across Darfur.

title: Artillery Strike Hits Dilling Market, Killing Four Amid Escalating Fighting
excerpt: Dilling, April 11, 2026 - At least four people were killed and 13 others injured after artillery fire struck a central market in the city of Dilling, in South Kordofan, as fighting continues between Sudanese forces and armed groups. Local sources reported that the shelling target
title_en: Artillery Strike Hits Dilling Market, Killing Four Amid Escalating Fighting
excerpt_en: Dilling, April 11, 2026 - At least four people were killed and 13 others injured after artillery fire struck a central market in the city of Dilling, in South Kordofan, as fighting continues between Sudanese forces and armed groups. Local sources reported that the shelling target
body_en:
Dilling, April 11, 2026 - At least four people were killed and 13 others injured after artillery fire struck a central market in the city of Dilling, in South Kordofan, as fighting continues between Sudanese forces and armed groups.
Local sources reported that the shelling targeted a busy market area, causing significant destruction. Four shops were completely destroyed, while at least seven others sustained partial damage. The attack is attributed to a coalition involving the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and a faction of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, although independent verification remains limited.
The incident forms part of a broader escalation in hostilities around Dilling, South Kordofan’s second-largest city. Armed groups have reportedly intensified their use of heavy artillery and drones in recent weeks, with repeated strikes affecting civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, schools, and industrial sites.
Despite periodic ground offensives by the RSF and allied fighters, the Sudanese army has so far maintained control of the city, repelling attempts to seize it.
Dilling remains heavily populated, as civilians displaced by surrounding violence continue to seek refuge there. However, the humanitarian situation has deteriorated sharply. Local activists warn that medical facilities are overwhelmed, with many healthcare workers having fled during prolonged periods of siege. Those remaining face acute shortages of essential medicines and equipment.
Access to the city has fluctuated amid shifting frontlines. After months of isolation, army forces and allied units reopened supply routes earlier this year, only for access to be disrupted again as fighting resumed. Renewed clashes in early April reportedly led to temporary gains by government forces in nearby strategic areas.
The situation in Dilling highlights the growing toll of Sudan’s protracted conflict on civilians, as urban centers increasingly become focal points of sustained military operations.

title: Drone Strike at Chad Border Crossing Kills Three, Injures Dozens
excerpt: Geneina, April 15, 2026 - At least three people were killed and dozens injured in a drone strike targeting a border crossing in West Darfur, as Sudan’s conflict continues to spill across strategic transit routes. According to local activists and emergency response groups, the str
title_en: Drone Strike at Chad Border Crossing Kills Three, Injures Dozens
excerpt_en: Geneina, April 15, 2026 - At least three people were killed and dozens injured in a drone strike targeting a border crossing in West Darfur, as Sudan’s conflict continues to spill across strategic transit routes. According to local activists and emergency response groups, the str
body_en:
Geneina, April 15, 2026 - At least three people were killed and dozens injured in a drone strike targeting a border crossing in West Darfur, as Sudan’s conflict continues to spill across strategic transit routes.
According to local activists and emergency response groups, the strike hit the Adukong crossing near the Chad border, killing three porters and injuring numerous workers, many of them reportedly Chadian nationals. The attack also caused damage to civilian vehicles, food supplies, and fuel stocks.
The incident is part of an intensifying aerial campaign by Sudanese armed forces across the Darfur region, much of which remains under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Recent strikes have targeted a range of locations, including markets, police stations, and facilities allegedly used by armed groups.
Military authorities maintain that the operations are aimed at degrading RSF capabilities, including the disruption of supply lines such as fuel shipments and cross-border logistics networks.
Local coordination groups reported that the Adukong crossing has been struck multiple times in recent days. Additional drone strikes were also reported in nearby areas, including villages north and east of Geneina, with claims that civilian sites were affected.
The crossing serves as a critical route not only for commercial transport but also for humanitarian assistance entering Darfur. Its repeated targeting has raised concerns about the impact on aid delivery and civilian access to essential goods.
The broader situation reflects increasing regional dimensions of the conflict, with Sudanese authorities accusing neighboring Chad of facilitating logistical support routes used by armed groups-claims that have not been independently verified.
The escalation underscores growing risks for civilians and cross-border communities, as aerial operations intensify in contested regions of western Sudan.

title: Fire in Darfur Displacement Camp Kills Five, Leaves Over 1,400 Homeless
excerpt: Zalingi, April 15, 2026 - At least five people, including two children, were killed after a fire swept through a displacement camp in Central Darfur, highlighting worsening humanitarian conditions for civilians uprooted by ongoing conflict. The blaze broke out on Wednesday in a t
title_en: Fire in Darfur Displacement Camp Kills Five, Leaves Over 1,400 Homeless
excerpt_en: Zalingi, April 15, 2026 - At least five people, including two children, were killed after a fire swept through a displacement camp in Central Darfur, highlighting worsening humanitarian conditions for civilians uprooted by ongoing conflict. The blaze broke out on Wednesday in a t
body_en:
Zalingi, April 15, 2026 - At least five people, including two children, were killed after a fire swept through a displacement camp in Central Darfur, highlighting worsening humanitarian conditions for civilians uprooted by ongoing conflict.
The blaze broke out on Wednesday in a temporary settlement in Rokoro, located in the North Jebel Marra area. The camp shelters thousands of people displaced by fighting in North Darfur, particularly from the city of El Fasher.
Local sources reported that the fire spread rapidly through the overcrowded camp, fueled by shelters constructed from highly flammable materials. Dozens of makeshift homes were destroyed, leaving more than 1,400 people without shelter.
The incident is the latest in a series of fires affecting displacement camps across the Darfur region, where living conditions remain precarious. Overcrowding, limited infrastructure, and the absence of basic safety measures have increased the risk of such disasters.
Humanitarian conditions in Darfur continue to deteriorate amid ongoing violence and restricted access to aid. Large numbers of displaced people are living in makeshift camps with insufficient support, exposing them to both environmental hazards and the broader impacts of the conflict.
Relief efforts remain constrained, raising concerns about the ability to respond effectively to emergencies such as fires, disease outbreaks, and food shortages in the region.

title: U.S. Sanctions Network Accused of Recruiting Foreign Fighters for Sudan’s RSF
excerpt: Washington, April 17, 2026 - The United States has imposed sanctions on a network of individuals and companies accused of recruiting foreign fighters to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in a move aimed at disrupting external involvement in the country’s war. The U.S. T
title_en: U.S. Sanctions Network Accused of Recruiting Foreign Fighters for Sudan’s RSF
excerpt_en: Washington, April 17, 2026 - The United States has imposed sanctions on a network of individuals and companies accused of recruiting foreign fighters to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in a move aimed at disrupting external involvement in the country’s war. The U.S. T
body_en:
Washington, April 17, 2026 - The United States has imposed sanctions on a network of individuals and companies accused of recruiting foreign fighters to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), in a move aimed at disrupting external involvement in the country’s war.
The U.S. Treasury Department identified what it described as a structured recruitment system that has facilitated the deployment of hundreds of foreign combatants-primarily former Colombian soldiers-into Sudan since 2024. These fighters are believed to have taken part in major military operations, including battles in North Darfur.
Among those sanctioned is Jose Oscar Garcia Batte, a former army colonel accused of using a private firm to recruit specialized personnel such as snipers and drone operators. His brother, Omar Fernando Garcia Batte, was also designated for his alleged role in managing a parallel recruitment structure operating under different corporate identities.
Authorities further targeted several entities accused of acting as fronts for these activities, including firms involved in personnel recruitment and financial facilitation. One Panama-based company was identified as a key intermediary used to channel funds and obscure transactions linked to the network.
According to U.S. officials, some of the sanctioned entities had attempted to evade earlier restrictions by rebranding and creating new corporate structures.
The sanctions were issued under an executive order targeting actors accused of contributing to instability in Sudan and undermining peace efforts. U.S. authorities stated that the recruitment of foreign mercenaries has intensified the conflict and contributed to the suffering of civilians.
The measures form part of broader efforts to curb external support to armed groups in Sudan, where the involvement of foreign fighters and financial networks continues to complicate prospects for a resolution to the conflict.

body_en:
Blue Nile, Sudan, April 29, 2026 - The Sudanese army has announced the recapture of the town of Mogja in the Blue Nile region following heavy fighting with a coalition of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied rebel groups.
In a statement, the army’s 4th Infantry Division described the operation as a “significant victory,” saying its forces successfully liberated the town after intense clashes that forced opposing fighters into retreat. The military added that the withdrawing forces suffered heavy losses in both personnel and equipment.
According to the army command, the operation is part of a broader military campaign aimed at securing the Blue Nile region and eliminating remaining RSF elements from strategic locations.
The Sudanese government has also renewed accusations against neighboring Ethiopia, alleging that RSF-linked camps are being hosted on its territory with financial support from the United Arab Emirates. Both Ethiopia and the UAE have previously denied any involvement in Sudan’s ongoing conflict.

title: Over 550,000 Sudanese Refugees Flee to Libya Since Conflict Began, UN Says
excerpt: Tripoli, April 20, 2026 - More than 550,000 Sudanese refugees are estimated to have entered Libya since the outbreak of conflict in Sudan in April 2023, according to the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR). The agency reports that approximately 559,920 Sudanese nationals have c
title_en: Over 550,000 Sudanese Refugees Flee to Libya Since Conflict Began, UN Says
excerpt_en: Tripoli, April 20, 2026 - More than 550,000 Sudanese refugees are estimated to have entered Libya since the outbreak of conflict in Sudan in April 2023, according to the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR). The agency reports that approximately 559,920 Sudanese nationals have c
body_en:
Tripoli, April 20, 2026 - More than 550,000 Sudanese refugees are estimated to have entered Libya since the outbreak of conflict in Sudan in April 2023, according to the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR).
The agency reports that approximately 559,920 Sudanese nationals have crossed into Libya. Of these, 74,934 were registered after the start of the war, bringing the total number of Sudanese registered at the UNHCR centre in Tripoli to 91,494.
UNHCR said tightened border surveillance by Libyan authorities has pushed many refugees to take longer and more dangerous routes, with daily arrivals via Chad now averaging around 70 people.
The agency also noted that accurately tracking arrivals remains difficult due to irregular migration patterns and Libya’s vast, porous borders with Sudan, Chad, and Egypt. Many refugees reportedly move quickly toward coastal cities after crossing the border.
Displaced Sudanese are facing significant challenges in accessing healthcare services, with many unable to obtain medical treatment due to lack of documentation and the high cost of care, often charged at foreigner rates.
The report further warned of worsening humanitarian conditions, including widespread psychological distress linked to instability and the constant threat of homelessness. It also highlighted ongoing maritime search-and-rescue operations, with 18 incidents recorded in March alone-10 in eastern Libya and 8 in the west.
Security operations in eastern Libya have intensified, increasing the risk of arbitrary detention and forced returns to Sudan. The UNHCR cautioned that women, children, and persons with disabilities are particularly vulnerable to exploitation, abuse, and gender-based violence.

title: Sudan Returns Risk Collapse Without Urgent Infrastructure Aid, IOM Warns
excerpt: Khartoum, April 21, 2026 - The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that the large-scale return of displaced Sudanese civilians risks becoming unsustainable unless urgent investment is made in rebuilding infrastructure and restoring livelihoods. In a briefing
title_en: Sudan Returns Risk Collapse Without Urgent Infrastructure Aid, IOM Warns
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 21, 2026 - The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that the large-scale return of displaced Sudanese civilians risks becoming unsustainable unless urgent investment is made in rebuilding infrastructure and restoring livelihoods. In a briefing
body_en:
Khartoum, April 21, 2026 - The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that the large-scale return of displaced Sudanese civilians risks becoming unsustainable unless urgent investment is made in rebuilding infrastructure and restoring livelihoods.
In a briefing on Tuesday, the UN agency said that nearly 4 million people have returned to their homes out of an estimated 11.5 million who fled since the conflict began three years ago. It noted that the return movement has been driven largely by the Sudanese army’s regained control of key areas, including Sennar, Al Jazirah, and Khartoum states.
The IOM cautioned that while many returnees are motivated by hopes of rebuilding their lives, these efforts could fail without rapid rehabilitation of essential services such as water, electricity, and healthcare, as well as broader economic recovery measures.
Returns have been concentrated in Khartoum and Al Jazirah, driven by relative improvements in security, economic pressures, and family reunification. However, the agency warned that both regions are under severe strain.
In Khartoum, the influx of returnees is placing additional pressure on already devastated urban infrastructure. Water systems, electricity grids, and health facilities have been heavily damaged by the conflict, limiting access to basic services.
In Al Jazirah, the destruction of agricultural equipment and irrigation systems is threatening food production at a critical stage of recovery, raising concerns over food security for both returnees and host communities.
According to IOM data, approximately 1.8 million people have returned to Khartoum and 1.1 million to Al Jazirah. The agency said these shifting population movements are also increasing pressure on eastern and northern states, which continue to serve as major hubs for displaced populations despite their own economic and climate-related challenges.
The report further highlighted growing strain on health systems and water infrastructure in host communities, warning of rising social and economic tensions.
IOM Deputy Director General for Management and Reform SungAh Lee, who recently visited Sudan, said that returning home should represent the start of recovery, but for many it has instead meant confronting destroyed services and renewed uncertainty.
She stressed the need for access to safe housing and sustainable livelihoods, warning that without such support, ensuring safe and dignified returns will become increasingly difficult.
The IOM said it is working with partners to support Sudan’s transition from emergency response to longer-term stability and peace, emphasizing that coordinated regional efforts are essential to track and manage the country’s evolving displacement and return dynamics.

title: Sudan Army Resumes Heavy Air Strikes in South Kordofan
excerpt: Dilling, April 22, 2026 - Sudanese military aircraft carried out heavy air strikes on Wednesday targeting positions of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) around the city of Dilling in South Kordofan, marking the return of fixed-wing air operations to the region after several months o
title_en: Sudan Army Resumes Heavy Air Strikes in South Kordofan
excerpt_en: Dilling, April 22, 2026 - Sudanese military aircraft carried out heavy air strikes on Wednesday targeting positions of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) around the city of Dilling in South Kordofan, marking the return of fixed-wing air operations to the region after several months o
body_en:
Dilling, April 22, 2026 - Sudanese military aircraft carried out heavy air strikes on Wednesday targeting positions of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) around the city of Dilling in South Kordofan, marking the return of fixed-wing air operations to the region after several months of suspension.
Eyewitnesses reported seeing MiG fighter jets flying over Dilling and its outskirts for the first time in months, with strikes hitting areas including Al-Dulaymah, Al-Hujayrat, and Birno. The army said the bombardments were directed at RSF positions and allied forces.
Military operations in Kordofan and Darfur had previously been scaled back after the RSF reportedly succeeded in downing several aircraft, including fighters and cargo planes, the last of which was lost near Babanusa in West Kordofan. Following those losses, the army had increasingly relied on drone warfare.
Unmanned aerial strikes have since been used extensively against RSF positions and those of its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), in and around Dilling as well as nearby towns such as Abu Zabad, Al-Fula, Al-Mujlad, and Lagawa, causing what military sources describe as significant casualties.
Dilling, the second-largest city in South Kordofan, remains a contested strategic hub and has repeatedly come under aerial and artillery fire from the RSF-SPLM-N alliance, which also conducts periodic ground assaults aimed at seizing control of the area.
Earlier this year, on February 10, the Sudanese army announced it had destroyed a K-2000 air defense system in Al-Dubeibat in South Kordofan and neutralized drones at Nyala Airport, operations it said were part of a broader strategy to degrade RSF defensive and offensive capabilities.

title: Sudanese Army Hits RSF Positions in Coordinated Multi-State Operations
excerpt: Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - The Sudanese army carried out coordinated air and ground operations targeting positions held by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) across six states on Thursday, striking weapon depots, ammunition stockpiles, and drone launch sites, according to military st
title_en: Sudanese Army Hits RSF Positions in Coordinated Multi-State Operations
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - The Sudanese army carried out coordinated air and ground operations targeting positions held by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) across six states on Thursday, striking weapon depots, ammunition stockpiles, and drone launch sites, according to military st
body_en:
Khartoum, April 23, 2026 - The Sudanese army carried out coordinated air and ground operations targeting positions held by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) across six states on Thursday, striking weapon depots, ammunition stockpiles, and drone launch sites, according to military statements.
The army said it has expanded its use of drone warfare in recent months, particularly in the Darfur and Kordofan regions, where it claims repeated strikes have inflicted significant losses on RSF personnel and equipment.
Military leadership described the latest operations as part of a broader strategy aimed at dismantling RSF air defenses, logistics networks, storage facilities, and airstrips, with the objective of weakening its overall combat capacity.
In parallel, groups aligned with the RSF accused the army of hitting densely populated civilian areas in parts of Kordofan and Darfur, alleging that the strikes have resulted in civilian casualties. These claims could not be independently verified.
A spokesperson for the armed forces stated that the military achieved what it called “decisive strikes” against RSF forces across multiple fronts over a 72-hour period. The army also announced the capture of the Muqaja area in the Blue Nile region, reporting the destruction of several combat vehicles and the killing or capture of dozens of RSF fighters.
In West Kordofan, the army said it intercepted an RSF mobilization involving tanks and armored vehicles in the Al-Sunut area, destroying a large number of military assets. Additional operations in North Kordofan reportedly resulted in the destruction of further combat vehicles.
The military further stated that strikes in South Darfur targeted RSF outposts, drone platforms, and fuel depots in an effort to disrupt operational logistics. Similar attacks in Central and North Darfur reportedly destroyed additional combat vehicles and caused further casualties.
According to the army, the operations reflect ongoing efforts to regain territorial control and restore national security amid continuing conflict.

title: Seven Killed in Drone Strikes on Sudan’s El Obeid
excerpt: El Obeid, April 25, 2026 - At least seven civilians were killed and several others injured on Saturday after drone strikes hit multiple areas in El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan State. Local medical sources reported that the attack also left 22 people wounded, with injurie
title_en: Seven Killed in Drone Strikes on Sudan’s El Obeid
excerpt_en: El Obeid, April 25, 2026 - At least seven civilians were killed and several others injured on Saturday after drone strikes hit multiple areas in El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan State. Local medical sources reported that the attack also left 22 people wounded, with injurie
body_en:
El Obeid, April 25, 2026 - At least seven civilians were killed and several others injured on Saturday after drone strikes hit multiple areas in El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan State.
Local medical sources reported that the attack also left 22 people wounded, with injuries ranging from moderate to critical. The strikes reportedly targeted residential neighbourhoods across the city.
El Obeid has increasingly become a strategic military hub for army operations in Darfur and Kordofan, and has frequently been subjected to drone attacks attributed to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which seek to disrupt military advances in southern and western Kordofan.
A medical advocacy network said the city was struck by what it described as “suicide drones,” alleging that the attacks deliberately targeted densely populated civilian areas rather than military installations. It condemned the strikes as a violation of international humanitarian law, citing the high number of civilian casualties.
The organization warned that the use of drones in residential zones reflects a growing disregard for civilian protection amid worsening humanitarian conditions and collapsing health services.
It also called on the international community and humanitarian organizations to pressure armed actors to halt repeated attacks on populated areas and ensure the protection of non-combatants.

Ed Damazin, April 25, 2026 - Fighting has escalated in Sudan’s Blue Nile region as the army and an alliance of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu continue to exchange heavy attacks amid conflicting claims of territorial control.
The RSF and its allied forces launched a major offensive in the southeastern part of the region last month, capturing the strategic town of Kurmuk along with several surrounding areas, according to local military reports.
In a statement, the army’s 4th Infantry Division in Ed Damazin said its forces, together with allied units, repelled an RSF-led assault on the Sali area. The army claimed it destroyed 36 combat vehicles, captured two others, and inflicted casualties on attacking forces.
However, RSF representatives said their allied troops had seized control of the strategic Al-Kaili area after intense clashes with government forces. They described the development as a significant shift in the balance of power in the region and part of a broader effort to weaken military control.
Pro-RSF channels circulated video footage appearing to show fighters inside a military installation in Blue Nile State, though the authenticity of the material could not be independently verified.
The renewed fighting, combined with increased drone activity in the western and southern parts of the region, has worsened an already fragile humanitarian situation. Aid monitors report that thousands of civilians have been displaced, with many fleeing toward the regional capital, Ed Damazin, in search of safety and basic services.

title: Sudan Authorities Resume Exhumation of War Victims in South Khartoum
excerpt: Khartoum, April 26, 2026 - Authorities in Khartoum locality have resumed the exhumation and transfer of human remains from informal burial sites in southern parts of the capital, following legal procedures and notification of victims’ families. The local administration said opera
title_en: Sudan Authorities Resume Exhumation of War Victims in South Khartoum
excerpt_en: Khartoum, April 26, 2026 - Authorities in Khartoum locality have resumed the exhumation and transfer of human remains from informal burial sites in southern parts of the capital, following legal procedures and notification of victims’ families. The local administration said opera
body_en:
Khartoum, April 26, 2026 - Authorities in Khartoum locality have resumed the exhumation and transfer of human remains from informal burial sites in southern parts of the capital, following legal procedures and notification of victims’ families.
The local administration said operations restarted on Sunday in coordination with forensic experts, focusing on areas including the Land Port and Jabra district, where large numbers of wartime burials were previously conducted in residential and public spaces.
Officials stated that more than 15,000 bodies have been transferred from homes, streets, and public squares across Khartoum since April 2025. The Forensic Medicine Authority aims to complete the relocation of all remains buried outside official cemeteries by mid-year.
In the latest phase of operations, 93 sets of remains were reportedly moved to designated cemeteries, including 87 recovered from Jabra Block 18 and six from the Land Port bus terminal area.
Authorities explained that the ongoing process involves relocating bodies from makeshift graves used by civilians during the height of the conflict, when access to burial services was severely disrupted and movement across the city was highly dangerous.
The exhumations are being carried out under directives from a higher committee overseeing the return of displaced persons to Khartoum, which is now operating under the Council of Ministers and coordinating broader recovery efforts, including the restoration of basic services such as water, electricity, health, and education.
Officials said all procedures are being conducted in accordance with legal requirements, including documentation of cases and notification of relatives. Unidentified remains are being reburied in official cemeteries.
The operation is expected to continue across multiple administrative areas until all identified sites are cleared before the onset of the rainy season, based on surveys conducted by specialized teams and local community committees.
Authorities added that priority is being given to densely populated areas, including residential neighborhoods, schools, markets, mosques, and public squares.
During the conflict in Khartoum, many residents were forced to bury relatives in improvised graves due to the collapse of funeral services and the dangers posed by ongoing shelling and street fighting.
