title: Sudan Army Accused of Drone Strike on Zalingei Displaced Camp
excerpt: Zalingei, April 27, 2026 - A Sudanese displacement advocacy group has accused the army of carrying out a drone strike on a crowded camp for displaced persons in Zalingei, Central Darfur, injuring at least 15 civilians. The General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees in
title_en: Sudan Army Accused of Drone Strike on Zalingei Displaced Camp
excerpt_en: Zalingei, April 27, 2026 - A Sudanese displacement advocacy group has accused the army of carrying out a drone strike on a crowded camp for displaced persons in Zalingei, Central Darfur, injuring at least 15 civilians. The General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees in
body_en:
Zalingei, April 27, 2026 - A Sudanese displacement advocacy group has accused the army of carrying out a drone strike on a crowded camp for displaced persons in Zalingei, Central Darfur, injuring at least 15 civilians.
The General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees in Darfur said the strike targeted Square 4 of the Hamidiya camp on Monday morning, with the injured taken to Zalingei Hospital for treatment. The group reported that several shelters were destroyed, triggering panic among residents, particularly women and children.
The incident comes amid a reported increase in drone operations across Darfur, where the Sudanese army has intensified aerial strikes in areas largely under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Groups aligned with the RSF have accused the military of targeting civilian locations, while the army maintains that its operations are directed at RSF positions, including weapons depots, fuel storage sites, and drone facilities.
The displacement coordination body described the attack as a serious violation of international humanitarian law, warning that continued strikes on civilian and humanitarian sites could have devastating consequences for vulnerable populations.
Humanitarian agencies have also raised concerns over the growing use of drones in the conflict. Recent incidents have included attacks on aid convoys and infrastructure, disrupting the delivery of essential assistance to displaced communities.
According to aid officials, millions of people remain internally displaced across Sudan, with hundreds of thousands more seeking refuge in neighboring areas. The targeting of camps and humanitarian operations has heightened fears over the safety of civilians and the sustainability of relief efforts.
The group called on international and regional organizations to take urgent steps to protect civilians, ensure safe access for humanitarian aid, and support independent investigations into alleged violations.

title: Fire Kills Four in Central Darfur Displacement Camp
excerpt: Golo, April 27, 2026 - At least four people, including children, were killed and 12 others injured on Monday after a large fire swept through a displacement camp in Sudan’s Central Darfur region. Local authorities in areas controlled by the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Abdul
title_en: Fire Kills Four in Central Darfur Displacement Camp
excerpt_en: Golo, April 27, 2026 - At least four people, including children, were killed and 12 others injured on Monday after a large fire swept through a displacement camp in Sudan’s Central Darfur region. Local authorities in areas controlled by the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Abdul
body_en:
Golo, April 27, 2026 - At least four people, including children, were killed and 12 others injured on Monday after a large fire swept through a displacement camp in Sudan’s Central Darfur region.
Local authorities in areas controlled by the Sudan Liberation Movement, led by Abdul Wahid al-Nur, confirmed the casualties, saying the blaze destroyed significant portions of the camp in Golo.
According to officials, the fire completely razed three blocks within the camp and partially damaged several nearby shelters, leaving many families without housing.
Authorities issued an urgent appeal to humanitarian organizations to provide emergency medical assistance and supplies for those injured in the incident.
The fire is the latest in a series of similar incidents affecting displacement camps across Darfur in recent months. Aid workers say such fires spread rapidly due to extreme heat, overcrowded conditions, and the widespread use of flammable materials in makeshift shelters.
The incident adds to the worsening humanitarian situation in the region, where large numbers of displaced people continue to live in precarious conditions with limited access to basic services and protection.

title: Sudanese Army Says It Repelled Rebel Attack in Blue Nile Region
excerpt: Ed Damazin, April 29, 2026 - The Sudanese army said Tuesday it repelled a renewed attack by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, in Sudan’s Blue Nile region. According to a statement from the army’s 4
title_en: Sudanese Army Says It Repelled Rebel Attack in Blue Nile Region
excerpt_en: Ed Damazin, April 29, 2026 - The Sudanese army said Tuesday it repelled a renewed attack by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, in Sudan’s Blue Nile region. According to a statement from the army’s 4
body_en:
Ed Damazin, April 29, 2026 - The Sudanese army said Tuesday it repelled a renewed attack by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, in Sudan’s Blue Nile region.
According to a statement from the army’s 4th Infantry Division, fighting erupted on the outskirts of the Sali area along the southern axis, where government forces, supported by allied units, pushed back the assault and inflicted heavy losses on the attacking forces.
The army said it seized 10 combat vehicles in usable condition and destroyed more than 15 others during the clashes.
Military operations in southeastern Sudan have intensified since March, following a large offensive by RSF and SPLM-N forces that led to the capture of the strategic border town of Kurmuk and nearby areas.
The renewed fighting has contributed to a rapid deterioration in humanitarian conditions across the region. Residents report increasingly frequent clashes and expanded use of drones, which have heightened insecurity in both rural and urban areas.
The escalation has also triggered new waves of displacement, with thousands of civilians fleeing toward the regional capital, Ed Damazin, where overcrowded shelters are struggling to absorb the growing number of displaced families.
Conclusion
The period between April 12 and 29, 2026, highlights a Sudan caught between intensified internal restructuring and a complex international diplomatic landscape. Domestically, the Sudanese military has undergone significant leadership changes aimed at consolidating command as the conflict enters its third year. Simultaneously, political alliances such as the Democratic Block are attempting to broaden their national representation to establish a viable path toward stability.
On the international stage, the crisis has become increasingly "internationalized," with major conferences in Berlin and Antalya seeking to mobilize humanitarian aid and build political momentum for de-escalation. While civilian groups have successfully adopted a joint peace roadmap, the exclusion of government authorities from key forums remains a point of contention that may challenge the effectiveness of these initiatives.
Economically, the country remains in a fragile state despite a slowing inflation rate and surging artisanal gold revenues. Massive industrial damage, a looming collapse of the strategic sugar sector, and a sharp depreciation of the national currency continue to erode the quality of life for the Sudanese population. These economic hardships are further exacerbated by a collapsing healthcare system, now struggling to contain simultaneous outbreaks of dengue fever and measles.
Ultimately, while the introduction of new UN sanctions and the defection of key paramilitary commanders signal shifting dynamics, a lasting resolution remains dependent on unifying fragmented international efforts and prioritizing national interests over external interference. The restoration of state institutions and the successful re-engagement with global financial entities like the World Bank will be critical prerequisites for any meaningful reconstruction and long-term peace.
By Jeff Buleli

title_en: Uganda Finance Ministry Inaugurates Public Investment Committee to Strengthen ReformsKampala April 17, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development has inaugurated the Public Investment Management Plus (PIMPLUS) Operations Technical Committee (OTC), in a move aimed at strengthening public investment management and advancing ongoing public finance reforms.
excerpt_en: The induction ceremony, held at Speke Resort Munyonyo, was presided over by the Ministry’s Director of Budget, Hannington Ashaba, who highlighted the committee’s strategic role in enhancing efficiency, coordination, and delivery of public investment projects. PIMPLUS is a flagshi
body_en:
The induction ceremony, held at Speke Resort Munyonyo, was presided over by the Ministry’s Director of Budget, Hannington Ashaba, who highlighted the committee’s strategic role in enhancing efficiency, coordination, and delivery of public investment projects.
PIMPLUS is a flagship initiative under Uganda’s Public Finance Management Reform Strategy (PFMRS), designed to improve the planning, execution, and oversight of public investments, as well as the management of public assets. The programme is closely aligned with the country’s Fourth National Development Plan (NDP IV) and its broader Tenfold Growth Strategy.
Strengthening Investment Governance
The newly constituted Technical Committee brings together 29 members from 17 government institutions, reflecting a multi-sectoral approach to investment coordination and oversight.
The OTC will serve as a central governance mechanism for the PIMPLUS programme, providing technical and operational support to ensure timely implementation of public investment projects across government entities.
Its core responsibilities include offering technical oversight, coordinating implementation efforts, and ensuring alignment between institutional investment plans and the Program Expenditure Framework (PEF).
Driving Efficiency and Accountability
Speaking at the event, Ashaba emphasized the importance of strengthening delivery systems across government.
“The establishment of this Technical Committee is critical to ensuring that public investments are well-prepared, properly coordinated, and effectively implemented in line with our national development priorities,” he said.
Officials say the initiative is expected to address longstanding challenges in project preparation and execution, while improving value for money in public spending.
Reform Agenda
The Ministry reaffirmed its commitment to deepening public financial management reforms aimed at enhancing transparency, accountability, and efficiency in the use of public resources.
The PIMPLUS initiative is seen as a key pillar in accelerating the delivery of priority development outcomes, particularly as Uganda advances implementation of its long-term economic transformation agenda.

title: Uganda Links Teenage Pregnancies to Rising Fistula Cases, Expands Maternal Health Response
excerpt: Kampala April 19, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Health has attributed the continued rise in obstetric fistula cases to high teenage pregnancy rates and delays in accessing emergency obstetric care, warning that most of the complications are preventable with timely medical intervent
title_en: Uganda Links Teenage Pregnancies to Rising Fistula Cases, Expands Maternal Health Response
excerpt_en: Kampala April 19, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Health has attributed the continued rise in obstetric fistula cases to high teenage pregnancy rates and delays in accessing emergency obstetric care, warning that most of the complications are preventable with timely medical intervent
body_en:
Kampala April 19, 2026 - Uganda’s Ministry of Health has attributed the continued rise in obstetric fistula cases to high teenage pregnancy rates and delays in accessing emergency obstetric care, warning that most of the complications are preventable with timely medical intervention.
Commissioner for Maternal and Child Health Richard Mugahi said one in four pregnant women in Uganda is a teenager, with some as young as 12 to 14 years old, a trend he linked directly to increased childbirth complications.
“These are young girls whose bodies are not yet ready to carry a pregnancy, and this leads to complications like fistula, death of the baby, or even the mother,” Mugahi said.
Obstetric fistula, a severe childbirth injury caused by prolonged or obstructed labour, remains a significant health challenge in underserved communities, often leaving survivors with long-term physical and social consequences.
Mugahi noted that limited access to sexual and reproductive health information is a key driver of early pregnancies, calling for stronger education and awareness programs targeting adolescents.
Beyond social factors, he also highlighted systemic gaps in the health system, particularly delays in referring mothers with complications from lower-level facilities to higher-level care centres. He warned that such delays often result in life-threatening conditions, including uterine rupture, fistula, or death.
In response, the government-working with the United Nations Population Fund and the Government of Iceland-is scaling up maternal health interventions in high-burden regions.
These include the construction of a Health Centre IV in Namayingo District, recruitment of additional health workers, improved medical equipment supply, and enhanced training for emergency obstetric care.
The programme also supports surgical repair for fistula survivors and provides reintegration support, including income-generating activities aimed at helping affected women rebuild their lives.
“Addressing both the social drivers and the health system gaps is critical if we are to eliminate fistula in Uganda,” Mugahi said.
The initiative was formalized during a signing ceremony in Kampala involving Iceland’s Head of Mission Hildigunnur Engilbertsdóttir and Kristine Blokhus.
The programme will focus on regions including Acholi, West Nile, Bukedi, Karamoja, and Busoga, targeting improvements in adolescent health education, reproductive health services, and response mechanisms for gender-based violence.
Engilbertsdóttir described obstetric fistula as both a public health and human rights issue, emphasizing that it reflects broader gaps in health system capacity.
“Fistula happens when a health system lacks the capacity to meet the full spectrum of reproductive health needs of women and girls. It is a human rights and gender equality issue,” she said.
Officials say the combined interventions are expected to strengthen maternal healthcare delivery, reduce preventable injuries, and improve outcomes for vulnerable women and girls across Uganda.

title: Museveni to Commission Major Cement Plant in Karamoja
excerpt: Moroto April 19, 2026 - President Yoweri Museveni is set to commission a new cement and clinker manufacturing plant in Karamoja, marking a significant milestone in Uganda’s industrialisation drive and regional economic transformation. The facility, developed by Yaobai Cement Ugan
title_en: Museveni to Commission Major Cement Plant in Karamoja
excerpt_en: Moroto April 19, 2026 - President Yoweri Museveni is set to commission a new cement and clinker manufacturing plant in Karamoja, marking a significant milestone in Uganda’s industrialisation drive and regional economic transformation. The facility, developed by Yaobai Cement Ugan
body_en:
Moroto April 19, 2026 - President Yoweri Museveni is set to commission a new cement and clinker manufacturing plant in Karamoja, marking a significant milestone in Uganda’s industrialisation drive and regional economic transformation.
The facility, developed by Yaobai Cement Uganda, is located in Moroto and represents an investment of more than US$300 million. Officials describe it as one of the largest industrial projects in northern Uganda, with the potential to reshape the country’s manufacturing landscape.
The commissioning ceremony is expected to draw a wide range of stakeholders, including government officials, private sector leaders, development partners, and cultural representatives from across the Karamoja sub-region and beyond.
Industrial Boost for Karamoja
The project is widely seen as a turning point for Karamoja, a region historically associated with insecurity and underdevelopment but now increasingly opening up to investment, infrastructure, and economic opportunities.
At its initial phase, the plant is producing more than 6,000 tonnes of clinker per day, significantly boosting Uganda’s domestic production capacity.
Officials estimate the facility will reduce the country’s reliance on imported clinker by more than 2.5 million tonnes annually, easing pressure on foreign exchange and strengthening local supply chains.
Impact on Construction and Local Economy
Industry stakeholders say increased domestic production is expected to stabilise cement supply and potentially lower prices over time, providing a boost to Uganda’s rapidly expanding construction sector.
Beyond industrial output, the project is already generating tangible benefits for local communities. Residents in and around Moroto are experiencing increased economic activity, improved household incomes, and expanded employment opportunities linked to the factory and its supporting infrastructure.
Symbol of Economic Transformation
The launch also highlights Karamoja’s evolving role in Uganda’s broader industrialisation agenda, as the region positions itself as a new frontier for investment and development.
Officials say the project reflects growing investor confidence in Uganda’s economic prospects and underscores government efforts to promote inclusive growth by extending industrial development to previously underserved regions.

title: Uganda Faces Rising Burns Crisis, Experts Urge Creation of National Specialist Hospital
excerpt: Kampala April 14, 2026 - Medical experts in Uganda are warning of a worsening burns crisis, citing rising numbers of cases and overstretched health facilities, and are calling for the establishment of a dedicated national burns hospital to improve survival rates and care outcomes
title_en: Uganda Faces Rising Burns Crisis, Experts Urge Creation of National Specialist Hospital
excerpt_en: Kampala April 14, 2026 - Medical experts in Uganda are warning of a worsening burns crisis, citing rising numbers of cases and overstretched health facilities, and are calling for the establishment of a dedicated national burns hospital to improve survival rates and care outcomes
body_en:
Kampala April 14, 2026 - Medical experts in Uganda are warning of a worsening burns crisis, citing rising numbers of cases and overstretched health facilities, and are calling for the establishment of a dedicated national burns hospital to improve survival rates and care outcomes.
Currently, Kiruddu National Referral Hospital remains the country’s only specialised burns treatment centre. Its 60-bed unit is under severe pressure, receiving more than ten new patients daily, with frequent surges during emergencies.
Health workers say the unit is increasingly overwhelmed, as critically injured patients require long-term and intensive treatment, often arriving faster than others can be discharged.
Dr. Rose Alenyo, a plastic and reconstructive surgeon heading the burns unit at Kiruddu, said most injuries are linked to preventable household accidents.
“These include open cooking fires, charcoal stoves, kerosene accidents, hot liquids, and unsafe electrical connections,” she said.
She noted that children under the age of 10 make up the majority of patients, largely due to exposure in home environments where cooking is often done at ground level. Women are also frequently affected because of their roles in household cooking activities.
Beyond the immediate trauma, survivors often suffer long-term consequences such as permanent disability, disfigurement, and psychological distress. Delays in treatment further increase the risk of infections and death.
Dr. Alenyo warned that the system is operating beyond capacity, with only about ten trained burns specialists available nationwide, a shortage she said is affecting the quality and speed of care.
“There is an urgent need to expand specialised care, train more personnel, and establish a dedicated national burns hospital to manage the increasing caseload,” she said.
Experts also highlighted prevention measures, including safer cooking practices, elevating cooking surfaces, proper storage of fuels, and improved electrical safety in homes. However, they stressed that prevention alone is not enough without stronger treatment capacity.
Medical professionals are now urging the government and development partners to invest in specialised infrastructure and training, warning that without urgent intervention, Uganda’s burns burden could continue to rise and result in avoidable loss of life.

title: Over 100 Suspects Arrested in Kampala Metropolitan Crime Crackdown
excerpt: Kampala , Uganda March 24, 2026 - Security forces in Uganda’s capital have arrested more than 100 suspects following a series of coordinated operations targeting criminal activity across the Kampala Metropolitan Area. The intelligence-led crackdown, carried out on Monday, March 2
title_en: Over 100 Suspects Arrested in Kampala Metropolitan Crime Crackdown
excerpt_en: Kampala , Uganda March 24, 2026 - Security forces in Uganda’s capital have arrested more than 100 suspects following a series of coordinated operations targeting criminal activity across the Kampala Metropolitan Area. The intelligence-led crackdown, carried out on Monday, March 2
body_en:
Kampala , Uganda March 24, 2026 - Security forces in Uganda’s capital have arrested more than 100 suspects following a series of coordinated operations targeting criminal activity across the Kampala Metropolitan Area.
The intelligence-led crackdown, carried out on Monday, March 23, involved joint efforts by the Kampala Metropolitan Police and other security agencies. The operations spanned multiple locations in Kampala and neighboring Wakiso District, focusing on areas flagged for rising crime and public disorder.
According to police, the initiative was launched in response to increasing complaints from residents over theft, drug-related offenses, and disturbances affecting community safety.
In Kira Division, officers conducted raids in Kito B Cell, Kito A Zone, and Kireku Main Zone, leading to the arrest of 34 suspects. In Entebbe Division, operations in Kawafu and Abaita Ababiri resulted in 46 arrests.
Additional operations in Kajjansi Town Council-covering KKB Zone, Ssanyi Village, Dewey Village, and Kawali Village-led to 17 suspects being taken into custody. Meanwhile, police in Jinja Road Division arrested seven individuals in Kilombe, with another seven apprehended in Namayumba by Kakiri Police.
Authorities said the crackdown primarily targeted criminal networks involved in burglary, phone snatching, substance abuse, and nighttime attacks on pedestrians. Officers also responded to reports of social disorder, including noise pollution and illegal gambling.
During the operations, security personnel recovered several items believed to be linked to criminal activity, including suspected narcotics.
All suspects remain in custody and are expected to face court proceedings.
Police have indicated that similar operations will continue as part of broader efforts to combat crime and restore order across Kampala and its surrounding areas.

title: Ugandan Lawyer Urges Rwanda to Maintain Security Measures Over FDLR Threat Concerns
excerpt: Kampala, 8 April 2026 - Ugandan lawyer and former East African Legislative Assembly member Fred Mukasa Mbidde has said that Rwanda should not lift its security measures until the FDLR is fully dismantled. Speaking in an interview with Radio 4 Uganda, Mbidde argued that the curren
title_en: Ugandan Lawyer Urges Rwanda to Maintain Security Measures Over FDLR Threat Concerns
excerpt_en: Kampala, 8 April 2026 - Ugandan lawyer and former East African Legislative Assembly member Fred Mukasa Mbidde has said that Rwanda should not lift its security measures until the FDLR is fully dismantled. Speaking in an interview with Radio 4 Uganda, Mbidde argued that the curren
body_en:
Kampala, 8 April 2026 - Ugandan lawyer and former East African Legislative Assembly member Fred Mukasa Mbidde has said that Rwanda should not lift its security measures until the FDLR is fully dismantled.
Speaking in an interview with Radio 4 Uganda, Mbidde argued that the current security arrangements remain necessary due to ongoing concerns about the armed group’s presence and influence in the region. He expressed skepticism about the ability and willingness of the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to fully implement commitments to disarm the group.
He stated that, in his view, the FDLR has established links within political and military structures in eastern Congo, making its complete dismantlement difficult to verify in practice. “I doubt the DRC government’s ability to dismantle the FDLR,” he said, adding that he would only support lifting security measures once verifiable proof of disarmament is provided.
Mbidde also cautioned against relying solely on formal agreements between states, stressing the need for concrete implementation rather than diplomatic assurances.
The FDLR, a militia formed by remnants of forces associated with Rwanda’s former regime after the 1994 genocide, remains a persistent security concern in the region. Its presence has been a longstanding point of tension between Rwanda and its neighbors.
The comments come amid ongoing regional debates over border security and the implementation of recent peace commitments aimed at stabilizing eastern Congo and improving relations between regional states.

Wakiso April 17, 2026 - Police in Wakiso District have arrested a boda boda rider following his alleged involvement in the defilement of an eight-year-old girl, an incident that was reportedly captured in a viral video circulating on social media.
The suspect, identified as Moses Ssebagala, was apprehended after being recognized in the footage, according to police.
Kampala Metropolitan Police spokesperson Racheal Kawala confirmed the arrest, stating that investigations are ongoing and the suspect will be presented before court.
“The suspect has been arrested and is currently in custody. He will be produced in court as investigations into the matter continue,” Kawala said.

Preliminary accounts indicate that the victim had been outside with her sister when the suspect allegedly approached them, gave them a mobile phone to watch cartoons, and later committed the offence.
Authorities have condemned the incident, describing it as a serious case of child abuse, and have urged parents and guardians to remain vigilant about the safety of children in their communities.
The case has sparked renewed concern over rising incidents of child abuse and exploitation, with law enforcement emphasizing continued efforts to track and prosecute offenders.

title: Mbarara Police Arrest Over 15 in Drug Crackdown in Kisenyi Suburb
excerpt: Mbarara April 17, 2026 - Police in Mbarara have arrested more than 15 suspects during a targeted operation against drug trafficking in Kisenyi suburb, an area authorities say has increasingly become a hub for criminal activity. The early morning raid followed intelligence reports
title_en: Mbarara Police Arrest Over 15 in Drug Crackdown in Kisenyi Suburb
excerpt_en: Mbarara April 17, 2026 - Police in Mbarara have arrested more than 15 suspects during a targeted operation against drug trafficking in Kisenyi suburb, an area authorities say has increasingly become a hub for criminal activity. The early morning raid followed intelligence reports
body_en:
Mbarara April 17, 2026 - Police in Mbarara have arrested more than 15 suspects during a targeted operation against drug trafficking in Kisenyi suburb, an area authorities say has increasingly become a hub for criminal activity.
The early morning raid followed intelligence reports identifying houses allegedly used as distribution points for narcotics. Security teams conducted coordinated searches, recovering cannabis and other illicit substances, along with drug-related paraphernalia. The suspects are currently being held at Mbarara Central Police Station pending further investigations.
The operation was led by Kenneth Kabwigo, who said the crackdown forms part of a wider strategy to address rising insecurity in the city.
“We are conducting these operations as a proactive measure to curb the insecurity in the city. The operation is specifically targeting areas raising concerns of attacks and where criminal elements congregate to plan their activities,” Kabwigo said.
Authorities say the raid comes amid growing concerns from residents over increased robberies and nighttime attacks in Mbarara. Local leaders have linked the rise in insecurity to drug abuse and the existence of drug dens, which they allege also function as coordination points for criminal gangs.
Kabwigo warned that the operation is part of a broader city-wide enforcement campaign aimed at dismantling illegal drug networks.
“We want to send a clear message to those engaged in illegal trade and terrorizing residents: Mbarara will not be a safe haven for you,” he said, urging the public to continue providing intelligence to security agencies.
Police say the suspects will be taken to court once investigations are complete, with charges expected to include possession of illegal substances and possible links to organized criminal activity.
Following the operation, security presence in Kisenyi has been reinforced, with increased patrols aimed at preventing the re-emergence of drug networks. Residents have welcomed the crackdown and called for sustained police presence to maintain improved safety in the area.

title: URA Customs Officer Exposes $10.2 Million Hidden in Cargo, Praised for Integrity
excerpt: Kampala April 16, 2026 - A Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) customs officer has been commended for uncovering $10.2 million (approximately Shs38 billion) in undeclared cash concealed within household items belonging to a passenger returning from Turkey. The discovery was made durin
title_en: URA Customs Officer Exposes $10.2 Million Hidden in Cargo, Praised for Integrity
excerpt_en: Kampala April 16, 2026 - A Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) customs officer has been commended for uncovering $10.2 million (approximately Shs38 billion) in undeclared cash concealed within household items belonging to a passenger returning from Turkey. The discovery was made durin
body_en:
Kampala April 16, 2026 - A Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) customs officer has been commended for uncovering $10.2 million (approximately Shs38 billion) in undeclared cash concealed within household items belonging to a passenger returning from Turkey.
The discovery was made during a routine cargo inspection, when the officer flagged a shipment that initially appeared to contain ordinary personal effects. Upon physical verification, she reportedly found bundles of foreign currency hidden inside sealed boxes.
The URA Commissioner General John Musinguzi Rujoki later publicly honoured the officer, praising her integrity and refusal to accept an alleged bribe offered in connection with the case.
According to URA, the customs officer-whose identity has been withheld for security reasons-encountered attempts to influence her decision shortly after the discovery, including offers of financial inducement.
“The moment I discovered the money, the clearing agent started convincing me not to escalate the matter, saying it was my time to get rich,” she was quoted as saying during an internal recognition ceremony.
URA officials said she resisted pressure and proceeded with enforcement procedures, leading to the seizure of the undeclared funds.
Musinguzi described her conduct as exemplary, saying it reflected the standards expected of enforcement officers in protecting public revenue and upholding institutional integrity.
“You have shown a high standard of accountability,” he said, adding that the action reinforced URA’s anti-smuggling and compliance mandate.
The interception occurred during inspection of a container belonging to a Ugandan traveler arriving from Turkey. Officials said the shipment contained multiple boxes that initially appeared to carry household goods, but further examination revealed concealed foreign currency.
URA emphasized that the case underscores the importance of physical cargo inspections alongside risk-based profiling systems used in customs clearance. These include red-channel physical inspections, documentary verification, and post-clearance audits.
The authority also reiterated its use of digital declarations and cargo scanning technologies aimed at strengthening transparency and reducing opportunities for smuggling or concealment of undeclared assets.
URA said the officer’s actions serve as an example to staff across the institution, reinforcing its mandate to safeguard national revenue through strict enforcement and professional conduct.

title: Crime Rate Drops by 10.2% in 2025, Police Report Shows
excerpt: Kampala , Uganda March 30, 2026 - The national crime rate declined by 10.2% in 2025, according to the latest annual police crime report, reflecting a broad reduction across multiple categories of offenses. The report indicates that total reported cases fell from 218,715 in 2024 t
title_en: Crime Rate Drops by 10.2% in 2025, Police Report Shows
excerpt_en: Kampala , Uganda March 30, 2026 - The national crime rate declined by 10.2% in 2025, according to the latest annual police crime report, reflecting a broad reduction across multiple categories of offenses. The report indicates that total reported cases fell from 218,715 in 2024 t
body_en:
Kampala , Uganda March 30, 2026 - The national crime rate declined by 10.2% in 2025, according to the latest annual police crime report, reflecting a broad reduction across multiple categories of offenses.
The report indicates that total reported cases fell from 218,715 in 2024 to 196,405 in 2025, signaling a significant improvement in overall public security.
Data from the report shows that assault cases dropped by 10.8%, decreasing from 29,580 in 2024 to 26,366 in 2025. Sexual offenses also registered a notable decline of 12.6%, falling from 14,425 to 12,606 cases. Similarly, domestic violence cases reduced by 12.2%, from 14,073 to 12,361.
Economic and corruption-related crimes recorded a 12.1% decrease, with reported cases falling from 13,132 to 11,548. Break-ins also declined, from 13,511 cases in 2024 to 11,818 in 2025, while incidents involving threats of violence showed a downward trend.
Police leadership attributed the overall decline to a combination of structural reforms and enhanced operational strategies within the force. Key measures included improvements in command and control systems, increased use of technology, and the expansion of community policing initiatives.
Authorities noted that the establishment of a clearer chain of command has streamlined decision-making processes, while stronger collaboration among security agencies has improved coordination and response capabilities.
The rollout of a sub-county policing model has also contributed to bringing services closer to communities, although officials indicated that implementation remains ongoing, with just over half of sub-counties currently covered.
In addition, investments in surveillance and investigative capacity-including expanded CCTV networks, canine units, forensic tools, and other technological resources-have strengthened law enforcement capabilities.
Police further credited sustained intelligence-led operations for enabling more proactive crime prevention and response.
Officials say the combined impact of these measures has played a central role in reducing crime levels, while efforts to expand coverage and reinforce systems are expected to continue.

title: Veteran Journalist Joe Nam Shot Dead in Kampala
excerpt: Kampala April 19, 2026 - A veteran Ugandan journalist, Joe Nam, has been shot dead in what police describe as a targeted attack in the early hours of Sunday morning. Nam, 55, a former features reporter with New Vision, was killed in Kawanda, Nabweru Division, in Wakiso District,
title_en: Veteran Journalist Joe Nam Shot Dead in Kampala
excerpt_en: Kampala April 19, 2026 - A veteran Ugandan journalist, Joe Nam, has been shot dead in what police describe as a targeted attack in the early hours of Sunday morning. Nam, 55, a former features reporter with New Vision, was killed in Kawanda, Nabweru Division, in Wakiso District,
body_en:
Kampala April 19, 2026 - A veteran Ugandan journalist, Joe Nam, has been shot dead in what police describe as a targeted attack in the early hours of Sunday morning.
Nam, 55, a former features reporter with New Vision, was killed in Kawanda, Nabweru Division, in Wakiso District, according to authorities.
Police said the incident occurred in the early morning hours when an unidentified armed assailant opened fire before fleeing the scene.
Luke Owoyesigyire, deputy spokesperson for the Greater Kampala Metropolitan Police, confirmed the killing and said investigations were underway.
“Preliminary information indicates that an unidentified armed assailant shot and killed him. The suspect, who was masked, fled the scene immediately after the incident,” Owoyesigyire said.
The motive for the attack remains unclear, and no arrests have been reported so far.
Nam was known for his work as a features journalist in the late 2000s, and his death has raised concerns among media professionals and observers about the safety of journalists in Uganda.
Police have urged anyone with information that could assist in the investigation to come forward as efforts continue to identify and apprehend the suspect.

title: Kira Road Police Admit Gaps in School Outreach, Shift Focus to Prevention
excerpt: Kampala April 19, 2026 - The Kira Road Police Division has acknowledged significant shortcomings in its school outreach programmes, revealing that several secondary schools within its jurisdiction have not been reached by community policing initiatives. Divisional Police Commande
title_en: Kira Road Police Admit Gaps in School Outreach, Shift Focus to Prevention
excerpt_en: Kampala April 19, 2026 - The Kira Road Police Division has acknowledged significant shortcomings in its school outreach programmes, revealing that several secondary schools within its jurisdiction have not been reached by community policing initiatives. Divisional Police Commande
body_en:
Kampala April 19, 2026 - The Kira Road Police Division has acknowledged significant shortcomings in its school outreach programmes, revealing that several secondary schools within its jurisdiction have not been reached by community policing initiatives.
Divisional Police Commander Suubi Sam said the findings have prompted a comprehensive review to assess the real impact of police engagement in schools, with a shift toward measurable outcomes such as crime reduction, improved reporting, and legal awareness among students.
“We have been active, yes-but we must ask ourselves: are we effective?” Suubi said, noting that the review will move beyond routine activity reports to focus on tangible results.
The reassessment comes as schools in densely populated suburbs such as Kamwokya and Kyebando face increasing urban challenges. Many institutions are located near areas associated with drug activity, betting centres, and higher crime rates, exposing students to risks including gang recruitment and substance abuse.
“This is not just about discipline; it’s about survival in these environments,” Suubi warned.
In response, the division is adopting a prevention-focused approach, introducing a mentorship-based policing model aimed at building trust and guiding students before issues escalate.
“A police officer should not only be seen when there is a problem,” he said. “We want to build relationships, guide students, and prevent crime before it happens.”
Authorities also plan to evaluate whether students feel confident reporting crimes, amid concerns that many incidents go unreported due to lack of trust.
“If students cannot trust us, then our presence in schools means very little,” Suubi added.
Anatoli Muleterwa, Commissioner for Community Policing, reinforced the emphasis on prevention, urging students to take responsibility for their choices.
“Success is built on discipline, hard work, and purpose,” Muleterwa said, cautioning against negative peer influence and warning of the consequences of criminal behavior.
“Crime does not bring pride; it brings fear, embarrassment, and isolation,” he added, noting that legal accountability applies to individuals from the age of 12.
Police are also encouraging greater community involvement, calling on students, parents, local leaders, and informal actors such as boda boda riders to play a role in maintaining security.
“Security is not just a police responsibility; it is a community responsibility,” Suubi emphasized.
As reforms take shape, the Kira Road Police Division says its priority is to transform schools into safer environments through prevention, accountability, and stronger community engagement.

“We have been active, yes-but we must ask ourselves: are we effective?” Suubi said, noting that the review will move beyond routine activity reports to focus on tangible results.
The reassessment comes as schools in densely populated suburbs such as Kamwokya and Kyebando face increasing urban challenges. Many institutions are located near areas associated with drug activity, betting centres, and higher crime rates, exposing students to risks including gang recruitment and substance abuse.
“This is not just about discipline; it’s about survival in these environments,” Suubi warned.

“A police officer should not only be seen when there is a problem,” he said. “We want to build relationships, guide students, and prevent crime before it happens.”

“Crime does not bring pride; it brings fear, embarrassment, and isolation,” he added, noting that legal accountability applies to individuals from the age of 12.
Police are also encouraging greater community involvement, calling on students, parents, local leaders, and informal actors such as boda boda riders to play a role in maintaining security.
“Security is not just a police responsibility; it is a community responsibility,” Suubi emphasized.

title: Fear Grips Kawempe as Wave of Night Attacks Spreads in Corner Zone
excerpt: Kampala April 19, 2026 - Residents of Nkere Village and Corner Zone in Kazo Angola Parish, Kawempe Division, are living in fear following a surge in violent attacks attributed to suspected local criminal groups, with some households considering abandoning their homes. The communi
title_en: Fear Grips Kawempe as Wave of Night Attacks Spreads in Corner Zone
excerpt_en: Kampala April 19, 2026 - Residents of Nkere Village and Corner Zone in Kazo Angola Parish, Kawempe Division, are living in fear following a surge in violent attacks attributed to suspected local criminal groups, with some households considering abandoning their homes. The communi
body_en:
Kampala April 19, 2026 - Residents of Nkere Village and Corner Zone in Kazo Angola Parish, Kawempe Division, are living in fear following a surge in violent attacks attributed to suspected local criminal groups, with some households considering abandoning their homes.
The community says insecurity has escalated to both daytime and nighttime assaults, leaving residents injured, traumatized, and increasingly unable to carry out daily activities.
“We no longer sleep. These criminals attack us at any time,” one resident said, describing repeated assaults and thefts.
According to residents, many of the suspected attackers are young people from within the same community, a development they say has made prevention and control more difficult. “These are our own children, but they have turned against us,” another resident said.
Locals have also pointed to what they describe as a breakdown in local leadership. They claim that the LC1 chairperson, Mathias Mulumba, relocated to Matuga, while his deputy also left the area, leaving administrative structures largely inactive.
“The LC1 office is always closed, and we have nowhere to report our issues,” one resident said.
Corner Zone, a densely populated area where many residents rely on vending, market trade, and small businesses, is said to have become increasingly vulnerable amid the leadership vacuum.
Residents further allege that the situation worsened following the arrest of a local defense official, Gerald Sande, who had previously coordinated night patrols in the area. “Since he was arrested, the criminals have returned and are now more aggressive,” a resident said.
Sande was detained in connection with allegations surrounding the death of a suspected criminal, identified as Yudah Kavuma, who was reportedly killed by a mob.
Several victims have shared accounts of violent attacks, including physical assaults and robberies. Vicent Mayengo, a trader at Nakasero Market, said he was severely beaten during one incident and continues to live with injuries.
“They attacked me and beat me badly. I still have scars on my body,” he said.
Residents also accuse a group of suspected gang members, locally identified as Musege, Dog D, and Owetanzaniya, of orchestrating a series of attacks, including an assault on a school security guard who was reportedly injured and robbed.
Despite the worsening insecurity, some residents have controversially called for the release of Sande, arguing that his presence previously helped stabilize the area.
“If it is possible, they should release him. We need security more than anything right now,” one resident said.
However, LC1 chairperson Mathias Mulumba dismissed claims that his relocation contributed to the security crisis, urging residents to follow proper administrative procedures.
“My leaving the area does not mean people should take the law into their own hands,” he said. “They should elect a new chairperson, and I am no longer responsible for the village.”
As fear continues to spread, residents are calling on security agencies to intervene urgently, warning that continued inaction could force further displacement from the area.

title: IGP Byakagaba Transfers 433 Police Officers in Major Nationwide Reshuffle
excerpt: Kampala April 17, 2026 - The Inspector General of Police, Abas Byakagaba, has announced a major reshuffle involving 433 officers across the Uganda Police Force, with immediate effect. The transfers affect multiple directorates and units, including Welfare, Production and Sports;
title_en: IGP Byakagaba Transfers 433 Police Officers in Major Nationwide Reshuffle
excerpt_en: Kampala April 17, 2026 - The Inspector General of Police, Abas Byakagaba, has announced a major reshuffle involving 433 officers across the Uganda Police Force, with immediate effect. The transfers affect multiple directorates and units, including Welfare, Production and Sports;
body_en:
Kampala April 17, 2026 - The Inspector General of Police, Abas Byakagaba, has announced a major reshuffle involving 433 officers across the Uganda Police Force, with immediate effect.
The transfers affect multiple directorates and units, including Welfare, Production and Sports; Human Resources Administration; the Chief Political Commissariat; Human Resource Development; Fire and Rescue Services; the Professional Standards Unit; Traffic Police; and the Criminal Investigations Directorate (CID).
Senior officers have been reassigned to strategic positions, including postings to the Inspector General’s office, Interpol, legal services, finance, and specialized operational units.
Among the key appointments, Senior Commissioner of Police Geoffrey Chombe has been posted to the Inspector General’s office, while Commissioner Alison Agaba has been assigned to Interpol. Commissioner John William Okalany has been deployed to the Human Rights and Legal Services Directorate, and Commissioner Richard Arumadri has been transferred to the Finance Department.
Assistant Commissioner of Police Richard Mugwisagye has been named Deputy Commander of the Professional Standards Unit.
The reshuffle also includes officers recently trained at the Oliver Reginald Tambo Leadership School in Kaweweta, with several receiving new postings across regions. Former Kampala Central Police Station operations commander, Assistant Superintendent of Police Ivan Nduhura, has been deployed to West Nile as Police Legal Officer.
Other notable changes include Commissioner Enock Baine, now heading the Police Duty Free Scheme and Supermarkets, and Assistant Commissioner Grace Ewiku, appointed Head of Crop Production in the Agriculture Police.
In specialized units, Senior Superintendent Bashir Siriba has been appointed Coordinator of the National Drowning Prevention Program within the Marine Unit, while Senior Superintendent Ahmed Kimera Seguya has been moved to the Railways Unit as Head of Operations.
Regional commands have also been significantly affected. Senior Superintendent Diana Nyamisango has been appointed Regional Police Commander for Katonga Region, while other officers have been reassigned across Kigezi, Busoga East, Kidepo, and other regional formations.
In the Traffic Directorate, multiple senior officers have been redeployed, including new appointments in vehicle inspection and transport monitoring sections.
The reshuffle also includes officers in the CID, where 132 personnel have been moved. Assistant Commissioner Moses Taremwa has been appointed Acting Commissioner of the Trafficking in Persons Department, while Assistant Commissioner Peter Muwonge has been reassigned to inspection duties at CID headquarters in Kibuli. Assistant Commissioner Charles Mutungi has been posted to the Uganda Anti-Money Laundering Task Force.
Authorities say the changes are part of ongoing efforts to strengthen efficiency, accountability, and operational effectiveness within the police force, following leadership training and institutional reviews.

title: Security Intensifies Crackdown on Illegal Mining in Kassanda
excerpt: Kassanda April 12, 2026 - Security agencies in Uganda’s Wamala Region have intensified operations against illegal mining activities in Kassanda District following a directive from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development ordering the suspension of operations under Explorati
title_en: Security Intensifies Crackdown on Illegal Mining in Kassanda
excerpt_en: Kassanda April 12, 2026 - Security agencies in Uganda’s Wamala Region have intensified operations against illegal mining activities in Kassanda District following a directive from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development ordering the suspension of operations under Explorati
body_en:
Kassanda April 12, 2026 - Security agencies in Uganda’s Wamala Region have intensified operations against illegal mining activities in Kassanda District following a directive from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development ordering the suspension of operations under Exploration Licence No. 00459.
The enforcement exercise, code-named Operation Safisha, is being jointly conducted by the Police Mineral Protection Unit and the Wamala Regional Police Command to restore order and ensure compliance with mining regulations.
According to regional police spokesperson Lameck Kigozi, the licence in question had been issued to Mugobwa Katugo Small Scale Miners strictly for exploration within a 0.34 square kilometre area in Bubali, Kitumbi Sub-county. However, authorities allege that the operators exceeded the scope of the permit by engaging in full-scale extraction without the required mining licence.
“This was purely an exploration licence. The law requires that after exploration, findings must be submitted to the Ministry before an extraction licence is granted. Unfortunately, this procedure was ignored, and illegal extraction commenced,” Kigozi said.
Following this breach, the Ministry ordered an immediate suspension of all activities, prompting the launch of the enforcement operation aimed at demobilising miners and clearing the site. Authorities say operators were initially given a two-week ultimatum to vacate the area and remove equipment, but several failed to comply.
“Despite the grace period given, some operators remained defiant. That is why security forces have now moved in to fully enforce the directive,” Kigozi added.
The crackdown involves multiple security units, including the Field Force Unit, the Criminal Investigations Directorate (CID), and Crime Intelligence teams, tasked with monitoring and investigating any related criminal activity.
Authorities have also warned both local and foreign nationals involved in the mining activities-including individuals from neighbouring countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania, Kenya, and South Sudan-to vacate the area peacefully.
Kigozi cautioned against illegal scavenging in abandoned mining pits, locally known as “okwekyokola,” describing it as both unlawful and dangerous, with several fatalities already reported.
“This kind of activity has already claimed lives due to poor safety practices. Security will remain on the ground to ensure no one returns to the pits. These areas will be backfilled to prevent further incidents,” he said.
He urged aggrieved parties to pursue legal remedies through the Ministry rather than resisting enforcement.
“If you feel dissatisfied, the law provides avenues for appeal. You can formally engage the Ministry and apply for an extraction licence through the right procedures,” he added.
Authorities say the operation marks a decisive step toward regulating the mining sector in Kassanda, improving safety standards, and ensuring compliance with Uganda’s legal framework for mineral exploitation.

title: Three Killed, One Injured in Night Attack in Adjumani as Police Launch Investigation
excerpt: Adjumani April 11, 2026 - Police in Adjumani District are investigating a deadly overnight attack that left three people dead and one seriously injured in Ukusijoni Sub-county, as security forces intensify efforts to track down the assailants and calm rising tensions in the area.
title_en: Three Killed, One Injured in Night Attack in Adjumani as Police Launch Investigation
excerpt_en: Adjumani April 11, 2026 - Police in Adjumani District are investigating a deadly overnight attack that left three people dead and one seriously injured in Ukusijoni Sub-county, as security forces intensify efforts to track down the assailants and calm rising tensions in the area.
body_en:
Adjumani April 11, 2026 - Police in Adjumani District are investigating a deadly overnight attack that left three people dead and one seriously injured in Ukusijoni Sub-county, as security forces intensify efforts to track down the assailants and calm rising tensions in the area.
According to a police incident report registered at Adjumani Central Police Station under CRB 191/2026, the attack occurred at around 2:30 a.m. on April 10, 2026, in Ofua East, Rubangabini Village.
The victims have been identified as Annah Abiria (48) and Susan Unzia (56), both residents of Acimari East in Ewafa, Obongi District, and Karulino Mamawi (64) from Onyire Afoji in Moyo District. Police said one of the bodies had not yet been recovered from nearby bushland at the time of reporting.
A fourth victim, Pastore Moroga (50), a farmer from Iyiri Village in Ukusijoni Sub-county, survived the attack but sustained injuries and is receiving treatment at Adjumani General Hospital.
North West Nile regional police spokesperson SP Collins Asea confirmed the incident, saying preliminary investigations point to an armed group that attacked residents using bows, arrows, and machetes before fleeing through the Zoka Forest.
“We strongly condemn this act of violence. Our teams responded promptly, but the suspects had already fled the scene. However, five individuals armed with bows and arrows have been apprehended to assist with ongoing investigations,” Asea said.
He added that joint security forces, including the army, assisted in rescuing the injured victim and have launched a manhunt for other suspects believed to be at large.
Police and local investigators have visited the scene, while the bodies of the deceased have been taken to Adjumani General Hospital for postmortem examinations. A search operation is ongoing to recover the missing body despite difficult terrain conditions.
Authorities have urged residents to remain calm and avoid retaliatory actions, calling instead for peaceful coexistence and cooperation with ongoing investigations.
“We urge both communities to remain calm and avoid retaliatory actions. Matters of this nature must be handled through lawful means as investigations continue,” Asea added.
